full_text:
Falcons quarterback Michael Penix Jr., the reigning NFC Offensive Player of the Week, has impressed when healthy this season. Kevin C. Cox / Getty Images
We’re going to start today’s Atlanta Falcons mailbag with the No. 1 question looming over this team: Is Michael Penix Jr. a franchise quarterback?
Safety Jessie Bates III started the conversation on Monday when he said, simply, “Yes.”
How Falcons president of football Matt Ryan, general manager Ian Cunningham and head coach Kevin Stefanski answer that question is the most important factor looking ahead, but none of the three is ready to answer yet. Neither Ryan nor Cunningham has spoken to the media since the preseason, and Stefanski, offensive coordinator Tommy Rees and even Penix himself essentially said this week that it’s not the time for the conversation.
“I just want to win football games,” Penix said when told of Bates’ comments. “All that stuff comes. When you’re winning, that’s when the good things happen.”
Penix is 11th in the NFL in expected points added per dropback (0.13), seventh in yards per attempt (7.0) and 10th in completion percentage (66.7) headed into Sunday’s matchup with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers (2-5), a game that could vault Atlanta (3-4) into the NFC South lead. He was named the NFC’s Offensive Player of the Week for the first time in his career on Wednesday following his terrific performance (25-for-34 passing for 213 yards, three touchdowns and no interceptions) in a win over the previously unbeaten San Francisco 49ers.
“You can’t do that by yourself,” Penix said. “It shows the guys I have around me, the guys we have in this building. They make my job easier, but it’s an awesome award, and I’m thankful for it.”
Penix will tie his streak of longest consecutive starts (six) when Sunday’s game kicks off, and his health is obviously a huge part of the equation.
“It’s been really rewarding as a coach to see him have success, and the enjoyment that he has playing this game and preparing right now,” Rees said. “The awards are great, and the recognition is great, but he’s got bigger things on his mind.”
Penix is not even thinking about a day off, much less anything beyond that, he said. He is playing on the third year of his rookie contract, and the Falcons have not yet exercised the fifth-year option on that deal.
“I know a lot of people are like, ‘You have to take time for yourself,’ and you do, but at the same time you’ve got something in you that is like, ‘I want to win so bad,’ that you want to put that work in,” Penix said. “I’m grinding right now. We’re locked in.”
Sunday will be Penix’s first professional game in his hometown.
“I imagine I should have a lot of people coming to the game,” he said. “My mom usually knows that head count. Can’t wait to get there. Hopefully, we’ll come out with a win.”
At what point do they trim to three quarterbacks instead of carrying a fourth? Surely, they will need that roster space for extra bodies as injuries occur. Unless Tua Tagovailoa or Andy Dalton can play special teams, maybe it’s time to cut bait on one of them or Jack Strand. (When they do, watch Penix get hurt in the next game.) — Stu A.
I do think that becomes an interesting question after the addition of Dalton, but my best guess at the moment is that they keep four throughout the season. Dalton is expected to compete with Tagovailoa for the backup job, but it’s unclear who holds the job at the moment.
I expect that Dalton will eventually, which would make Tagovailoa expendable because his health will always be a question and his preseason play wasn’t inspiring.
However, Rees said something this week that was interesting. Unsolicited, Rees praised Tagovailoa for his support of Penix and everyone in the quarterback room and said Tagovailoa’s laid-back approach has been beneficial for Penix.
I have noticed over the last few weeks that Penix seems more comfortable and relaxed in media settings. He has always been a pleasant guy — but pretty reserved. As he has played better, he jokes more and seems more comfortable in his own skin.
That might be valuable enough that Rees doesn’t want to do anything to upset the vibe this year. The entire premise of this question rests on how valuable the quarterback position is in the NFL. You have to have a guy playing well at that position to have any chance of winning. That’s why the mere possibility that Strand might be good makes him valuable enough to keep on the roster.
If it comes down to it, it makes more sense to keep Strand than Tagovailoa because of age, health and potential.
Will we draft a quarterback or an offensive lineman in the first round in 2027, assuming we exercise Penix’s fifth year and he makes it through the season healthy? — Seaborn H.
Will this be Jake Matthews’ last year? — Stephen S.
This question hits on a topic I’ve been going on and on about for years: drafting a tackle.
There are so many benefits that would come if Penix turns out to be the answer at quarterback, and I think being able to use next year’s first-rounder on a tackle is at the top of the list. I don’t think this will be Matthews’ last season, but it is (past?) time to address the future of the position.
Free-agent addition Jawaan Taylor has played better than I expected, and he’s only 28. But he’s on a one-year, $5 million contract, and there’s no guarantee he’ll be back next year.
Matthews is 34 and in his 13th season, and he has looked his age at times this season. The advanced statistics paint a pretty clear picture of where Matthews is. He has given up a lot of quick pressures but fares much better in pure pressure rate allowed, which means when he gets his hands on pass rushers, he’s doing well — but he’s not getting his hands on as many as he gets older.
I think the Falcons would certainly be open to trading Strand or Tagovailoa if either had any trade value, but I don’t think they do. Strand’s development is hard to measure because we don’t see any of the team work in practice during the season, but he does consistently spend an extra 30 minutes after practice throwing by himself.
Do you think the Falcons will be buyers or sellers at the trade deadline? — John K.
I hate to be boring, but I think the answer is “holders.”
There were scenarios where I could have seen either Bates or Kyle Pitts being available for the right offer, but the Falcons are still viable contenders in the NFC South. I don’t think this team has to make the playoffs this year, but it would be beneficial as proof of concept for the new coaching staff and personnel office.
With that still a reasonable possibility, I don’t think Atlanta ships out a key piece.
At the same time, I can’t see Cunningham giving up any future draft capital to be a buyer for a team that is still well short of being a championship contender.
What are the team’s travel plans for Spain next week? Are they leaving straight from Tampa on Sunday or treating it like a “regular” game and leaving late next week? — Gary C.
They are splitting the difference. Atlanta’s traveling party will leave on Tuesday evening, fly through the night and arrive in Madrid early Wednesday morning local time. The team will go straight to the practice fields at Real Madrid’s facility and get in a walk-through. From there, the Falcons will simply stay on local time because the game will be a 2:30 p.m. kickoff in Madrid.
How do you see James Pearce Jr. reintegrating with the team after this weekend? Will he be on the plane to Madrid? — Matt L.
The Falcons have been hesitant to discuss their plans for Pearce, so we don’t know the answer, but my guess is he will be on the plane. The bigger question is if he will be added to the 53-man roster during the week.
Atlanta is fourth in the league in quarterback pressure percentage (41.4 percent), and defensive coordinator Jeff Ulbrich has credited the defensive linemen’s willingness to “rush as one” and stick to a specific plan on each snap. It will take a while to integrate Pearce into…

Walter Nolen III's Outlook For Cardinals-Cowboys is Concerning
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Arizona Cardinals , for a second straight day, did not see defensive lineman Walter Nolen III practice.
Nolen missed Arizona's Week 7 matchup against the Denver Broncos with an ankle injury and is now on track to suffer a similar fate for Week 8's road test against the Dallas Cowboys barring a strong turnaround in the next 48 hours.
The Cardinals' defense is much different when Nolen is healthy and in the lineup, as his ability to disrupt both the run and pass is crucial for Arizona to control the line of scrimmage. The former first-round pick, unfortunately, continues to deal with injuries early in his career.
With a loaded Cowboys offense playing host to Arizona on Sunday, the Cardinals' chances of slowing them down could take a turn.
“They have a lot of talent, I know that," Cardinals head coach Mike LaFleur said of Dallas' offense.
"I’ve always had a lot of respect for Dak. I’ve had a lot of respect for ‘Schotty’ (Cowboys Head Coach Brian Schottenheimer) — he’s as good a human in this league as there is. You know they’re always going to be a talent-filled team. It’s always fun to go into that stadium (AT&T Stadium) and play those guys for obvious reasons. We have our hands full like you do every week but yes, these guys are talented.”
The Cardinals will rely on Roy Lopez and Darius Robinson to step up if Nolen can't go. Both players have had respectively nice 2026 campaigns. Dante Stills likely gets the nod inside while Andrew Billings could find himself active.

title: Where Cardinals, Josh Sweat Trade Stands After NFL Blockbusters
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Arizona Cardinals are expected to make Josh Sweat readily available for trade ahead of the NFL's Nov. 10 trade deadline.
We've already seen two defensive front players dealt for picks in DeForest Bucker (49ers) and Jeffery Simmons (Bears) with more moves potentially on the way.
What the recent deals mean for Sweat and the Cardinals:
Giving up two future first-round picks for a player essentially pushes you out of the running for any other major moves, and that's what stamped Chicago's deal for Simmons this morning. The Bears were also interested in Buckner and reportedly offered a better package than the 49ers for Buckner before the player himself reportedly only wanted the 49ers.
Chicago appeared to be serious on acquiring some sort of pass rush help. That's what they're getting in Simmons, and barring a "forget those picks" mentality from the Bears, they're out of the running for Sweat.
Even after getting Buckner, ESPN 49ers reporter Nick Wagoner says another move is still on the table for San Francisco:
"An addition such as Mack -- or other potentially available edge rushers like the Jets' Will McDonald IV, Cardinals' Josh Sweat or Bucs' Yaya Diaby -- would make sense to round out San Francisco's rotation for a reasonable cost in terms of what they need to give up," he wrote .
However, it would have to cost the 49ers.
Trading Sweat inside the NFC West would only happen if the receiving team would add a sweetener to the deal, as the Cardinals wouldn't be in the business of helping out a rival get a Super Bowl ring now without it paying dividends in the future.
The Cardinals' reported asking price of a second-round pick should remain the same, even after other deals on the defensive front market in recent days. One could make an argument Sweat's value for interested teams goes up due to other top names now off the market.
While Arizona should stay firm on their asking price of a high Day 2 pick, there also may be a sense of urgency to strike a deal now as opposed to waiting next offseason, where Sweat will be 30 and demanding a new contract with zero money guaranteed on the final two years of his deal.
If there was ever a time for the Cardinals to trade Sweat, it would be in the coming days.
The Cowboys are naturally a team that has been connected to Sweat in recent weeks. With a Dallas defense that needs another pass rusher on a team that conceivably wants to win now, Sweat's name makes sense.
However, Dallas doesn't quite have ample 2027 draft capital to make some moves — owning Green Bay's first-round pick, their own second and Pittsburgh's fourth to begin festivities next offseason.
That's not quite exciting if you're the Cardinals, and if you're Dallas, are you really looking to empty the clip on a guy who you'll have to pay more in the coming years?

title: Cardinals' Michael Wilson Gets Surprising Week 8 Practice Update
full_text:
ARIZONA — There were a handful of notable Arizona Cardinals missing from the team's Wednesday practice , and though Michael Wilson wasn't one, we did get a surprising update during the period open to reporters.
Wilson was spotted wearing a yellow non-contact jersey on Wednesday, which signals Wilson is dealing with an injury. In public knowledge he emerged clean from Week 7's loss to the Denver Broncos and didn't appear to be dealing with any injuries, nor did head coach Mike LaFleur mention anything about Wilson in his morning press conference.
Wednesday #AZCardinals practice report: HERE: Carson Beck, Jeremiyah Love, Andrew Wingard, Max Melton, Darius Robinson, NOT HERE: Walter Nolen, Budda Baker, Josh Sweat, Isaac Seumalo, Elijah Wilkinson, Tyler Allgeier A bit of a surprise… Michael Wilson spotted in a yellow… pic.twitter.com/IVB2Ri361Z
Players wearing this jersey signals to teammates that he cannot be blocked or hit.
While this doesn't automatically mean Wilson is in concussion protocol, players progressing through protocol are typically the ones that don the non-contact jerseys during practice. Reporters are not able to ask LaFleur about his status until Friday when he holds his next press conference.
The Cardinals travel to face the Dallas Cowboys in Week 8. Arizona will reveal their first injury report of the week later today, which will provide us clarity on what exactly Wilson is dealing with.
Wilson's production has slowed down a bit since Marvin Harrison Jr. was traded, which is something LaFleur was specifically asked about earlier this week:
“I think if you take away the stats from it, he’s running good routes and he’s separating. He has drawn quite a few penalties this year as well. I mean that got us going there on that third drive (of the game). With that being said, I know he can still make that play — for himself too, but (it’s) just kind of the momentum of making a play as opposed to a penalty," LaFleur said, reflecting back on his performance against the Broncos.
"I mean he (Broncos CB Riley Moss) held him. We told the official it was going to be a double move. He ran the double move. It was a really good route and the guy held him. That was clearly a penalty, but again, I know we can make that play. Then he drew another one a little bit later, but our pocket collapsed right away. To me, when we’re clicking on all cylinders, those are touchdowns. He ran right by the guy off the double move. He’s doing a lot of good things. He obviously hasn’t had the stats and that’s kind of what you’re insinuating right there.
"Again, all he can do is control what he can control — win his one-on-one matchups when the ball’s thrown to him, catch it, and then obviously try to stay grounded and make as much ‘YAC’ (yards after the catch) as he can.”
This would be a massive blow for the Cardinals' offense if Wilson isn't available.

title: Walter Nolen III Gets Injury Update Ahead of Cardinals-Cowboys
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Arizona Cardinals will not see Walter Nolen III practice on Wednesday, head coach Mike LaFleur told reporters.
Nolen is dealing with an ankle injury that kept him out of Arizona's Week 7 loss to the Denver Broncos.
"He's doing good. He'll will be DNP today, but he's getting better," LaFleur said of Nolen.
The Cardinals will practice twice more (Thursday and Friday) this week before being required to declare Nolen as out, questionable or doubtful.
Arizona travels to face the Dallas Cowboys in Week 8. The Cardinals are 2-5 while the Cowboys are 3-4.
Nolen, a second-year defensive lineman, has shown the ability to wreck offensive gameplans on a weekly basis. The one drawback? He's battled injuries since entering the league.
Nolen suffered a calf injury before training camp of his rookie season, which saw him miss the beginning of 2025 before returning halfway through the year. He played a handful of games and showed massive promise before suffering a knee injury that landed him on injured reserve, ending his year.
Nolen had surgery (later revealed to be a meniscus) but made a full recovery and was healthy for 2026's training camp, though he suffered a minor lower body injury during the team's time at State Farm Stadium.
Last week was the first regular season game Nolen missed for this year.
Nolen holds potential to be one of the best young defensive linemen in the NFL, and Arizona certainly needs it. Their defensive line pressure rate of 24.7% ranks dead-last in the league. In a front seven that's been largely uninspiring, Nolen's presence has been noticeable on a weekly basis.
The Cardinals, typically precautious with injuries, are going to be smart and hold Nolen out of action today. We'll see if that changes throughout the week, though it's clear the former first-round pick will be somebody to watch this week as things progress.
In six games this season, Nolen has 14 tackles, one sack and three quarterback hits.

title: Cardinals Set Asking Price for Josh Sweat as Trade Rumors Heat Up
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Arizona Cardinals sit at just 2-5 on the season, positioning themselves as prime selling candidates ahead of the NFL's Nov. 10 trade deadline.
Their recent deal that sent Marvin Harrison Jr. out to the Houston Texans for a second-round pick signaled Arizona would be willing to do business if the price is right for just about anybody, and if recent trade rumors have any merit, Cardinals outside linebacker Josh Sweat could very well be on the move.
Sweat being involved in trade discussions is nothing new. The beginning of the offseason saw Arizona's top pass rusher involved in chatter after the Cardinals fired head coach Jonathan Gannon, who played a big role in landing Sweat last offseason.
What would the Cardinals want for Sweat?
PHNX's Johnny Venerable tweeted out the following:
"The Cardinals are aware of Josh Sweat’s trade market and are believed to be seeking a high Day 2 pick for the veteran pass rusher, per source. Sweat previously requested a trade following the firing of Jonathan Gannon and is signed through 2028."
The Cardinals are aware of Josh Sweat’s trade market and are believed to be seeking a high Day 2 pick for the veteran pass rusher, per source. Sweat previously requested a trade following the firing of Jonathan Gannon and is signed through 2028. pic.twitter.com/LmOdKqKuwe
Sweat is in the second year of a four-year, $76 million contract that does not feature any guaranteed money in 2027 and 2028 — which are the final two years of his deal. He's reportedly looking for a new contract.
The new deal could play a big part in how teams approach Sweat and a potential trade. He's turning 30 next offseason and it appears as degenerative knee issue will be something that needs to be closely managed by Sweat wherever he's at in the coming years.
Sweat's production also hasn't been up to par. The Cardinals saw him tally 12 sacks last season but have rarely seen their star pass rusher get to the quarterback in 2026, bringing down the quarterback just twice.
A high Day 2 pick makes sense for Arizona's asking price, but will that be met?
The good news for the Cardinals is demand for a top pass rusher will only push Sweat's price tag up, especially after DeForest Buckner is now traded and off the market.
It's possible we see Sweat traded for a conditional third-round pick that could turn into a second based off various incentives, whether it be playing time, sacks, whatever the two teams strike a deal on.
There's serious trade buzz around Sweat, and if a desperate team wants to match Arizona's reported asking price, the Cardinals could very well do business.

title: NFL Insider Reveals 3 Top Teams in Cardinals' Josh Sweat Trade Talks
full_text:
ARIZONA — The NFL's Nov. 10 trade deadline is rapidly approaching, and the Arizona Cardinals figure to be massive players.
With a 2-5 record and Marvin Harrison Jr. already traded, the Cardinals very much feel open for business within the next few weeks. Whether a deal can be struck remains to be seen, though Arizona clearly has some available talent if the price is right.
No name is bigger — or generating more buzz — than edge rusher Josh Sweat , who has been no stranger to dominating trade headlines entering 2026.
According to ESPN's Jeremy Fowler, the Dallas Cowboys , Chicago Bears and San Francisco 49ers are teams to watch for Sweat.
Josh Sweat is being linked to the Cowboys, Bears, 49ers ahead of the NFL Trade Deadline, per @JFowlerESPN . Should the Arizona Cardinals trade their most productive pass rusher? pic.twitter.com/UFqpqcnMZK
Sweat is in the second of a four-year, $76 million contract that doesn't have any guaranteed money in the final two seasons of his deal. He's reportedly looking for a new contract that will fix that.
After signing with the Cardinals in 2025, Sweat tallied 12 sacks and nearly was a Pro Bowl player before being snubbed. Arizona fired head coach Jonathan Gannon after the year, which reportedly prompted a trade request from Sweat.
The Cardinals ultimately held on to Sweat (despite intensified trade buzz heating up around training camp), though with Arizona now trending in the wrong direction, general manager Monti Ossenfort may find it the appropriate time to sell.
Sweat is expected to fetch a Day 2 pick on the trade market, which very well could be met by a team looking to push themselves over the top. Dallas, Chicago and San Francisco all match those molds.
However, the Cowboys are 3-4 on the season and truly need a turnaround to save their playoff chances. The Bears' interest in Sweat and other defenders is acceptable with hopes of balancing their offensive side of the ball while the 49ers would have to massively overpay for a trade to happen within the division.
Arizona already snagged a round two pick for Harrison — is a similar fate in store for Sweat?
Sweat's about to enter his 30s and has just two sacks on the season while he's clearly got some knee injury management that will slow him down. Sweat, after not practicing in any form this offseason, has only shown flashes of the typical damage he can do.
If that magically is fixed after being traded remains to be seen, though Sweat's one of the hottest names in the market right now.

title: Cardinals Big Losers in NFL Week 8 Power Rankings
full_text:
The Arizona Cardinals dropped to 2-5 after their Week 7 loss to the Denver Broncos.
Ahead of Week 8, the Cardinals (expectedly) tumbled down various NFL power rankings:
Josh Weinfuss on Kendrick Bourne being the best offseason addition: "The veteran wide receiver, who signed a two-year deal this offseason, has been a reliable third or fourth option for quarterback Jacoby Brissett. That has been especially true after Marvin Harrison Jr. was traded away three weeks ago, as tight end Trey McBride and wide receiver Michael Wilson have gotten a significant amount of attention from defenses. Bourne has 234 yards on 25 catches in seven games. He's on pace for a career high in catches and the third-most receiving yards of his career."
Conor Orr : "Man, the Broncos defense will put you in a terrible headspace."
Pete Prisco : "The high of beating the Rams last week went by the wayside as they were blown out by Denver at home Sunday. They just lack the talent to compete week in and week out."
Nick Shook : "Arizona’s performance in Sunday’s loss to Denver was too predictable. The Cardinals once again became a chuck-and-pray offense on third down, gave up an inexcusable, 62-yard scramble touchdown to Bo Nix, and produced a calamity of errors in the clubhouse leader for worst goal-to-go possession of the year. I feel for Jacoby Brissett, who was brutalized by Denver’s defense. It’s tough to be a Cardinals fan right now."
Mike Florio : "It’s Carson Beck time."
Gary Davenport : "Beck probably isn't the long-term answer at quarterback, but he was a three-year starter at Georgia and then Miami. The Redbirds thought enough of him to spend a Day 2 pick on him.
"And if they're going to get him some game reps, now is the time. After the Cowboys' non-existent defense in Week 8, the Cardinals face Seattle, the Rams and Kansas City.
"This will be a 3-8 team (at best) by the end of November."
Chad Graff on their pass rush being spooky: "The Cardinals have the league’s third-worst passing defense in part because they struggle to generate pressure. The group ranks 27th in pressure rate and 26th in quarterback hits."

title: Cardinals Sign Familiar Face to Address WR Room Injuries
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Arizona Cardinals are bringing back a familiar face.
After losing Jalen Brooks to injured reserve, the Cardinals are signing veteran receiver Zay Jones – who previously played for Arizona for two seasons (2024-25) before not being re-signed this past offseason.
After Brooks was officially placed on IR today following wrist surgery, Jones (who spent time with the Houston Texans in training camp before being cut) was signed to help a depleted receivers room that also lost Marvin Harrison Jr . due to a trade weeks ago.
In related moves today, Arizona officially re-signed offensive lineman Austin Deculus and safety Wydett Williams Jr. to the practice squad and has released safety Jerrick Reed II from the practice squad.
Jones has nine years of NFL experience with over 300 receptions and 3,000 receiving yards. His familiarity with Cardinals general manager Monti Ossenfort most certainly played a role in helping him get back to the desert.
While current head coach Mike LaFleur doesn't have prior working experience with Jones, former Arizona head coach Jonathan Gannon always sang Jones' praises when asked in press conferences.
“He does his job. He's in the right spot. He can play three spots. He's fast and he's explosive. (He’s a) really good, contested catch guy," Gannon said of Jones last season.
With Jones arriving to a new Cardinals offense under LaFleur, there is some continuity already established with personnel. Jones played with Michael Wilson and Trey McBride previously. Behind Jones, presuming he's eventually worked into Arizona's X receiver role, is fifth-round rookie Reggie Virgil and Simi Fehoko.
LaFleur, asked about replacing Brooks, told reporters it would be done by a committee approach.
“Next man up. I mean, the show goes on, right?" LaFleur said.
"(WR) Reggie’s (Virgil) got a few reps there versus L.A. Didn’t get as many yesterday, but a good week of practice by him. You can do it by committee. (WR) Kendrick (Bourne) can play some X too if we need that. Obviously, (WR) Simi (Fehoko) has done kind of both, but it’ll be by committee.”
The Cardinals, currently 2-5, are dead last in explosive play rates and yards after reception after seven weeks of football. While Jones' presence probably doesn't change those numbers, he does add another veteran presence to a young and overall inexperienced Cardinals' wide receiver room.
Arizona will play the Dallas Cowboys in Week 8. Jones could potentially be caught up to speed enough to be active for Sunday.

title: 7 Alarming Stats the Cardinals Must Fix Immediately
full_text:
The Arizona Cardinals are 2-5 through just seven weeks of football, and while stats don't always tell the story, it does sprinkle in some context into how a team is performing.
Take for example their latest red zone struggles , which has stalled their offense and overall ability to win games to begin the regular season. Seven weeks is more than enough to gather data and establish a foundation of what a football team is.
While there's a few good things the Cardinals are doing at this point in time, there's several categories where Arizona ranks near the bottom of the league — if not completely alone at No. 32.
Seven alarming stats the Cardinals have to fix, fast:
What it means : The average time quarterbacks spend in the pocket before throwing or moving out.
Why it matters : Jacoby Brissett is getting the ball out at incredibly fast rates, which does keep turnovers and sacks down to a minimum. However, this usually means teams aren't able hit big plays down the field and are often only hitting the first read... which is exactly what Arizona's offense has evolved into with Brissett under center.
What it means : The percentage in which the defensive line is pressuring a quarterback on dropbacks.
Why it matters : The Cardinals have seemingly only been able to manufacture sacks and pressure from exotic looks or blitzes from defensive coordinator Nick Rallis. Great defenses can rush four and drop seven, and Arizona has tried that with little success for far too long. This number only suffers the more time Walter Nolen III misses due to injury.
What it means : The average amount of yards a pass catcher gains after a reception.
Why it matters : If the Cardinals can't hit deep plays down the field, they have to rely on receivers making defenders miss after the catch — which hasn't happened. While Arizona has strong options in Trey McBride and Michael Wilson, neither are exactly known for making defenders miss in the open field. The Cardinals need a spark in their WR room.
What it means : The percentage of explosive plays an offense has. Ten yards for a rush and 20 yards through the air qualifies.
Why it matters : The Cardinals have been forced to dink-and-dunk their way during drives, failing to hit a big play more than any other team in the league. Arizona can't take the top off the defense, make defenders miss after the catch, or block well enough to spring big plays. This falls on a mix of execution and scheme from head coach Mike LaFleur.
What it means : The percentage of drives a defense allows the offense to score on.
Why it matters : The Cardinals' defense is allowing some sort of score on nearly half of their drives, operating in true feast or famine territory. Arizona's defense has unfortunately met low expectations this season by allowing the most amount of points through seven weeks at 208, which is 29.7 points per game. It's basically a coin flip to see if an offense will score against Rallis' unit, and that's not good.
What it means : The percentage of plays where the defense pressures a quarterback on a passing attempt.
Why it matters : Arizona simply isn't getting to the quarterback. Whether it be their defensive line as highlighted above, outside linebackers or whoever else, opposing offenses aren't being pressured nearly close enough  by Arizona's defense to make an impact. Rallis is solid at generating blitzes to manufacture pressure, he just isn't aggressive enough.
What it means : How often a rushing attempt is stopped at or behind the line of scrimmage.
Why it matters: The Cardinals can't run the ball. For what reason remains to be seen, though missing starters along the offensive line doesn't help while LaFleur hasn't found the recipe for success in terms of scheme. Bam Knight's found some success while Tyler Allgeier has been disappointing. Would love to see what Jeremiyah Love can do when he's fully healthy.

title: Bears Jeffery Simmons Trade Makes Prior Falcons Trade Look Like Robbery
full_text:
The Tennessee Titans and Chicago Bears executed a blockbuster trade on Thursday, but Atlanta Falcons general manager Ian Cunningham came out a winner.
In late August, the Falcons sent cornerback Clark Phillips III and a 2027 fifth-round pick to the Bears for interior defensive lineman Gervon Dexter . The Bears then turned around and made this lucrative deal for Jeffery Simmons (two first-rounders and a fourth-rounder to the Tennessee Titans for Simmons and a fifth-rounder) just a few months later.
Simmons is an elite player who deserves this sort of capital, but that is an expensive deal for a player whose output has been eerily similar to the one they just sent away.
Dexter, 6-foot-6 and 326 pounds, has been a force for the Falcons since coming to Atlanta ahead of the regular season. He boasts a pass-rush win rate of 15.8, with 18 hurries, four quarterback hits, two sacks, and 24 pressures – which is right in line with Simmons’ pass-rush win rate of 14.3, with 14 hurries, six quarterback hits, four sacks, and 24 pressures.
Dexter's numbers match Simmons, despite the former Titan playing nearly twice the snaps (425-279). Dexter's run defense, a sore spot in Chicago, also matches up well against Simmons.
Not that far apart in dbl team rate. pic.twitter.com/sRab1khSMW
The Bears’ new interior piece is an elite player and has been for several years (three-time All-Pro), but the Falcons might have found a similar player in Dexter, who's four years younger,  for considerably less. It’s why they felt compelled to extend him just a month after making that deal.
“He repped our style at the highest level: strain, effort, toughness, violence, awareness, instinct, all of that,” Falcons defensive coordinator Jeff Ulbrich said after Dexter signed that deal. “He proved a lot before he got here, and then he's just validated it, because you never know until you get your hands on a guy and you're really around him on a day-to-day capacity, what his makeup is – and his makeup is elite.”
Atlanta needed to get bigger and stronger in the trenches, and Cunningham made that a priority this offseason. The process, which included adding Dexter from the Bears, has paid off in a big way. The Falcons have been one of the NFL’s best defensive lines this season, generating pressure at a high clip without sending added blitzers and stuffing the run.
This isn't the first time in the recent past the Bears and Falcons have been linked at the position. Prior to the 2025 season, the Falcons waived stalwart Grady Jarrett for salary cap reasons. The Bears quickly pounced on Jarrett and gave him a three-year, $43 million contract.
The 33-year-old Jarrett started just four games for the Bears last year and has 12 tackles in seven starts this season.
The Falcons' four-man rotation at defensive tackle costs less than Jarrett's $18.9 million cap hit combined. And they have been one of the most productive units in the NFL.
Falcons have 4 guys in the top right. It gives me another opportunity to say that ranking them the 32nd DL was ignorant. https://t.co/mrOWz5zD6O
Does all this mean that Dexter is as good a player as Simmons? Maybe not, but he is four years younger, matches his production, and it didn’t cost the Falcons a pair of first-rounders to get him. You be the judge.

title: Falcons QB Michael Penix Jr. Ready to Step Into Familiar but Uncharted Territory
full_text:
Third-year NFL quarterback Michael Penix Jr. now has a season’s worth of starts at 17.
But there’s one thing the Atlanta Falcons signal-caller hasn’t done yet.
This Sunday, Penix will be about 40 miles north of his hometown, Dade City, when Atlanta (3-4) heads to Raymond James Stadium for a Week 8 NFC South road clash against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers (2-5) .
“It’s exciting,” Penix told reporters Wednesday. “I imagine I should have a lot of people coming to the game. My mom usually knows that headcount. But it’s going to be exciting to be able to get out there.”
Penix was originally born in Cookeville, Tennessee, where his father, Michael Sr., starred as a running back and his mother, Takisha, was a track and field athlete at Tennessee Tech. The family then relocated to Dade City and later to Riverview.
In a 2019 interview with Indiana Hoosiers on SI , Penix Sr. shared that his baby, Penix Jr., took his first steps in the end zone of a local football field.
“His very first steps as a baby – they were actually in the end zone,’’ Penix, Sr. told Tom Brew. “His first steps were right out there on the football field, right there in the end zone with me. How’s that for a start?’’
Penix played prep football at Pasco High School and then finished his final two years at Tampa Bay Technical High School.
He hasn’t played a game at home since.
Before transferring to finish his college career at the University of Washington, Penix’s Hoosiers team played in the 2021 Outback Bowl, hosted by Raymond James Stadium. The quarterback watched from the sidelines with a torn ACL, the second of three in his football career.
As a rookie, Penix was backing up Kirk Cousins before taking over as the starter for the final three games of the 2024 season in what was planned to be a redshirt year. Last year, when the Falcons made the trip to Tampa, Penix had already torn his ACL and was ruled out for the season less than a month earlier.
“It’s happening,” Penix said of finally playing near his Central Florida home. “Can’t wait to be out there. We want to come out with a win.”
Penix has faced the Bucs before, though, in the 2025 season opener. Atlanta hosted, but dropped the game 23-20. The quarterback went 27-for-42 for 298 passing yards and threw a touchdown.
Now 26, Penix was two years old when the Bucs won their first Super Bowl in January 2003 to cap off the 2002-2003 season. But he added he was never a fan of the team growing up.
Penix enters his homecoming on a heater, turning in two consecutive three-touchdown games for Atlanta.
He’s fresh off what’s arguably his best performance of his career as the Falcons knocked off the unbeaten San Francisco 49ers 29-20 last Sunday, Oct. 25. Penix went 25-for-34 for 213 passing yards and tossed three touchdowns in the comeback win . On Wednesday, the NFL named him the NFC Offensive Player of the Week for the outing.
A large credit for Penix’s standout game was clean pockets from flawless offensive line protection. He wasn’t sacked or hurried, and barely took any contact at all from the Niners’ defense.
The Falcons will now face a Tampa Bay team with a 38% blitz rate, the fourth-highest in the NFL, according to Pro Football Focus.
“You practice it, you look over all the looks that they’ve brought, you go years back, and just be ready for everything,” Penix detailed the preparation. “We try to make sure we don’t miss any pressure looks that we possibly can see. And every week, a team comes in with a new pressure. And once we figure that out, we make adjustments on the sideline or at halftime. We’ll be ready.”
Falcons-Bucs kicks off at 1 p.m. from Raymond James Stadium. FOX will televise the game.
Gerald Thomas, III, is a national award-winning reporter contributing to Atlanta Falcons On SI. He has several years of writing and editorial experience, including covering college athletics under the USA TODAY umbrella.

title: Michael Penix Jr. Explains How New Offensive Coordinator Helps Fuel Falcons Offense
full_text:
The Atlanta Falcons have found an offensive rhythm with Michael Penix Jr. back under center, and the quarterback's growing relationship with offensive coordinator Tommy Rees has played an important role in that progress.
The Falcons have averaged 31 points per game since Penix returned to the starting lineup in Week 3, the best in the NFL in that span. His most recent performance earned him an NFC Offensive Player of the Week nod and strengthened the optimism surrounding Atlanta's offense .
For Penix, that success starts with communication and trust between himself and Rees.
"We've been very close since he got here. It's always been, with the quarterback and offensive coordinator, y'all got to be hand in hand," Penix said.
That connection extends to the weekly game plan, where Rees has encouraged Penix to speak openly about the game plan with him
"With Tommy, he's always like, 'Hey, tell me things that you don't like, and it won't be called. We'll take it off the play sheet.' So he's always thinking about the things that I like," Penix explained.
Penix also has a say in which plays receive priority during games.
"Obviously, I give him my favorite play calls, so I will get those plays called first, and then he starts drizzling in some of the things that he likes based on the game plan and stuff like that," Penix said.
The results have been encouraging. Through Week 7, Penix had recorded nine touchdown passes against just one interception, demonstrating the efficiency Atlanta needs from its starting quarterback.
Rees believes that confidence in the play call is critical to getting the most out of Penix. The coordinator has emphasized the importance of seeing the game through the same lens and ensuring his quarterback trusts the offensive approach.
"I never want to call a play that you don't have full belief or confidence in," Rees said.
That philosophy has helped the two build a partnership that goes beyond their responsibilities on game day.
"As we've grown together and as we've gone through some battles together, you form this closeness. You start to build a bond off the field," Rees said.
As the Falcons continue their season, the relationship between Penix and Rees will remain an important part of Atlanta's offensive development. Their willingness to communicate and incorporate each other's perspectives has established a foundation built on trust.
With Penix producing and Rees tailoring the offense to his strengths, Atlanta has reason to believe their growing partnership can continue fueling the team's success.

title: Khalil Herbert Hopes to Find a Home With Falcons After Long NFL Journey
full_text:
Khalil Herbert has spent the past year searching for stability in the NFL, moving between teams while trying to prove he can still make an impact.
After helping the Atlanta Falcons earn victory over the San Francisco 49ers, the veteran running back hopes his latest opportunity can turn into something more permanent.
Herbert signed with the Falcons on September 16th, and he was elevated from Atlanta’s practice squad ahead of Sunday’s matchup. He made the most of his opportunity. He finished with 3 touches for 28 yards and contributed on special teams, including a 38-yard kickoff return to open the second half. His return helped give Atlanta favorable field position during a key stretch of the game.
The Falcons scored a touchdown to give them their first lead of the game, a lead they wouldn't relinquish.
For Herbert, simply being back on the field and finding ways to help his teammates was meaningful.
“It felt good. It felt good, you know, coming out there with the team, doing what I can. So it just felt good to be out there,” Herbert said.
The running back also joked about whether he had scored on a 19-yard reception, where he was ruled to have stepped out of bounds at the one-yard line. “I think so. I think so. Everybody else is telling me that, too. They have to go check the tape.”
Herbert entered the NFL as a sixth-round pick by the Chicago Bears in 2021. He spent four seasons with Chicago before his career took several turns, including stops with the Cincinnati Bengals and New York Jets. He also spent time with the Indianapolis Colts, Seattle Seahawks and San Francisco 49ers, according to his account of his recent journey.
The constant movement has made finding a consistent role difficult. Rather than focusing on what has happened, however, Herbert is concentrating on making the most of his opportunity in Atlanta.
“It’s been a little journey the last year, just trying to get in where I fit in, contribute where I can, and, you know, hopefully stick it out here,” Herbert said.
The victory over San Francisco carried additional significance because Herbert had been with the 49ers during training camp before joining the Falcons. Getting a win against a team he previously worked with made the experience even more rewarding.
Atlanta’s decision to elevate Herbert also came at a useful time. With Brian Robinson Jr. sidelined by a hamstring injury, the Falcons needed additional depth behind Bijan Robinson. Herbert provided another option in the backfield while contributing on kickoff returns.
Herbert understands that his role could change from week to week, particularly as he continues to work to establish himself on the roster.
“I take the same approach whether I’m in or not,” Herbert said. “Honestly, preparing, always being ready mentally, practice, walkthrough, whatever. Any reps I’m not in, walking through, taking my steps, doing it.”
That preparation becomes especially important for a player whose opportunities can arrive with little notice. Herbert knows he cannot control when his number is called, but he can control how prepared he is when it happens.
“You never know. So just trying to stay ready and everything,” he said.
One performance will not guarantee a permanent role, but Herbert has given Atlanta another reason to consider what he can offer moving forward. After spending much of the past year searching for the right fit, he now has a chance to turn a short-term opportunity into a lasting home in Atlanta.

title: Jessie Bates III Sends Strong Message on Falcons QB Michael Penix Jr.
full_text:
The Atlanta Falcons have faced plenty of questions about their long-term future at quarterback, but All-Pro safety Jessie Bates III believes the organization already has its answer in Michael Penix Jr.
“You can sleep good at night when you got Michael Penix playing quarterback for you,” Bates said.
The veteran safety did not stop there, making it clear that his confidence in Penix extends beyond the quarterback’s physical ability.
“I really, truly believe that he’s a franchise quarterback,” Bates said.
Bates’ comments arrive as Penix continues to establish himself as Atlanta’s quarterback of the future. Although the Falcons invested a first-round pick in Penix in 2024 despite having just signed Kirk Cousins to a $100 million guaranteed contract, questions about the team’s long-term quarterback situation have persisted as Penix works to prove he can consistently lead a contender.
Atlanta’s decision to select Penix with the eighth overall pick surprised many observers because the team had signed Cousins to a lucrative contract just weeks earlier. The move immediately created questions about the organization’s plans at quarterback, particularly with Cousins expected to be the starter when the 2024 season began.
Penix took over the starting job with three games left in his rookie season, putting the spotlight on whether he could justify the organization’s significant investment and establish himself as Atlanta’s long-term answer.
Now, as the Falcons continue evaluating their future, Bates’ endorsement offers an encouraging sign of the confidence Penix has earned inside the locker room.
Through his first five starts of the 2026 season, Penix has completed 66.7 percent of his passes for 1,157 yards, nine touchdowns, and just one interception. He has posted a 109.1 passer rating, placing fourth in the NFL among quarterbacks with at least five starts.
Penix appreciated the endorsement, especially because of the respect he has for Bates and their relationship inside the locker room.
“It means a lot that a guy that’s been doing it at a high level in this league for a long time would have that belief in me and the offense as well as a collective,” Penix said.
The Falcons quarterback also talked about the relationship.
“It’s awesome to be able to hear that. That was my first time hearing that. But he’s my locker mate. I talk to him every day. We always try to pick each other’s brains. I love Jesse, man. That’s my guy,” Penix said.
That relationship is important as Penix continues navigating the expectations that come with being a first-round quarterback.
However, being viewed as the franchise quarterback requires more than draft position or support from teammates. Penix must continue demonstrating that he can stay healthy, make consistent decisions, and lead Atlanta to meaningful victories.
For his part, Penix is not interested in getting caught up in the speculation surrounding his future.
“Nah, I just want to win football games. All that stuff comes. You got to win, and when you win, some of the good things happen,” Penix said.
If Penix delivers consistent production and helps Atlanta compete for championships, many of the questions surrounding the quarterback position will quickly disappear.
Until then, the conversation about whether he is the Falcons’ long-term answer will continue.
Now Penix must turn that belief into sustained success and give the Falcons the winning quarterback they envisioned when they selected him.

title: Baker Mayfield Gives Blunt Answer On Kevin Stefanski Before Falcons Game
full_text:
A reunion is set for Week 8 in Tampa, and it’s not just the Atlanta Falcons and Buccaneers. Falcons head coach Kevin Stefanski and Buccaneers quarterback Baker Mayfield will meet for just the second time since parting ways in 2021.
Stefanski coached Mayfield, the Browns' first overall pick in 2018, during the 2020 and 2021 seasons. Their first year together was a resounding success, as Cleveland went 11-5 and won its first playoff game since 1994. Stefanski won NFL Coach of the Year, while the Browns appeared to have finally identified their future franchise quarterback.
But their second season unraveled. Mayfield played through multiple injuries as the Browns finished 8-9, and Cleveland's public pursuit of Deshaun Watson the following offseason ultimately led Mayfield to request a trade.
After the now-Falcons coach was hired in January, his former quarterback made some comments that raised some eyebrows. However, Mayfield walked back those comments a month later.
Mayfield was asked about those comments again on Wednesday as he prepares to take on his former coach for the first time since Week 1 in 2022. He kept it brief.
“No, I haven’t spoken to him since 2021,” Mayfield said.
He was then asked whether any lingering emotion remained that ‘ate at him.’
As for what he expects from Sunday's game, Mayfield had plenty of positive things to say about the challenge of facing this Falcons defense.
“ (Jessie) Bates is a hell of a player . (Xavier) Watts, I think, is extremely good as well. Those guys are so instinctive, and they disguise well,” Mayfield said. “But what really jumps out on tape is their front. They’re rotating a lot of guys in – obviously, (Jalon) Walker’s done for the year and (James) Pearce isn’t back yet – but who they have in there right now, they’re creating chaos. They’re jetting off the ball, attack-front style.
“A lot of different movement and keeping you on your toes (as an offense). They’re doing a good job of mixing up their pressures and fronts from different looks, so you can’t really get a beat on where it’s coming from.”
Atlanta has had the upper hand in the matchup, going 4-2 against Tampa Bay with Mayfield at quarterback. For Mayfield, flipping that trend starts with ball security. The Falcons are +3 in turnover margin in their last two trips to Raymond James Stadium, and they spurred Atlanta to a pair of wins.
After forcing four turnovers in Sunday's win over San Francisco , the Falcons will look to carry that defensive momentum into another divisional test.
“It comes to taking care of the rock,” Mayfield said. “In division games like that, when it’s a tight ball game, you gotta do that.”

title: Where Atlanta Falcons Stand in NFC South Ahead of Division Clash with Buccaneers
full_text:
The Atlanta Falcons have an opportunity to change the NFC South race over their next four games, beginning this Sunday with an important divisional matchup against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers.
Atlanta improved to 3-4 after defeating the San Francisco 49ers in Week 7. The victory provided a much-needed confidence boost, but the Falcons cannot afford to let that momentum disappear as they prepare for a challenging stretch.
With the Carolina Panthers currently leading the division at 3-3, the Falcons have ground to make up. Tampa Bay and the New Orleans Saints are both 2-5, leaving the division race open as the season progresses.
Atlanta’s next game comes against Tampa Bay on Nov. 1 at Raymond James Stadium. The Buccaneers are coming off a dominant 43-13 victory over Carolina, making this an important opportunity for the Falcons to gain ground in the division.
A victory would move Atlanta to .500 while giving Tampa Bay another divisional loss. It would also help the Falcons improve their divisional record.
The Buccaneers have already demonstrated their ability to compete within this division, and Atlanta will need another strong performance on both sides of the ball to leave Tampa with a victory.
Following that matchup, the Falcons travel to Madrid, Spain, to face the Cincinnati Bengals on Nov. 8 before hosting the Chiefs on Nov. 15. Atlanta then has its bye week before traveling to Minnesota to face the Vikings on Nov. 29.
Those three non-divisional games will be important for Atlanta’s overall record and playoff positioning. However, the Falcons must balance those challenges with the importance of their remaining NFC South matchups.
Carolina remains atop the standings despite its blowout loss to Tampa Bay. At 3- 3, the Panthers have the division lead, but their advantage over Atlanta is small enough that the race could change quickly. Carolina faces the Green Bay Packers on Thursday night. The Packers have won three of four since being blown out by the Falcons.
Tampa Bay’s victory over Carolina was significant because it improved the Buccaneers’ division record.
New Orleans, meanwhile, sits at 2-5 and has ground to make up. The Saints remain a factor in the division race, particularly with another matchup against Atlanta scheduled for Week 17. New Orleans is on a bye this week.
The Falcons will also host Tampa Bay in Week 16 before closing the regular season on the road against Carolina in Week 18. Those games could prove decisive if the division remains competitive.
The next four games will help determine whether Atlanta can turn its victory over San Francisco into a sustained push toward the playoffs.
With Carolina leading and Tampa Bay gaining momentum, Atlanta cannot afford to overlook the importance of its divisional games. Winning those matchups could ultimately determine whether the Falcons challenge for the NFC South crown or spend the final weeks trying to catch up.

title: NFL Stands Up, Takes Notice of Michael Penix Jr.'s Ascendancy
full_text:
The Atlanta Falcons are coming off one of their biggest victories of the season , and quarterback Michael Penix Jr. is receiving recognition for his performance against the San Francisco 49ers.
Penix was named NFC Offensive Player of the Week on Wednesday after leading the Falcons to a victory over the 49ers in Week 7. The honor marks the first time in his NFL career that Penix has received a Player of the Week award since entering the league in 2024.
The third-year quarterback delivered one of his most efficient performances of the season, completing 25 of 34 passes for 213 yards and three touchdowns without throwing an interception. His 73.5 percent completion rate and 118.9 passer rating highlighted an impressive outing against one of the conference's top teams.
Penix's passer rating was his second-highest of the season. He also extended an encouraging stretch for Atlanta's young quarterback, throwing three touchdown passes for the second consecutive game. He recorded three touchdowns in the Falcons' Week 6 loss to the Chicago Bears before matching that total against San Francisco.
Penix was the only quarterback in the conference in Week 7 to record at least three touchdown passes without an interception while completing at least 70 percent of his attempts.
Falcons head coach Kevin Stefanski praised Penix's ability to make smart decisions against a talented San Francisco defense.
“I thought Mike was really good throughout the day. You know, that's a very, very good defense. I mean they're excellent and they don't give up big plays. And we took our shots when we had them, and when we didn't, I thought Mike saw it really well,” Stefanski said after the victory.
His decision making helped Atlanta overcome an early deficit and secure a much needed victory.
After falling behind 14-3, the Falcons rallied and scored 26 unanswered points during a stretch that carried them into the fourth quarter. Atlanta's protection also played a significant role, allowing Penix to operate without being sacked against the 49ers.
The victory snapped Atlanta's two-game losing streak and provided a boost heading into a crucial divisional matchup.
The Falcons will travel to face the Tampa Bay Buccaneers in Week 8, with the opportunity to build momentum and strengthen their position in the NFC South standings.
For Penix, earning his first career Player of the Week award represents a significant milestone. His recent production gives Atlanta reason for optimism as the quarterback looks to carry his improved play into another important game.

title: Falcons Could Trade for Key Weapon in Colts Fire Sale
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts are open for business, but could the Atlanta Falcons want in?
After Colts ownership fired Chris Ballard last week, the franchise has started selling off roster assets in quick succession. In a matter of hours, interim general manager Ed Dodds shipped All-Pro guard Quenton Nelson to the Seahawks for a pair of picks (a 2027 third-rounder and a 2028 fifth-rounder) and All-Pro interior defensive lineman DeForest Buckner to the 49ers for a 2027 fourth-rounder.
With Indianapolis tearing down its roster, teams across the league are looking to pluck a piece from a teardown franchise.
The Falcons could add wide receiver depth at the deadline, and Josh Downs immediately comes to mind.
At 25, the Georgia native is entering the final year of his rookie contract and has developed into a solid route runner. The Falcons would need to send a mid-round pick in 2027 for Downs.
Lining up mostly in the slot, Downs could replace Olamide Zaccheaus in the rotation, since the free-agent addition hasn't made a significant impact so far (four catches for 17 yards). The addition could make sense, but his presence would also impede rookie Zachariah Branch. Atlanta would also be competing with other wide receiver-needy teams (e.g., the Chiefs, 49ers, etc.), and the Colts would look to maximize their return.
If the Falcons looked deeper on the Colts’ roster, they could also target wideout Keenan Allen. He is no longer the elite threat he was, but the 14-year veteran would still be a red-zone threat for Michael Penix Jr. and a valuable locker-room addition for a young rotation.
Ian Cunningham has already shown a willingness to make trades, and the first-year general manager has already made four.
Over the offseason, he acquired Wanya Morris from the Chiefs, Sydney Brown from the Eagles, Gervon Dexter from the Bears , and Maason Smith from the Jaguars . These were aggressive deals by the Falcons, and three have worked out beautifully. Cunningham was intentional with these deals, some player-for-player and others straight draft capital, but each addressed a specific need the roster didn’t already have.
For now, the Falcons aren't in a position to be hyper-aggressive.
At 3-4, they are around the middle of the NFC and aren't expected to be contenders this season. They are also well-positioned to spend big in free agency in 2027 ($141.4 million in cap space, the most in the NFL) and, if they choose, could compete for these assets on the open market instead of giving up draft capital.
Downs would also be in the market for a lucrative extension. With the Falcons already paying three skill players big money, they are unlikely to pony up what it would take to retain him.
The Colts' sell-off could create opportunities, but Cunningham should only make a move if the price and long-term fit make sense. He's shown a willingness to be aggressive, but patience may be the better play.
Garrett Chapman is a sports broadcaster, writer, and content creator based in Atlanta. He has several years of experience covering the Atlanta sports scene, college football, Georgia high school football, recruiting for 24/7 Sports, and the NFL. You can also hear him on Sports Radio 92.9 The Game.

title: Falcons Head Coach Kevin Stefanski Could Join NFL Royalty
full_text:
Atlanta Falcons head coach Kevin Stefanski is earning national recognition for his work in Atlanta, with ESPN analyst Ben Solak making the case that the two-time Coach of the Year winner deserves another award.
In his Week 8 column, Solak praised Stefanski’s impact on quarterback Michael Penix Jr., the Falcons’ rushing attack and a defense that has helped Atlanta remain competitive in the NFC South.
"I think ... Kevin Stefanski should win Coach of the Year," Solak wrote on ESPN . "Three coaches in NFL history have won the AP Coach of the Year award at least three times: Don Shula (3.5, as he shared a win in 1967), Bill Belichick (three), and Chuck Knox (three). I think Stefanski should become the fourth this season."
The endorsement follows Atlanta’s 29-20 victory over the previously undefeated San Francisco 49ers in Week 7. The Falcons improved to 3-4 after overcoming an early 14-3 deficit, scoring 23 unanswered points to secure an important win.
For Solak, however, Stefanski’s candidacy goes beyond one impressive performance. He believes the coach has helped establish an offensive identity that maximizes Atlanta’s personnel.
One of Solak’s biggest reasons for supporting Stefanski is Michael Penix Jr.’s development . The quarterback has increasingly embraced a quicker passing approach rather than consistently relying on deep throws.
“That the Falcons have readily gotten Penix to think about football in a different fashion altogether is impressive,” Solak wrote.
Atlanta has incorporated more quick passes and designed rollouts to help Penix operate efficiently. Solak says that Penix leads the NFL in designed rollout rate, highlighting the coaching staff’s willingness to tailor the offense to its quarterback.
The Falcons have also established a productive ground game behind Bijan Robinson.
“His running game is getting the best out of Robinson that we’ve ever seen,” Solak wrote.
That rushing production gives Atlanta another way to control games and takes pressure off Penix as he continues developing.
Solak also praised Stefanski for retaining defensive coordinator Jeff Ulbrich, whose unit has contributed to Atlanta’s recent success. Against San Francisco, the Falcons forced four turnovers and limited one of the NFC’s strongest teams to 20 points.
Stefanski previously won Coach of the Year honors in 2020 and 2023 with Cleveland. A third award would place him among a select group of coaches to accomplish that feat.
Solak believes Atlanta’s position in the NFC South gives Stefanski a realistic opportunity to strengthen his candidacy. He pointed to a potential 10-7 finish and a home playoff game as a compelling case for another award.
The Falcons still have work to do at 3-4, but their victory over San Francisco provided encouraging evidence of their potential.
If Stefanski can maintain the offensive progress and guide Atlanta into the playoffs, Solak’s thought could become a reality.

title: The Case For The Ravens Being NFL Trade Deadline Sellers. And Who Should Go ASAP
full_text:
The Baltimore Ravens might be three weeks away from truly pivoting to playing their youngsters and embracing the fact that the alleged Super Bowl contender carried 20 percent of its roster with rookies to open the season in the first place.
If they lose to the Bills and Jaguars in the span of a few days, and if their second-half defense continues to be historically suspect, and if their novice coaches continue to looks horribly overmatched after halftime ( they should have hired them help ), and if Jesse Minter keeps wondering why his $370M roster can’t display any heart and leadership, then it just might be that this team is a mere extension of last year's disaster, and that general manager Eric DeCosta is one of the biggest frauds in the NFL, and that Baltimore is doomed again.
This might just be a bloated, complacent roster that is the handiwork of an entitled, stubborn, egomaniacal fake smart guy (just like Mike Elias), who skirts accountability and blames others and curries favor with checked-out billionaires. Meantime John Harbaugh and Todd Monken – the men allegedly holding back DeCosta’s treasure trove of talent – compete for NFL Coach of the Year honors elsewhere.
DeCosta tends to put own self-interest ahead of the team, wanting “his guys” to make him look good for rewarding them with unnecessarily rich extensions while primo young talent leaves the building (which is why the baby-faced coach is forced to start guys, who are replacement-level talent, at best, making top-10 money at their positions).
But imagine if the Ravens had an honest broker running the team. Someone clear-eyed – not a politician obsessed with his media clippings who is constantly working to hone that image – who could see this Frankenstein roster for what it is. What would they do? Well, as longtime NFL GM Marty Hurney suggested on “The Daily Flock” several times this year and again this week, this was always going to be the final year in Baltimore for a legion of starters and key reserves, and this organization might need to shift into player-development mode soon.
“At some point if things still have not gotten right, I do think you have to make that switch and start playing more of the young guys,” Hurney told me, “and try to make that transition. Because I think that every team hits it and the Ravens do a really good job, as good as anybody of really turning it over and not having the ‘window; philosophy, because they've always drafted well and had a lot of draft choices. But right now, you kind of feel like this is a time where the young guys need to step up and it feels like there's a little bit of a transition taking place in Baltimore."
Indeed, so, wouldn’t it make sense to load up on draft picks – even very low draft picks because these are more salary dumps than football trades (again, blame DeCosta and blame a half-interested owner for not rebuilding his decaying front office when he fired Harbaugh). Getting DeCosta-ed 17 times since this guy was handed the reigns from Ozzie Newsome is a sign that even Lamar Jackson can’t overcome this mess, isn’t it?
There are some moves they could make to buy on the fringes ... but DeCosta may have created more problems already with a desperate deal for Cam Jurgens . Not sure he should be trusted to add more.
DeCosta is beyond a failure when it comes to extending his QBs contract like any half-assed GM would. So Jackson can decide if he wants to go to Miami, or whatever, and DeCosta knows it, which explains why he acted like a fool at his pre-season press conference when pressed on this topic.
But if Jackson doesn’t want to take their money, he doesn’t have to, and with an $85M cap hit the Ravens would have to move him. So there’s that. Then consider that it’s painfully obvious that Ronnie Stanley, Mark Andrews, Derrick Henry, Roquan Smith, Marlon Humphrey, Rashod Bateman and Calais Campbell are at the end here (and would be if this team had a real GM in charge). And that of their young players on rookie deals, only Tavius Robinson (on season-ending IR) and Trent Simpson would be making a case for an extension.
That’s bleak folks. But that’s DeCosta, who would rather give Humphrey the 10th most money of any corner in the NFL, than admit he did another stupid contract structure and acknowledge his obvious decline  just pay him $4M to leave.
And in terms of blue chip players on a contract extension, there’s Kyle Hamilton and Zay Flowers and Nnamdi Madubuike and that’s it. Not much.
But their culture is clearly warped - DeCosta is at the core of that - and it’s not getting better and I’d be perfectly fine with taking whatever you can get for Smith and Andrews and Bateman and Humphrey right now and embracing a future without them. Move Simpson to Smith’s spot, or Teddye Buchanan, give TJ Tampa a run for Humphrey, and they drafted two tight ends who are already better than Andrews.
Now, let's be real - no one wants those veterans. No one would give DeCosta anything for Andrews after the 2024 season and he insisted in paying him again, anyway. Oh, and the real problem is his drafts have stunk too, so the next man up at these positions could be perilous.
Sending a message to the locker room and starting to position for the future isn’t crazy. If those guys can’t lead – and Minter says he’s desperately searching for leaders – then empower your youth. I don’t think the drop-off would be significant in most cases (maybe not even going from Stanley to Carson Vinson)
They're going to need to convince Jackson why he should stay, and almost none of those veterans will be back here in 2027, whether the QB is or not.

title: Ravens Thursday Injury Report Includes Major News For Lamar Jackson
full_text:
The Ravens have been coy in their handling of Lamar Jackson’s ankle injury for a month now.
Since the two-time MVP suffered the injury on a sack from behind at the end of the first half in Week 4, Baltimore’s offense has fallen onto a major funk, and rookie head coach Jesse Minter has walked a verbal minefield about conveying some semblance of the extent of the injury to his paying customers – through the media – but also needing to respect the player’s reputation and make it clear this is a significant setback for him to navigate that.
Ravens public relations has a poor reputation in such matters, throwing a novice head coach into the mix has only exacerbated the messaging issues, and Minter would barely saying anything on Wednesday about his quarterback other than the team would be issuing an injury report – as mandated by the NFL – and Jackson would be listed on it in some capacity. Lesson learned, it seems (be careful who you take counsel from in The Castle, rook; they’ll hide and cower and let you take the fall).
Turns out Jackson practiced in full on Wednesday , the first time he did so since before facing the Titans on Oct. 4, and he did the same on Thursday. The longer this situation played out – it was obvious he was going to miss at least two games from the onset – it became clear that Jackson was going to have to get through a full week of full practices before being activated to return to play. He is checking those boxes now.
Kyle Hamilton, the Ravens best defensive player, returned to practice Thursday as did rookie guard Vega Ioane, who just suffered a knee inury that some reported would be multiple weeks (Minter did not close the door on him playing Sunday) and middle linebcker Roquan Smith was back on the field, too, as all did not take part in any capacity Wednesday.
Should Jackson practice fully on Friday – it’s a limited workday and barring some totally unforeseen circumstance that will be the case – it’s fair to expect he will have no injury designation on Friday’s injury report. He was ruled out on Friday on each of the first two weeks after his injury – which Jackson has described as a “very, very painful” high-ankle sprain. Last week he was listed as questionable and then the team announced on Saturday afternoon that he had been downgraded to out (which raised anew questions about their public handling of this situation all along).
While Ravens rookie offensive coordinator Declan Doyle was being hailed as a “genius” all summer, he was quick to point out himself on Thursday he is only seven games into calling plays and is trying to adjust his processes with one of the worst second-half offenses in the NFL. Jackson is the genius, he covers up the warts on a roster that is 7-14 without him, while wins 70% of the regular-season games he starts. And if this offense rebounds, it’s because the best player in the league returned (and if it doesn’t out late-summer prediction that Doyle is going to end up calling plays from the sidelines and trying to connect better with his players is going to look sage ).
How much Doyle is willing to lean into Jackson’s legs to boost a moribund run game will be telling; he’s already riding Derrick Henry at an historic rate for any age 32 RB in NFL history , with diminishing returns. The ability to generate explosive plays will be back – Jackson leads the NFL at 10.1 yards/attempts (no one else is above 8.8) – as backup Snoop Huntley doesn’t average even six yards per pass in his NFL career.
Henry has averaged just 3.4 yards per rush the last four weeks (35th in the NFL). Getting rookie “Joker” Adam Randall (a hybrid RB/TE/H-Back/WR ), off Injured Reserve could add wrinkled for Doyle, too. Something has to change in a major way for Baltimore in the second half and this young staff better figure it out quickly. Consider that without Jackson the Ravens have fallen to 31st in second-half scoring, dead-last in third-down conversions in that half and 29th in three-and-out percentage.
Also consider how it came to pass again that Ravens struggling general manager Eric DeCosta (better do something at the deadline, hoss )  let Jackson enter a potential walk season without a contract extension after the QB had to dangle on a non-exclusive franchise tag and demand a trade to get a fair-market deal after his rookie deal expired, which Baltimore made him play out.
The Miami Dolphins badly need a quarterback and a superstar to market the team around and an identity and they are loaded with draft capital. I’m just sayin .

title: Is Ravens GM Eric DeCosta At The Core Of Their Losing Ways? Longtime Coordinator Wink Martindale Thinks So
full_text:
There’s a reason so many Ravens defensive stars from the past took to social media in the aftermath of Baltimore’s pathetic second half Sunday, allowing 35 unanswered points to the Bengals and looking like quitters in the process.
Guys like Ed Reed and Terrell Suggs seemed appalled by it all , the franchise DeCosta-ed for the 17th time since 2019 (blowing a double-digit lead in the second half in a loss), and the one constant during this entire uninspired brand of Ravens football is the general manager, Eric DeCosta, who curries favor with the billionaire boss and divides the organization and plays favorites in the locker room and creates a culture that continually produces spineless results.
Yet that billionaire chose to empower him even more than ever before when he fired John Harbaugh (needed to fire them both ), and with an overmatched novice head coach on board they keep hitting new lows. Rookie coach Jesse Minter is stuck with a legion of bad contracts DeCosta handed out all over that defense, and while there are some schematic changes he is going to have to make (as we discussed with longtime head coach Marvin Lewis here ), he’s also going have a hard time altering the psyche and heart of a football team poisoned by the guy who controls the salaries.
Longtime former Ravens defensive coordinator Wink Martindale, who has known Minter forever and was invited to Ravens practices this offseason and whom Minter helped create the defensive packages that make the hub of this 2026 Ravens defense, is aghast at what’s going on in Baltimore. He knows the role that DeCosta has played in this mess better than most, and kept it real with me on “The Daily Flock” this week.
“This isn't good enough,” Martindale said. “This is not the standard. This is not Baltimore defense.  And you know, I was there first, you know, in 2012 when we won the Super Bowl with Ray Lewis. You think Ray Lewis would put up with that [crap]? You think Ed Reed would put up with that [crap)? You think (Terrell) Suggs would put up with that [crap]? You think Haloti Ngata would put up with that [crap]? …
“You can still hold people accountable and you can still say, ‘This guy's better than this guy because of this this and this. And this guy's got to play, not because of what they get paid, you know, (but because they deserve it). They got a left tackle that's been paid a [crap] ton of money who needs to step up and be a leader, you know, with Ronnie (Stanley). And I love Ronnie, and these guys I’m talking about.
“They’re good people, but God damn it, we want to win in Baltimore. And that's where I was at the longest in my career ever in coaching. I was there for 10 years. So, like my kids who were born in Ohio think they're from Maryland because that's the longest we were in place …  And I just think that they need to step up and say, ‘Here's who we're going to be."’ Yeah. And if they don't, they're going to continue to do the [crap] they're doing.”
Martindale believes $19M corner Marlon Humphrey probably needs to move to safety or just play considerably less, though the team is short of corners despite it being one of DeCosta’s primary fetishes. He wouldn’t play overpaid $30M pass rusher Trey Hendrickson on early downs as much as Baltimore is (but DeCosta demands it with that salary!). Wink believes Minter needs to start blitzing more even though it runs counter to some of his core philosophies. (DeCosta better explore some of these cheap trade deadline options , ASAP)
He gives deep explanations for such on the show. The biggest reason for the organizations falloff, he believes is the move from longtime general manager Ozzie Newsome to DeCosta. And like so many around the NFL know, DeCosta built a reputation and career off of Newsome’s accomplishments, used it to get promoted repeatedly and ingratiated himself incredibly well with Steve Bisciotti back when he was still a minority owner in the team.
“I think the biggest impact was when it went from Ozzie to Eric,” Martindale said, noting DeCosta likes to hang on the sidelines and in the locker room and fraternize with certain players in a way Newsome never considered. And I know what (Owner) Mr. Steve Bisciotti wanted to do with Eric, but I also think it's time to for Eric to step up and win a Super Bowl because, you know, Ozzie’s last draft class (2018, when he selected Lamar Jackson) you can look at his last pick – it was (defensive lineman) Zach Sieler, who’s had three contracts down at Miami now.
“And I know their (scouting and evaluation) system and I would do the same system that they have there. But there's also times where you’ve got to come to dinner and say here's what it is, and not just keep patting yourself on the back because you get an A++ in every draft (from the media).”
Truthbombs. The show is loaded with them. Not everybody can stomach frauds.
