title: Here’s Why Packers WR Christian Watson Returned from Broken Rib
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – Green Bay Packers receiver Christian Watson had just made a 53-yard catch to put his team in position to take the lead on Thursday night against the Carolina Panthers.
There was one problem as he laid on the ground. He couldn’t breathe. Watson laid motionless on the grass at Lambeau Field, not knowing what had happened to him.
“I think I just came down on the ball or my elbow or something,” Watson said. “I couldn’t breathe on the field. I got the wind knocked out of me. I got back to the sideline and I was kind of spitting up some blood or something like that.”
Watson revealed that he had a broken rib that presumably was going to knock him out of the rest of the game. Watson was taken to a hospital for precautionary reasons, despite his objections.
“So, the doctor said I had to go get a CT. I was trying to beg them to not make me do that, but it is what it is,” Watson said. “Thankfully, I was able to get the CT, everything looked good. I got a rib, that’s all. The major stuff was all good. No internal bleeding or anything like that, so I was able to get back out there. That was an experience, for sure.”
Football is a game in which violence is glorified. Players run into each other for a living. Playing with pain is an expectation.
That’s especially true in the Watson family, where all three men have played at the professional level. Watson grew up with an older brother and father who would chide him into getting up as soon as he was laying on the field. That was a rule in the Watson household. Playing through pain once you’re standing? That’s the expectation, as well.
“We would always kind of chirp at each other if you know anyone was laying on the ground too long,” Watson said. “We just always had the mentality to get up, anyway. So, yeah, if you can get up, you have to get up.”
With Watson headed to the hospital, the assumption was that he would miss the rest of the game, considering the situation was similar to the one that he faced last year in Denver. Ultimately, Watson injured his shoulder and did not miss any time last year.
One hour after being unable to breathe, Watson returned to Lambeau Field in a scene that was straight out of WWE. The only thing missing was entry music for The Undertaker with the way Watson re-entered the game.
“Yeah, it was pretty remarkable,” coach Matt LaFleur said. “He was coughing up blood, and so they took him for precautionary reasons and had to check him out. Obviously, he cleared that, and the grit to go back in the game, he had a heck of a night. I can’t imagine what he would have had (statistically) had he not missed so much time.”
Watson’s night was off to an excellent start when he left the game. In about 21 minutes, he had eclipsed 100 receiving yards and was asserting himself as the best player on the field, his fumble notwithstanding.
When he returned to the stadium, the Packers were leading 27-10. Why did he return to the field?
Simply put, that’s the expectation.
“Honestly, I feel like before I even left, I wanted to get back out there,” he said. “This means everything to me, to be out there on the football field. Like I said, I’ve had injuries that I was not able to go back out on the field after for, and I missed a significant amount of time with injuries.
“So, any chance I get to go out there on the football field, I’m going to be out there on the football field. everyone’s hurting somewhere. Everybody is feeling something. Just got to fight through it and keep on going.”
Watson finished the night with eight catches for 113 yards. His final catch was a big third-and-2 conversion in the fourth quarter.
Watson had rotten injury luck earlier in his career with soft-tissue injuries along with the ACL injury he suffered in the season finale of 2024. The question with Watson has never been ability, but whether his body would allow him to showcase his obvious talent.
Through eight games, Watson is well on pace to shatter his career highs in receptions, yards and touchdowns. According to the team, he is the first Packers player with 40-plus catches, 700-plus receiving yards, six-plus receiving touchdown and an average of at least 16.5 yards per catch in the first eight games since Jordy Nelson in 2013.
He is Green Bay’s best receiver on the field, but also sets the standard off of it.
His football character is sky high. His teammates rave about him. He’s blossomed into a leader of his position group.
When the game ended, his teammates were both in awe, but not surprised that Watson returned to the lineup in order to play through pain.
“I think it’s incredible. I think it shows resiliency, I think it shows toughness and I think it just shows the love that he has for this team,” safety Xavier McKinney said. “Sometimes, you might see that happen and he had his 100 yards and he could’ve just sat it.
“But the fact that he wasn’t satisfied and the fact that he felt like and he knew that we still needed him out there and he still said, OK, I love this team and I want to be able to go out here for this team and do that, that gains our respect. We respect him for that and sh**, we love him for that, we appreciate him for that.”
What about his quarterback? What did Jordan Love think about his top receiver returning to the lineup?
“That just speaks and is a testament to who he is and what type of player he is,” Love said after the game. “But not only that, what kind of will he has because, man, that’s crazy. A lot of people would never, especially a receiver, but for him to come in and keep playing and then still make plays, I mean that’s huge.”

title: Packers’ Josh Jacobs Clarifies Viral Touchdown Celebration vs. Panthers
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – After the first of two touchdowns against the Panthers on Thursday night, Green Bay Packers running back reacted with what seemed like a provocative celebration in which his hands were behind his back.
The Amazon Prime Video cameras didn’t show the “whole celebration,” Jacobs said after the game.
Packers RB Josh Jacobs, who was arrested on misdemeanor battery in May, pretended that he was being handcuffed after his touchdown run. (🎥: Amazon Prime Video) pic.twitter.com/kUJEnLsXpM
“Sh**, it was f***ing 1 second that they just showed me,” Jacobs said after a 27-19 victory in his second game back with the team after spending six weeks on the exempt list for an incident with a woman.
“But, anyways, me and Savion (Williams) came up with a celebration – if they would’ve seen the whole celebration. Basically, last week, we said the first celebration when I score, I was going to thank God; that’s what I did last week. The second one was going to be “ Break Every Chain .” It’s a gospel song, that was going to be the next celebration. It’s just a correlation, but like I said, the media [is] going to run with it. They’re going to make it something that it wasn’t, but it is what it is.”
The cameras only showed Jacobs with his hands behind his back as if he’d just been handcuffed.
“That wasn’t the whole celebration. It was more to it than that,” Jacobs said. “They stopped showing the celebration after that. So, like I said, it is what it is.”
Jacobs has not saved the running game . It was the worst in the league without him and it’s been the worst in the league with him.
Against a Carolina defense that entered Week 8 ranked last in the NFL in rushing yards allowed per game and per carry, Green Bay’s abysmal running game managed just 66 yards on 26 carries – a feeble 2.5-yard average.
Williams had a game-high 18-yard run. Otherwise, Jacobs mustered just 39 yards on 21 carries – a woeful 1.9-yard average – with a long run of 6.
“I felt pretty good with what I could do,” Jacobs said. “I tried to make the plays when they was there. It wasn't a lot out there, but I tried to make the plays when they was there.”
He made a couple of key plays. On third-and-goal at the 1 midway through the second quarter, he used a jump cut to get him into space for an easy touchdown run that put the Packers ahead to stay at 13-10.
Then, midway through the third quarter, the Packers faced a third-and-1 at the 4. Jacobs was wide open for an easy touchdown catch from Jordan Love.
Jordan Love (17) to Josh Jacobs (3) Green Bay Packers 4 yards pic.twitter.com/e68Q3B4c1J
Those touchdowns were part of the Packers going a season-best 3-of-3 in the red zone.
“Just the dynamic player that he is in the pass game and the run game, it’s amazing to have him back out there,” Love said. “It’s two games in for him – he missed a lot of games – so he’s going to keep getting rolling.
“We talk about it, you look at the stats, our run game isn’t where it needs to be, but he had two touchdowns tonight. Just looking at that, that’s what he’s capable of and that’s what he helps bring to the offense. We’ll keep leaning on him, keep finding ways to get him the rock, but he’s a dynamic player. He does it in the pass and the run game. So, it’s great to have him back.”
The hope is Jacobs will get better as he gets into a groove and the line will get better once it gels. It’s possible the guard combo the Packers rolled out on Thursday for the first time, with Aaron Banks back in the lineup at left guard and Laken Tomlinson flipping to right guard, will have some staying power to help get things cranked up.
“It’s a lot of turnover,” Jacobs said. “Obviously, we got a lot of injuries in that (OL) room, so it’s a lot of guys trying to get a feel for each other. But I just try to make the plays when they’re there and then, when they’re not there, still try to create and get the most out of every play.
“But definitely when they’re there, I just try to make the play and it’s just something I feel like as a unit we got to be better at, just more intentional with, straining a little longer, me running a little harder. All those things correlate.”
For Jacobs, it was his first home game since the incident over Memorial Day, which wrapped up legally with him pleading no contest to misdemeanor battery and criminal damage to property. Officially, the league says the investigation is ongoing, though the reality is the league shut it down weeks ago other than waiting to see if it will get access to video of the incident.
While there are fans who no longer want Jacobs on the roster, the reaction during introductions was mostly positive.
“It was good, man. I think it was good,” Jacobs said. “I think it was good for the team. It was good to be out there – Thursday night, electric, stadium packed. As an offense, we had our little lull moments but the defense held it down in this game.”
Asked what it meant personally, Jacobs mostly focused on the Packers winning the game and improving to 5-3.
“Oh, yeah, definitely a lot, man,” he said. “Being able to go out there and make some plays, still a lot to clean up, still a lot to work on, but it’s still positive. We’ll never apologize for winning.”

title: Packers Winners and Losers: Christian Watson Goes From Ambulance to Starring vs. Panthers
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The Green Bay Packers needed to bounce back against the Carolina Panthers after Sunday’s loss to the Detroit Lions. A win would keep them within striking distance in the NFC North. A loss would put them at risk of falling four games behind the Minnesota Vikings in the loss column.
As has become the norm for this year’s version of the Packers, sloppy football followed. They lost two fumbles and missed an extra point in the first half alone. Jordan Love’s red-hot start, however, allowed the Packers to take a 10-point lead into halftime.
The second half started with Jordan Love throwing a touchdown pass to Josh Jacobs to give the Packers a 27-10 lead that despite some of their best efforts, they would not relinquish.
He was excellent most of the night, and leads off our weekly list of winners and losers.
How good was Jordan Love in the first half? Well, he started 17-of-20 passing. All three of his incompletions were on dropped passes by Matthew Golden and Christian Watson. Maybe you could argue Watson’s drop was a pass breakup, but the point stands. He was dealing in the first half. That performance comes behind a bad offensive line and a run game that cannot find any traction no matter the opponent.
The Packers know better than anybody what can happen when asking a quarterback to carry the entire ship.
Usually, that ship sinks because quarterbacks, like everyone else, are human. The evidence came in the second half as Love threw an interception on the second play of the fourth quarter to give the Panthers some life.
Matthew Golden on 2nd down: Drops a TD Matthew Golden on 3rd down: Catches a TD. Jordan Love didn't hesitate going back to him. 💯 pic.twitter.com/eJwpUEg1kB
Apart from that critical mistake, the second half was much of the same for Green Bay’s offense. Love continued to dice apart a Panthers defense that was missing some of its stars. The first drive of the second half finished with a four-yard touchdown pass to Josh Jacobs to give the Packers a 27-10 lead.
Love finished the night 281 yards on 40 pass attempts, three touchdowns and one interception. The entire offense, as it has for most of the season, fell on him.
He looked like he was in total control of the offense most of the night. Nothing seems to faze him, no matter what happens during the game.
Yes, they were playing a Carolina defense that was decimated, but those are the teams that great quarterbacks light up.
Love lit up the Panthers in prime time and was the single biggest reason his team got to 5-3.
In what looked straight out of a WWE script, Christian Watson left the game in an ambulance in the first half, and returned with just over four minutes to play in the third quarter.
Yes, you read that right. Watson laid motionless on the Lambeau Field grass after catching a 53-yard bomb and you could hear a pin drop in the stadium.
Christian Watson is back!! 🚨 What a moment. (via @packers ) pic.twitter.com/xOv1db19bQ
As everyone feared the worst, Watson had to leave the stadium in an ambulance for precautionary testing.
The official announcement was a chest injury, and it felt like a near certainty he’d miss the rest of the game if not more.
Instead, Watson returned to the game in the third quarter. Playing hurt in the NFL is an expectation, not an exception. Still, the toughness is admirable.
Oh, and on the field before he left the game, he was the Packers’ best receiver. He’d caught six passes for 100 yards before leaving the game in an ambulance.
His final catch of the game also helped the Packers pick up a critical first down to essentially run out the clock and avoid disaster. Watson is someone held in high regard by his teammates, and Thursday's game was a big reason why.
In a season full of next men up, Ty’Ron Hopper became the latest one last week after a freak injury to Zaire Franklin came to light in practice. Hopper replaced him and played solid in his debut as the Packers’ new linebacker next to Isaiah McDuffie.
Hopper had a huge first half against Carolina. On the second series of the game, Hopper was sent on a pressure and decked Bryce Young on a vicious hit that forced an incompletion and a punt.
Later in the game he was locked up in coverage on Chuba Hubbard before forcing an incompletion as Young threw the ball down the field. His biggest play was a case of being in the right place at the right time.
Lukas Van Ness batted a pass from Bryce Young into the air that fell into the waiting arms of Hopper with the Packers leading 13-10 in the second quarter.
He added a sack in the second half by chasing down Bryce Young.
Hopper is going to need to play well for the team with Edgerrin Cooper out for the season and Franklin having an unclear return date.
If he keeps making the plays he made in the first half on Thursday, the Packers may keep him on the field when Franklin returns.
Through the first month of Zeitler’s tenure in Green Bay, it made sense that Zeitler would not be ready to play due to sitting on the couch for most of the offseason.
The sense of that decision ended on Sunday in Detroit. It made less sense on Thursday against the Carolina Panthers.
Travis Glover, the person who has been starting at right guard since Zeitler signed in Green Bay, was inactive with a knee injury.
It felt like Zeitler was set to make his debut as the starting right guard. That was not to be. Aaron Banks was active, and took his place at left guard.
The starting right guard was someone who had 13,920 fewer snaps than him at right guard. Those snaps all came in 2026. Laken Tomlinson took the starting role.
Zeitler was paid real money to save Green Bay’s offensive line after a disastrous performance at the end of September against Atlanta.
He was likely under the impression he was going to play when he was ready. Zeitler has said he’s ready to play, but remains on the bench.
Nobody can seem to figure out why.
The Packers lost their one free possession of the game. How? Their new kickoff returner, Coleman Owen was hit by Jackson Kuwatch of Carolina, forcing a fumble.
Owen’s snap was his first as a kick returner. He had been returning punts and was signed to the active roster thanks to the high ankle sprain for Skyy Moore, who remains on injured reserve.
He replaced J. Michael Sturdivant in that role, who had been solid if unspectacular in Moore’s absence.
The Packers’ defense would hold the Panthers to a field goal attempt when a third down sack from Devonte Wyatt ended the Panthers’ opening series.
It’s difficult to generate explosive returns as a kickoff returner, so ball security has to be a priority.
At some point, questions need to start getting asked. Trey Smack was given virtually no competition this offseason, and quieted some questions with a perfect preseason.
Smack came into play Thursday with five missed kicks in the last three games. Last week, he cost the Packers six points in a game they lost by three.
His first attempt to kick on Thursday he hit the left upright. He followed that up by kicking the ball into the end zone, gift wrapping the Panthers great field position for the ensuing possession that ended in a touchdown.
If there were any example of how bad things have gotten for Smack, Matt LaFleur bypassed a 53-yard field goal that would have given the Packers an insurmountable lead to have Daniel Whelan pooch punt with 30 seconds left in the game. He does not trust his kicker.
Smack currently leads the league in missed kicks with eight. Five field goals and three extra points. For those that are good at math, that’s 18 points that have been left on the field this season.
The next time the Packers play, the calendar will have flipped to November. That means that the games are getting more important. The more important the game, the smaller the margin for error.
The Packers cannot afford to have their kicker lighting points on fire.
If it’s not going to happen against the Dallas Cowboys or Carolina Panthers, it’s probably not going to happen at all…

title: Christian Watson Returns from Hospital, Packers Beat Panthers
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – With 9 minutes left in the second quarter on Thursday night, Christian Watson caught one of those majestic deep passes from Jordan Love. It was a beautiful throw and a beautiful catch.
And a violent ending as Watson and cornerback Will Lee IV tumbled to the turf, with Lee falling on Watson. Both players stayed on the turf for a couple minutes before Watson – in full uniform – stepped into an ambulance to go to a hospital for testing.
The Green Bay Packers trailed the Carolina Panthers 10-6 at the time. Less than 20 minutes of game time later, with the Packers leading 27-10, Watson jogged through the stadium, ran out of the tunnel and joined his teammates on the sideline. After Carolina capped its drive with a field goal, Watson was back in the game. He was targeted on his first play back in the game and caught a short pass later in the series.
Highlighted by Love’s early destruction of the Panthers’ depleted defense, Watson’s remarkable return to the lineup and the World Series champion Milwaukee Brewers soaking up the cheers and doing Lambeau Leaps during a TV timeout, Green Bay overcame a sloppy start to beat the Panthers 27-19 on Thursday night at Lambeau Field.
The Packers have won four of their last five games to improve to 5-3. The Panthers, who started the night leading the NFC South, fell to 3-4.
The Packers took a 27-10 midway through the third quarter. Along with the theatrics of Watson’s return, a blowout win seemed like a formality.
But nothing is ever for these Packers.
Trailing 27-13 and facing a fourth-and-3 with about five-and-a-half minutes left, Bryce Young hit Jalen Coker over the middle, and he dodged a couple would-be tacklers for a 26-yard touchdown. Carolina went for two but Isaiah McDuffie broke up Young’s pass, keeping the score 27-19.
The Packers then had a horrendous three-and-out. A 21-yard screen to Tucker Kraft was wiped out by an ineligible-man-downfield penalty and Love was flagged for intentional grounding on third-and-10 following a wayward shotgun snap by John Williams.
After the punt, Carolina started at its 45 with 4:35 to go. But Green Bay’s defense wouldn’t budge. Devonte Wyatt’s tackle for loss on first down set the stage for Young’s incompletion on fourth-and-5. Defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon sent six and the Panthers picked it up, but Young’s pass to Tetairoa McMillan was short of its destination.
The Packers entered the game with the worst rush offense in the NFL. The Panthers had the worst rush defense. Carolina won the matchup decisively, but it all came down to the end and whether Green Bay could run out the clock.
Jacobs gained 8 yards on two tries, setting up third-and-2 with 2:33 to go. With the game on the line, Love connected with Watson over the middle for 7 yards and the pivotal first down.
Green Bay needed one more first down to officially put the game away, but Jacobs was buried for minus-3 on first down, with the clock winding down to the 2-minute warning. His second-down run got stuffed. His third-down run was lucky to gain one. So, with 29 seconds left, coach Matt LaFleur sent out the punt team.
Dani Dennis-Sutton’s sack essentially ended the game.
Even while losing Christian Watson to a chest injury and two early fumbles, the Packers led the Panthers 20-10 at halftime.
Jordan Love was on fire against a Panthers defense playing without their two starting cornerbacks, a fill-in starting cornerback and their top pass rusher. Love ended the half 18-of-24 passing for 192 yards and two touchdowns. Two of the incompletions were drops by Matthew Golden.
Golden made amends for the second. After dropping a 24-yard touchdown pass in the right corner of the end zone, he caught a 24-yard touchdown pass to the left on the next play. That gave Green Bay its 10-point halftime lead – a remarkable feat considering Coleman Owen fumbled the opening kickoff return, Watson fumbled later, Trey Smack missed an extra point and Josh Jacobs had 14 rushing yards on 10 carries against the worst run defense in the NFL.
Carolina got the ball to start the second half and drove out to midfield. Coach Dave Canales went for it on fourth-and-2 but rookie defensive tackle Chris McClellan stuffed running back Chuba Hubbard for a turnover on downs.
The Packers wasted no time in scoring what seemed like the clinching touchdown. Jacobs got the ball six times on the drive, including a 4-yard scoring pass from Jordan Love. The play, which gave the Packers a 27-10 lead, pushed Jacobs over 10,000 scrimmage yards in his career.
Carolina won the toss and deferred. The Packers had been going with Bo Melton and J. Michael Sturdivant on kickoff returns. This time, it was Melton and Coleman Owen. Owen did a nice job fielding the bouncing kick but got blasted by linebacker Jackson Kuwatch. Owen fumbled and the Panthers recovered at Green Bay’s 29.
The defense did well to limit the damage to a field goal. After giving up one first down, Lukas Van Ness set the edge on a first-down run, Ty’Ron Hopper had great coverage on a second-down checkdown and Van Ness and Barryn Sorrell corralled Bryce Young in the pocket so Devonte Wyatt could get the sack.
After an exchange of punts, the Packers took advantage of good field position to score the go-ahead touchdown. On third-and-8, Jordan Love ripped a post to Christian Watson for a gain of 24. Then, on third-and-8, Tucker Kraft got open on a post against safety Nick Scott for a 12-yard touchdown.
Trey Smack’s extra point hit the left upright, and the rookie heard the boos as he walked off the field.
Smack’s kickoff was a touchback, giving the ball to Carolina at the 35. Bryce Young hit tight end Tommy Tremble for 19 on third-and-3 (17 yards after the catch) and Chuba Hubbrd for 11 on third-and-10 (16 yards after the catch with two missed tackles) to get the ball into scoring position.
Brewers in the house and doing Lambeau Leaps. pic.twitter.com/hZ7Eiqydkk
With the Brewers being celebrated between quarters, the crowd was going nuts on second-and-goal at the 1. Hubbard silenced them immediately with a touchdown.
Green Bay had a drive going on its ensuing possession but Watson fumbled after a third-down catch. The defense, once again, did the job. Brenton Cox and Karl Brooks had pressures to force a three-and-out punt.
The Packers then drove 90 yards for the go-ahead touchdown. The big play – and the costly play – was a 53-yard bomb to Christian Watson. It was a perfect throw and excellent catch, but Panthers cornerback Will Lee IV fell on Watson at the end of the play. Both players stayed on the turf for a couple minutes before Watson walked off the field, into the blue medical tent and then the locker room.
On the next play, Savion Williams gained 18 on an end-around; Tucker Kraft and Anthony Belton had big blocks. Finally, on third-and-goal at the 1, Josh Jacobs used a wicked jump cut to find space for an easy touchdown. The crowd roared, then roared even louder when Trey Smack made the kick to give Green Bay a 13-10 lead.
Watson had 100 receiving yards in about 21 minutes before the injury.

title: Packers WR Christian Watson Hospitalized for ‘Precautionary’ Testing
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – Green Bay Packers receiver Christian Watson was taken to a local hospital for “precautionary testing” following a chest injury sustained in the second quarter against Carolina.
Watson made a 53-yard catch midway through the second quarter. Rookie cornerback Will Lee IV, who gave up the catch, fell on Watson at the end of the play.
Jordan Love dropped a moon ball in the bucket for Christian Watson, but Watson and #Panthers CB Will Lee were down and injured after the play. Both players are now in the locker room. (📽️ @NFLonPrime ) https://t.co/txSDGTN8PY pic.twitter.com/a78ATh8Oi2
Both players were shaken up; Watson stayed on the turf for a couple minutes before walking to the blue medical tent. After a few minutes inside the tent, he walked to the locker room and then walked into the back of an ambulance.
Video of #Packers WR Christian Watson getting into the ambulance to be taken to the hospital: pic.twitter.com/15ggu6GXak https://t.co/ukOaj2TZvY
The same thing happened at Denver last season; he played the next week.
Watson had six catches for 100 yards in less than a quarter-and-a-half of action. He did fumble once, though the defense prevented the Panthers from scoring any points.
Watson entered the game tied for 17th in the league with 34 receptions but seventh with 595 yards, second with 17.5 yards per catch and tied for second with six touchdowns. Along with Thursday’s production, he has 40 catches for 695 yards and six touchdowns in eight games. That’s a 17-game trajectory of 76 receptions for 1,477 yards and 13 touchdowns.
“It definitely motivates me to keep going,” he said recently of a blistering pace to start the season. “But I mean, I'm just trying to continue to be the best version of myself, and I want to look back at the end of the season and be able to have those same comparisons rather than looking at it during the season.”
Before Thursday night’s game, Watson had played 17 games since the ACL injury that ended his 2024 season. He caught 69 passes for 1,206 yards and 12 touchdowns during that span.
“I’d probably say the toughest is those first couple days after surgery,” he said of his comeback. “Just the amount of pain that you're in, dealing with the uncomfortableness of it. But I mean, yeah, probably like just like a month or two into it when you can't really do anything. You're kind of doing the same basic things every day, and it doesn't really seem like there's that much progress.
“And honestly, I'd say another one of the toughest parts of it is when you're getting down to the wire. You're getting like month six or seven where you feel like you should be able to do a lot more, and there's still that last hump you have to get over. And it seems like it's, I don't want to say out of reach, but it seems like, ‘Two months isn't that long of a time. I should be able to do more,’ but it's kind of just trust in the process, and you get to that point eventually.”
Without Watson against Carolina, the Packers were down to Matthew Golden, Savion Williams, Bo Melton, J. Michael Sturdivan and Coleman Owen as the receivers.
Despite a couple late incompletions, Jordan Love ended the first half 18-of-24 passing for 189 yards and two touchdowns, one apiece to Golden and tight end Tucker Kraft.
The Packers took a 20-10 lead into the break.

title: Packers Makes Most Unexpected Change Imaginable on Offensive Line vs. Panthers
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The best offensive lines are the lines that practice together and play together.
Well, so much for that for the Green Bay Packers.
On Thursday night against the Carolina Panthers, their eighth game of the season, they will roll out a sixth different starting combination this year that will include an 11th starter.
With center Sean Rhyan inactive with an ankle injury and right guard Travis Glover inactive with a knee injury, the Packers based on pregame warmups will roll with John Williams at center, Aaron Banks at left guard and, in a surprise, Laken Tomlinson moving from left guard to right guard. They will join Jordan Morgan, the pillar of the line at left tackle, and Anthony Belton, who will be making his sixth start at right tackle.
The Packers entered Week 8 having used a league-high 10 individual starters, one more than the Ravens, Patriots, Chargers and Eagles. Now, Williams, they’re up to an absurd total of 11.
Laken Tomlinson at right guard, Aaron Banks at left guard. pic.twitter.com/TLbDRRmJBU
The Packers lost to the Lions last week, but it had nothing to do with losing the top centers, Sean Rhyan and Jacob Monk, after one series.
That’s because John Williams rode to the rescue in the first snaps from scrimmage in his NFL career.
“That was one of the cooler things I’ve seen in a really long time,” offensive coordinator Adam Stenavich said on Wednesday. “Obviously, when Sean and Monk both went down after the first drive, I was extremely concerned with just us being able to operate, especially on the road, and against that defensive line. What he did, it wasn’t perfect, but he did a great job. So, I can’t say enough about how he stepped up for the team.”
His work against the Lions put him in position to make his first career start at a relatively foreign position.
Williams played left tackle in addition to being an aerospace engineering major at Cincinnati. The Packers drafted him in the seventh round last year but he spent his entire rookie season on injured reserve with a back injury. From the moment he was drafted, his only practice time last year was the final three weeks of the regular season after being designated for return.
Williams spent the offseason practices and start of training camp playing center before being moved out to left tackle for the entire preseason.
“It was kind of out of necessity,” Stenavich said of the trial at center in the spring. “Monk was down and we just needed guys to train to snap. Obviously, it’s kind of one of those jobs, anyone that’s available that you think can handle it, you want to get them some reps in there just for that instance right there.
“John’s the utility guy every game, where he can play tackle, he can play guard and obviously go in and play center, too. That’s just one of those deals where you’ve just got to get guys ready for that situation.”
Williams played well. Pro Football Focus charged him with only one pressure allowed.
“Obviously, I’ve been switching around a little bit,” Williams said. “Getting to focus on center, that’ll be good for me to just focus on one position.”
For the first time since Week 2, Aaron Banks will play. The $77 million free agent played 22 snaps in that game and zero since. After being saddled with a knee injury throughout training camp, an injury that kept him out of Week 1, Banks was inactive the next four games with knee and toe injuries. He was active last week at Detroit but only played special teams.
This week, he was projected as full participation at Wednesday’s practice, a first this season.
So, would the Packers continue to roll with Laken Tomlinson, who played well the past four weeks at left guard, or go back to Banks, who was given a $77 million contract in free agency last offseason?
Instead, the answer was both.
Banks is back in the saddle at left guard. The move was to switch Tomlinson to right guard. It’s in line with the Packers’ best-five philosophy but bizarre from an experience perspective.
Tomlinson entered the NFL in 2015. He has played 10,731 snaps at left guard and 65 at right guard. The last time he played a line position other than left guard was 2016. Moreover, the Packers didn’t even practice this week, so it’s not as if Tomlinson got an abundance of reps at right guard, though he might have gotten them last week, when Banks was practicing.
Of all the uncertainty up front this season, and especially this week, Stenavich said:
“It’s been difficult. And not only that, but there’s been instances where it’s like, ‘All right, let’s split reps with these two guys and let’s see who has a better week of practice.’ We have an idea of where we’re going, but then it’s not always cut and dried until we get to Friday, usually. Then we know what we’re doing.
“So, yeah, it’s been a really weird year from that standpoint, but again, it doesn’t matter. We’ve got to make sure we put the best five out there and get the results.”
After the team’s first Thursday night debacle, a blowout loss to Atlanta in which their offensive line was demolished, the Packers signed veteran guards Laken Tomlinson and Kevin Zeitler to the 53-man roster and Mekhi Becton to the practice squad.
Tomlinson started right away at left guard with Travis Glover plugged in at right guard. The Packers gave Glover four starts, with the team going 3-1 but playing only marginally better on the offensive line. With Glover out with a knee injury that he played through at Detroit, the stars were in alignment to give Zeitler the start.
After all, Zeitler has started 213 games in his 15-year career, including all but one game for the Titans last season and all but one game for the Lions in 2024. He had played almost 14,000 snaps at right guard in his career.
In four weeks with the Packers, he was a healthy scratch during his first week, played special teams the next two weeks, and was inactive against Detroit.
“He’s ready. He’s preparing to play,” Stenavich said this week.
The Bears went all-in on Jeffery Simmons today. Almost exactly 14 months ago, the Packers went all-in on Micah Parsons. The Bears obviously see a Super Bowl window. The Packers with Parsons should see the same. ⬇️ https://t.co/9XLKZ2UEAe

title: Packers-Panthers Inactives: Big Wins for Jordan Love
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The Green Bay Packers did not practice this week. If they would have, Matthew Golden would not have participated on Monday or Tuesday.
“I sure hope so,” coach Matt LaFleur said about Golden being available for Thursday night’s game against the Carolina Panthers.
LaFleur got his wish. Golden, who was limited participation on Wednesday and questionable on the final injury report, is active and will be in the lineup against the Panthers’ depleted pass defense.
Green Bay’s inactives are starting linebacker Zaire Franklin (shin), tight end Jonnu Smith, running back Kaleb Johnson, starting center Sean Rhyan (ankle), starting right guard Travis Glover (knee) and backup lineman Donovan Jennings.
Smith, Johnson and Jennings are healthy scratches. Johnson, clearly, is the odd man out in the backfield with the return of Josh Jacobs. He really could be the odd man out once Chris Brooks returns from injured reserve in a couple weeks.
The big news from earlier Thursday was the Packers adding cornerback Keisean Nixon to the injury report as questionable with a shoulder injury. Nixon, who is having his best season, will play.
He has not missed a game since signing with the Packers in 2022.
“It’s starting corner-caliber play from him right now,” defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon said on Wednesday. “Like (Brandon) Cisse, like all our guys, you’re going to give up some plays, that’s like in the NFL, but I think his point of attack is where it needs to be. He’s making a lot of plays for us.
“I love his demeanor, not only on gameday, but during the week of practice. He’s competitive. He really is competitive and he plays the game with an edge. He doesn’t back down. I love that about him. He’s ready to compete tomorrow night.”
Three starters were ruled out by Carolina on Wednesday: cornerback Akayleb Evans (triceps/knee), left guard Damien Lewis (knee) and outside linebacker Jaelan Phillips (hamstring). On Thursday, the Panthers put Evans on injured reserve.
Akayleb’s absence is another blow to a Panthers secondary that has starting cornerbacks Jaycee Horn and Mike Jackson on injured reserve. Moreover, Phillips is their top pass rusher. While with the Eagles, he crushed the Packers last season.
Added together, Carolina’s pass defense, which ranks fifth in yards allowed per pass play, might be a paper tiger.
The only other cornerbacks on the roster are Malcolm DeWalt IV, an undrafted free agent who had a predraft visit with the Packers, and Chau Smith-Wade. Smith-Wade was a fifth-round pick in 2024. He’s started 11 games in three seasons with two career interceptions.
Starting defensive tackle Bobbby Brown III (hand) was questionable on the injury report and is out, as well. Also out is former Packers running back AJ Dillon.
With such a beat-up defense, it's no wonder why the Packers are favorites at FanDuel Sportsbook and in position for a bounce-back win .
Inactive for the Panthers tonight: TE Ja'Tavion Sanders OLB Jaelan Phillips QB Haynes King (emergency third QB) RB AJ Dillon G Damien Lewis G Torricelli Simpkins DT Bobby Brown
With Carolina’s depleted pass defense, the Packers could have some opportunities to make some hay through the air.
Golden is 14th with 36 catches, ninth with 540 yards, 14th with 15.0 yards per catch and 16th with three touchdowns. He’s dropped a league-high seven passes, but he’s made a lot more big plays than he’s flubbed. He has three 100-yard games and three consecutive games with six catches.
With Christian Watson eighth with 571 receiving yards, second with a 17.5-yard average and tied for second with six touchdowns, Green Bay’s dynamic duo of receivers could be in line for big nights.
Golden might play limited snaps, but the coaches say they’re confidence in who’s behind their impact starters.
“Well, obviously, we’ve seen Savion out there the last few weeks make some plays,” offensive coordinator Adam Stenavich said. “He’s made some crucial third-down and fourth-down conversions and he’s looked really nice out there, so he’s one of those guys that has really stepped up in his second year. So, if he has to play a bigger role, I feel very comfortable with that.
“Bo (Melton) has been around and been a good role player for us. And then, obviously, J-Mike (J. Michael Sturdivant), he’s done a nice job as a rookie coming in and just trying to earn it every single week. If any of those guys have to be out there and play, I feel comfortable with that.”

title: Why Texans May Not Miss Jaylin Noel as Much as Expected
full_text:
The Houston Texans' latest injury to their roster is one that certainly stings.
Earlier this week, the Texans placed second-year wide receiver Jaylin Noel on injured reserve with a toe injury that's expected to sit him out for the remainder of the regular season .
Seeing any player go down with a season-ending injury is a tough pill to swallow, but that's especially so when losing out on a talent like Noel after the year he's put together. Noel has actually led Houston's offense in total receiving yards (331) and yards per reception (17.4) through their first seven games.
However, while losing Noel does take a hit to the Texans' overall offensive ceiling, it's certainly not time to panic as to how this passing attack is able to move forward.
In fact, the Texans might be able to stay afloat within their air attack pretty easily–– and that's because of the recent developments around their wide receiver position as a whole.
Sure, losing out on the explosiveness and playmaking ability that Noel provides is going to be hard to replace within the offense. He is the Texans' leading receiver on the year for a reason after all.
But the Texans' wide receiver room, which once was void of depth within the first few weeks of the regular season, has now turned a corner in a big way heading into their Week 8 bye.
That's because of the acquisition of not only Marvin Harrison Jr., who was brought in via trade after Houston's Week 5 win over the Tennessee Titans, but also the return of Tank Dell , who officially made his way back onto an NFL field for the first time in nearly two years this past weekend against the New York Giants.
Those two factoring into the mix are massive pieces of the puzzle for the Texans' offense. That pairing has a great chance to supplement that playmaking ability and depth that has since been lost at the position without Noel, which wasn't quite as available just a few games ago.
In Weeks 2 and 3, the Texans' leading contributors at wide receiver while Nico Collins was sidelined with a hamstring strain were none other than Kayshon Boutte and Xavier Hutchinson. A little over a month later, now with Dell and Harrison Jr. as a part of the equation, Houston's fate at the position has taken a full 180.
The hurdle sitting between that playmaking really coming to fruition is for the Texans to find a way to get them on the field in longer stints. This past weekend against the Giants, the two failed to combine for more than 30 snaps on the offense , which is expected given their respective situations.
But that outcome could certainly change in a big way after the bye. Harrison Jr. will have another week of learning the Texans' playbook under his belt. Dell will be even more comfortable coming off of his knee injury and create a much more potent attack for Houston to lean on through the air.
When you add that pairing alongside an already bonafide top wideout like Nico Collins, there's more than enough reason to believe that the Texans' passing offense can stay steady, even without one of their most potent pass-catchers.
So of course, not having Noel on the field for the next two weeks is a noteworthy loss for the Texans, and takes away yet another high-potential receiver out of this offensive attack right next to his draft classmate in Jayden Higgins.
But if the Texans can continue to get Harrison Jr. and Dell involved in the game plan, and they hold up their end of the bargain, that'll be their best course of action in hopes that this offense can rebound moving forward. Time will tell if it'll come to fruition as expected.

title: 3 Concerning Texans Stats That Need to Improve After the Bye Week
full_text:
The Houston Texans are a 2-5 football team heading into their Week 8 bye .
Needless to be said, there's much work to be done heading into the second half of the season if the Texans want to get back on track for a similar late-season run like they put together around this time last year.
And to do that, the Texans have some clear flaws within their game plan and overall production to iron out; issues that can be clearly seen by looking at a select few stats in which Houston has not exceled in through their first seven games of the year, thus leadin to their roster looking like what it does now.
So with all of that in mind, let's take a look at three different stats from the Texans' pre-bye week slate that need to turn around in the right direction for the weeks ahead. Or else, it'll be really tough to picture Houston racking up the necessary wins for a surprise push to the postseason.
Now, to the Texans' credit, they've been able to run the ball a bit better over the past three weeks since Woody Marks has been leading the charge in the backfield .
Marks has been averaging 3.8 yards per carry over the past three weeks that David Montgomery has been sidelined with an average of over 80 yards from scrimmage throughout. He's been a big-time playmaker for this offense and a capable lead ball-carrier on the ground, while helping their run game lift from the depths they were previously at through the first quarter of the season.
However, even while Marks has been taking care of business on the ground, the Texans' offensive line could still serve to make some improvements from the level they're at now when factoring in a nearly 20% run stuffed rate.
For reference, only six other teams rank ahead of the Texans for run-stuffed rate. Over half of those teams have a record under .500, and that's a crowd that Houston currently falls right into.
If Houston wants to continue to progress on the offensive side of the ball, gaining more momentum on the ground and finding more positive runs is a critical step in the process.
The Texans' defensive turnovers as a whole have not been to the level that they were at throughout their dominance of 2025.
Through seven games of last season, Houston's defense had recorded a total of 11 turnovers, even with the early struggles they faced in the year. Seven games in 2026, Houston's total is nearly half that, with just six.
And a large part of that regression for the Texans' turnover numbers has surrounded their failure to attack the air for those giveaways.
Houston's only three interceptions on the year have been to backup linebacker Jake Hansen, along with safeties Calen Bullock and Reed Blankenship getting a pair of their own as well. As for the Texans' top two corners, Derek Stingley and Kamari Lassiter, they haven't seen any takeaways coming their way.
Simply put, the Texans need to take advantage of the turnover battle more than they have so far this season. And with a defense as talented as the one this roster has on paper–– especially within the secondary–– there's little excuse for Houston to have just three interceptions in seven weeks.
More often than not, teams who win the turnover battle can win a lot of football games. The Texans' offense has taken care of the ball extremely well, but now comes the time for the defense to hold up their end of the bargain.
An issue that really showed itself for the Texans in their latest game against the New York Giants : penalties.
Last week, Houston gave up 80 total yards for the eight penalties they accumulated throughout the day, which has turned into a common trend for this Houston roster to look both unorganized and undisciplined––especially on the line of scrimmage offensively.
The Texans are currently the third-highest number of total flags in the NFL behind only the Green Bay Packers and the Cleveland Browns, who each have 73. Houston is one of only two teams to have given up over 500 total yards on the season because of penalties.
When factoring in the flaws that the Texans have had on early downs running the ball, getting even further behind because of frequent penalty issues ends up setting this offense back even further. Penalties have to be cleaned up for Houston, and DeMeco Ryans knows it .
However, time will tell if the Texans are able to get this group of tight ends up in time to make a run for the second half of the season.

title: Should Texans Trade WR Nico Collins? Here's What It Would Cost
full_text:
The Houston Texans have seen a few big trades circle around them in the AFC South in recent days.
The Indianapolis Colts traded away Quenton Nelson and DeForest Buckner –– and there could be more pieces on the move sooner rather than later. The Tennessee Titans just moved off of their franchise cornerstone Jeffery Simmons to the Chicago Bears in exchange for a haul of draft picks.
TRADE: Titans trading DT Jeffery Simmons to Bears. (via @AdamSchefter , @RapSheet ) pic.twitter.com/ZJnwnUtA9w
So naturally, as the trade deadline looms closer, the Texans could be another AFC South team to consider making a big shake-up to their roster. They already did make a move to add Marvin Harrison Jr. a few weeks ago, but maybe Houston opts to sell a piece or two off in the right circumstances.
And surprisingly, one name on the Texans' roster that's surfaced amongst some fans as a potential trade candidate to watch is star wide receiver Nico Collins, who's coming off his worst game of the season against the New York Giants where he hauled in just two of his five targets for six yards .
Collins is in a deep receiver room , hasn't been as involved in the game plan as he has been throughout the past three seasons with the Texans, and is due for a lucrative extension as soon as this offseason to cement his long-term future as a part of the franchise.
However, if the Texans wanted to be proactive on Collins' future, perhaps the front office could consider getting ahead of his situation by searching around the trade market for an appealing return. Wide receivers are a hot commodity, and Houston could certainly bring in a noteworthy package if they were to truly shop around.
So should the Texans even entertain a move to send out Collins? And if they do, what type of package could they get send their way? Let's break it all down:
There is reason to at least ponder a trade involving Collins from the Texans' perspective–– simply from a contractual perspective.
With the Texans' cost of the roster bound to get pricier over the next two seasons when factoring in the defensive talent and C.J. Stroud's pending extension, the cost to keep Collins around on a new deal might prove to be too much for Houston to pay out once the time comes .
So if the Texans simply wanted to cash in on Collins as an asset, perhaps now is the time to trade him if an extension wasn't in the cards next season.
However, what's also important to factor in is where the Texans stand as a franchise. They shouldn't be looking to recoup or build upon their pile of assets; this roster should be looking to do what they can to win games now.
Trading Nico Collins doesn't help the Texans get better. They're simply planning further for the future. And while there is value in keeping a forward-thinking mindset in any front office, shipping out a top 10 to 15 receiver in a year where Houston has invested a ton in this current core seems to be thinking too many steps ahead.
Over the next two years, this Texans roster might be equipped with the most talent they've had–– and will have–– in a while. Once Stroud gets his massive extension that could eclipse $60 million annually , it'll be much harder to build a roster with this type of talent on both sides of the ball.
If the Texans are truly committed to winning this season, trading Collins signals the opposite approach. And based on Houston's past offseason, and even their recent move to bring in Marvin Harrison Jr. for a second-round pick, this team is more equipped to be buyers on the market. Not sellers.
Now, to play devil's advocate for a moment, what might be an intriguing enough package to at least make the Texans really consider a move to ship out Collins?
The starting point for such a move feels like it'd have to be a first-round pick, and perhaps even more on top of it.
Just this offseason, we saw another similar star wideout on the move in the form of A.J. Brown being shipped to the New England Patriots in exchange for a 2028 first-round pick and a 2027 fifth-round pick.
Collins, being two years younger and just as productive as Brown, might be worth even more than that, and especially so given that the Texans don't exactly need to trade their star wideout unless a team offers a package they can't refuse.
So with that in mind, the Texans might need a future first-round pick, and maybe a third-round pick to play with the idea of sending Collins to another team via trade.
That still might not be enough to lead to Houston pulling the trigger, but such value seems pretty reasonable in the event a team had its eyes dead set on acquiring the two-time Pro Bowler.

title: Jaylin Noel Injury Could Mean Bigger Role for One Texans WR
full_text:
The Houston Texans are likely to be without one of their biggest bright spots on the offensive side of the ball for the remainder of this season, as it was announced that wide receiver Jaylin Noel would be placed on injured reserve with a turf toe injury on Wednesday.
It's a big loss for the Texans' wide receiver room. No doubt. Noel began to come alive in recent weeks as one of Houston's most electric downfield playmakers at the position, and it now seems as if his inspiring year-two campaign has come to a close a bit earlier than expected.
However, as deep as the Texans' wide receiver room currently looks––even without Noel––his absence does create a bit of an opening when it comes to both overall snaps and targets at the position.
And while being without Noel could mean that several names around the Texans' receiver room are due to get more attention in the weeks ahead, one player in particular sticks out as someone who could benefit the most from a potential expanded opportunity: and that's Tank Dell.
Now, perhaps it's a little bullish to project a larger role for Dell just one game after his long-awaited return to the field after 670 days.
Odds are, the Texans are still going to be cautious surrounding the usage and snap count for Dell in his first few weeks back on the field. Houston's remained careful with Dell all throughout his recovery process , and that shouldn't be expected to change in the early stages of his return to the field.
However, you can't help but get a little bit intrigued by what Dell's usage could look like for the Texans moving forward this season without having to work alongside Noel to get snaps within the offense.
Dell, if truly back to full health in the weeks ahead, could be a potent third wide receiver to complement Nico Collins and Marvin Harrison Jr. in this heavy passing offense that the Texans seem eager to try and lean into for the second half of the season.
While Dell is someone that has primarily lined up as an outside receiver throughout his time in Houston, he certainly has the quickness and the frame that matches up well with a slot receiver as well–– which is the role Noel typically filled into and excelled in .
Collins and Harrison Jr. work best as outside weapons themselves, but can also occasionally work inside the slot, and might also have even more routes to do so with another versatile threat like Dell coming back into the lineup.
So if the Texans wanted to truly lean into their strengths at wide receiver, Houston can roll with a potent trio of Collins, Harrison Jr. and Dell, with each being capable of playing on the outside or in the slot.
Each of them bring their unique superpowers to the table–– Collins' physical jump-ball ability, Harrison Jr.'s route-running, Dell's run after-the-catch ability–– and really give opposing defenses trouble when this scoring attack is really clicking.
Don't be mistaken: without Noel, Xavier Hutchinson and Kayshon Boutte will have their respective roles in the offense as well.
In fact, both of them got more snaps than Dell did in their most recent matchup against the Giants in Week 7, which makes sense given the implications of Dell's first game back in nearly two years.
But as Dell continues to get more comfortable and adjusted to the Texans' offense over the next few weeks, he stands out as the one name to benefit most from the newly opened opportunities at the wide receiver position.
He has the chance to be the best playmaker behind Collins and Harrison Jr., fits the physical profile and skillset that the Texans could use without someone like Noel, and is certainly hungry for any expanded role that he can get in the offense, which he made clear after his first game back last weekend .
"Y'all know me. I'm ready for the role," Dell said of getting an expanded role after facing the Giants. "I've been in the role to be that guy already and, y'all know how it gets. So, man, I'm ready for it. Next man up. Prayers for J. He's going to rehab his toe, and pick up where he left off."
Now, the time has arrived a bit sooner than expected for Dell to get those extra snaps and targets his way. We'll see how long it takes for the Texans to get him involved further, and when the time comes, whether or not he'll be able to help keep Houston's offense afloat without the presence of Noel.

title: Texans Sign Former Cowboys RB Amid Backfield Depth Concerns
full_text:
The Houston Texans have made a new addition to their backfield on Wednesday despite being in the middle of their Week 8 bye .
And that signing just so happens to have come via waivers from their in-state neighbors in the Dallas Cowboys.
According to the Texans' transaction log, the team has claimed running back Emari Demercado off waivers after he was let go by the Dallas Cowboys earlier in the week.
We have claimed Emari Demercado off waivers and made other roster moves. pic.twitter.com/2V0C9WcsDm
Demercado, a 5-foot-9, 215-pound running back who's been in the league for the past four seasons. He spent his first three years pro with the Arizona Cardinals, where he played a total of 40 games and recorded over 1,100 yards from scrimmage throughout that span.
More recently, Demercado had been with the Kansas City Chiefs earlier this year as a part of their 90-man roster leading into the regular season.
He was ultimately sent to waivers by the Chiefs at the end of August, and would quickly be scooped up by the Cowboys, where he would play two games over the course of this season.
In those two games he played in between Weeks 1 and 2, Demercado put together five carries for 15 yards on the ground, but would not be activated past those pair of appearances.
Now, Demercado is able to land on his feel with the Texans heading into the second half of the season, as he'll be able to provide some sense of backfield depth that Houston was left without during their most recent game against the New York Giants.
Since the Texans' Week 5 win vs. the Tennessee Titans, the offense has been without their lead veteran in the backfield in David Montgomery, as he's been dealing with a groin injury to keep him sidelined for Weeks 6 and 7.
Montgomery has still yet to log a limited, let alone full practice, for the team since going down with his injury. And while the Texans do have a bye week ahead of them that provides extra time for him to get right, there are no guarantees he'll be ready to go before their next game in Week 9 against the LA Chargers.
Without Montgomery, the Texans were currently left with just two active running backs on their roster in Week 7. RB3 British Brooks has been on injured reserve since Week 4 with a hamstring injury, and Jawhar Jordan was just placed on Houston's practice squad injured reserve after suffering an injury in Week 6 vs. Jacksonville.
That meant Woody Marks and Dare Ogunbowale were the only names the Texans could lean on in their backfield for Week 7. And while that setup worked relatively well for most of the contest against New York, an injury scare for Marks in the second half put that need for a third rostered running back on full display.
Therefore, the Texans now have another running back on their 53-man roster to lean on in Demercado, who brings depth, experience, and another ball carrier to utilize in the event that Montgomery–– or any other running back in the mix–– is due to miss any more time moving forward.

title: Texans WR Jaylin Noel's Foot Injury Update Is Worst-Case Scenario
full_text:
In the midst of the Houston Texans' Week 7 loss to the New York Giants, the wide receiver room would see one of their key contributors leave the game early with a toe injury: second-year wideout Jaylin Noel.
Noel would inevitably not return to the game, was said to have been suffering from turf toe from head coach DeMeco Ryans after the game, and was waiting further testing to see just how long he would be sidelined.
And it turns out, Noel will be out for a significant amount of time. The Texans have announced that Noel will be placed on injured reserve due to the toe injury he sustained this weekend against the Giants.
But that's not all. According to the Houston Chronicle 's Jonathan M. Alexander , Noel's toe injury is expected to be serious enough to sideline him for the rest of the season.
It's yet another tough injury blow for the Texans to sustain to be without Noel for what appears to be the rest of the season.
Houston has seen multiple starters on both sides of the ball deal with extended absences over the past few weeks. That includes injuries to Jalen Pitre, Reed Blankenship, and David Montgomery, and now, the newest issue is within their wide receiver room.
But those injuries are expected to subside within the next few weeks. Noel, however, now seems to have reached the end of what's been a really inspiring second season when he's gotten a chance to be on the field.
Noel has gotten off to at hot start for his second season in Houston, finding his way to become a gradually more involved piece within the Texans' passing attack–– especially for the past three weeks.
On the season, Noel has put together 19 receptions on 23 targets, 331 yards and two touchdowns, while currently leading the NFL in yards per target (14.4).
But now, the Texans will be forced to move forward for the next 10 games on the schedule without him. Noel now joins his draft classmate, Jayden Higgins, on injured reserve while being expected to miss the season; both of whom entered this season expected to make a big leap in terms of their development.
And while Houston does have a deep wide receiver room to bank on in his absence, not having Noel does take away a big-time explosive piece offensively who was just beginning to catch his stride within the passing attack.
The silver lining for the Texans in a rough turn of events for Noel is the fact that their wide receiver room is extremely deep compared to where things stood at the start of this season.
They've got Nico Collins leading the way, Xavier Hutchinson and Kayshon Boutte due to remain key parts of the Texans' passing attack, and Marvin Harrison Jr. and Tank Dell are just beginning to catch their stride within the offense within their respective situations.
The two names that remain the most compelling to keep an eye on now that Noel is due to miss the rest of the season will be both of Harrison Jr. and Dell.
While both pass-catchers were extremely limited in Week 7's game plan against the Giants, their usage and involvement should only be expected to increase in the weeks ahead. Harrison Jr. is still learning his way around the Texans' playbook and overall offensive scheme, while Dell just came back for his first NFL game in over 670 days .
So the Texans might be able to navigate the storm offensively, even without one of their biggest bright spots on the offensive side of the ball so far this season. But there's no doubt that losing Noel's explosiveness and downfield ability is going to sting for C.J. Stroud and the rest of the surrounding offense.

title: Texans' DeMeco Ryans Has a Simple Plan to Reset During Bye Week
full_text:
The Houston Texans have officially arrived at their bye in Week 8 –– a mid-season break that many would consider much-needed for this team after a rough 2-5 start to their 2026 campaign.
DeMeco Ryans and the Texans' staff will have an extra week at their disposal to take a step back, evaluate what's working and what's not through this team's up-and-down start to the season, and hope that this ship can be turned around in time for their Week 9 meeting facing the LA Chargers .
But when it comes to the Texans' plan for their players and any practice over the next week, it seems that Houston is putting a major emphasis on rest, recovery, and resetting rather than doubling down on any work on the field.
Ryans recently appeared on Texans Radio earlier this week to break down what the Texans' plans will be over the course of the bye as they try to rebound from their slow first half of the season.
And overall, Ryans' message was simple: take a deep breath, reset, then come back recharged for next week.
“Yeah, for the bye week, I think it comes at the right time, getting it right in the middle. I think guys just need to take a deep breath; just reset,” Ryans said.
“I think it's not going out and practicing four times this week, that's going to help us get better. I think everybody just needs to hit a reset mentally, see where they are mentally, physically, get their bodies recovered, heal up, and then we'll come back next week.”
Some who have seen the Texans' performance over the past several weeks may argue that more time on the practice field and in the weight room will be able to help Houston turn around in their desired direction.
After all, the Texans have lost five of their first seven games, so maybe more on-field work at the bye could be an approach to consider.
But for Ryans, he sees the situation as quite the opposite.
Instead of putting further strain on the players through what's already been a challenging start to the new year, Ryans wants his guys to really take this time off as a true bye week, then hope that extra rest can spark some new energy once the Texans are back at practice next Wednesday.
“Our plan this week isn't to go out on the field and do more practices. It's truly to give the guys a break,” Ryans continued.
“Let them get out of here. Make sure they're taking care of their bodies the right way. Get a couple days to themselves to just, ‘Hey, reanalyze yourself as a player, as a man. Like, where are you? What do you need to do?’"
The bye week also gives the Texans' staff some extra time to work through some of their own successes and failures that they may have encountered through the first seven games––and they certainly aren't without their own mistakes, just like the players.
Whether it revolves around their defensive scheme and their woes in pass coverage, some of their offensive plays or personnel that might not be working, this week has the chance to be even more constructive for the Texans' coaches than it is for the players.
So Ryans and the rest of the staff on the Texans' sidelines will also make sure to take some time to decompress throughout the bye. But the time will also give Houston a perfect opportunity to work through what aspects of their game plan are or aren't working as expected.
“Yeah, for the bye week, I think it comes at the right time, getting it right in the middle. I think guys just need to take a deep breath; just reset,” Ryans said.
“It's extremely important that we go all in on the self-scout,” Ryans continued. “We can look at certain things from a coverage standpoint. Hey, we're giving up explosive passes. I know what we probably want to do. What was the intentionality behind this scheme going into this game, and did we do it well? Is that working for us right now?”
“So, it's a really good week to just hit reset, refocus. You don't have to game plan, but you look internally and truly look at it. I tell coaches, look at it without feelings. Take your feelings out of it. Like, what does the film actually say? Does it say jumbo is working? Does it say man coverage is working? If that's not it, then we got to adjust.”
There's still so much more time to go this season, which means there's certainly an opportunity for the Texans to turn things around in time for a late run like they did around this time last year .
But this bye week is a pivotal point in the season where the Texans can get some coveted time off to really be ready for the second half of the year that could arguably be more challenging than the first few games Houston's had to endure.
So for Ryans, this week will mark a perfect time to step away, and thus offers the best chance for the Texans to try and rally for the second half of the schedule, starting with Week 9 against the Chargers.

title: Predicting Texans' Next 4 Games After Disappointing 2-5 Start
full_text:
The Houston Texans are heading into the bye week with an ugly-looking 2-5 record over their first seven games.
That's not where anyone expected the Texans to be at this point in the year. Many viewed this Houston roster to have one of the league's best defenses and a much-improved offense to rank towards the top of the AFC, but Houston now is just hoping that they can hang onto a spot in the Wild Card.
So now, the pressure is on for the Texans to kick it into high gear after the bye, and put some wins together and climb out of the deep hole they've since dug themselves into. Only four more losses would guarantee Houston finishes the year under .500, and pretty much ends any hopes of being one of the final playoff teams in the conference.
But just how well might the Texans fare through their next four games on the schedule? Is there any hope that Houston can run the table for a perfect 4-0 stretch? Or is that post-bye-week success just wishful thinking?
Let's pass some of the time through the Texans' Week 8 bye by predicting how each of Houston's next four games on the schedule could go, and what their record could end up looking like coming out of that Week 12 matchup:
The Texans have no choice but to take care of business in this game against the currently winless Chargers. And even while taking the long road trip to the West Coast, it feels like Houston should still be able to do so.
They'll be well-rested after the bye, with guys such as Jalen Pitre, Reed Blankenship, and David Montgomery possibly returning , and have an ideal matchup against a struggling Chargers offense for their defense to have a bounceback from the woes they encountered against the New York Giants.
The Chargers currently average the lowest points per game in the NFL (15.0), are bottom five in total yards per game (287.2), and are one of two teams to have not recorded 10 touchdowns or more through the first seven weeks of the season.
If the Texans can't get their defense right against this team, it'll be hard to find a better matchup for them to do so.
The Deshaun Watson revenge game... maybe?
The Texans have only faced off against their former quarterback once since they shipped him to the Cleveland Browns in 2022, and it was in that one matchup that Watson actually got the last laugh in a 27-14 victory over Houston back in December of 2022.
Fast forward to 2026, and Watson gets another chance to face his former team. And there's no question that both sides will be looking significantly different than they did from that last meeting four years ago.
Each team has cycled through some head coaches. C.J. Stroud will get his first opportunity to face the Texans' former signal-caller, and the Browns are surprisingly coming together for one of their more solid seasons in recent memory with a 5-2 record through seven weeks.
Heading into the season, many probably would've picked the Texans to take home a victory here pretty convincingly. However, considering how each of these teams has kicked off the first half of their schedule, and how inconsistent Houston has been on both sides of the ball, it's a whole lot harder to have that same confidence here.
Based on what we've seen through seven games, the Browns might just have the upper hand with a respectable defense, strong coaching, and momentum on their side to give Watson a 2-0 record against Houston.
Prediction: Texans Lose, 20-21
We'll keep this one quick. The Texans, at this point in the season, would be desperate to cling onto a victory against the Colts to try and go on a late-season run, especially after having dropped their last meeting against Indianapolis to find themselves 0-3.
The Colts have been the trade deadline's biggest sellers thus far with moves to already send out Quenton Nelson and DeForest Buckner. And with two more weeks to go, this roster could be down even more key contributors like Josh Downs, or even Jonathan Taylor.
The Texans have little excuse not to split the season series against Indianapolis. It was a shock that Houston couldn't claw out a victory in Week 3 after Daniel Jones had committed a total of three turnovers through the day, and it'd be even more surprising to see the Colts get another win here with a worse roster for meeting number two.
Houston should win this one rather convincingly on their home field, and perhaps even in a bit of a blowout fashion. It'd certainly be a plus for team morale.
Prediction: Texans Win, 33-10
There's no doubt that this game is the toughest Houston has on the schedule through the next four weeks: Houston gets to host Lamar Jackson and the Baltimore Ravens on their home field at Reliant Stadium with their backs against the wall to try and avoid another loss on the books.
Perhaps the Texans have a fighting chance in this one. If their offense can pick up a bit more steam compared to what they showcased against the Giants, and the defense looks healthy and at least a little bit closer to their 2025 status, Houston can pull out a much-needed win against a tough Ravens opponent.
But the Texans' defense hasn't exactly shown to be a reliable force when it comes to stopping some of the best quarterbacks on their schedule right now. They've fallen flat against Josh Allen, Joe Burrow, and Dak Prescott, and Jackson finds himself right on the same caliber as those guys.
Last year, the Texans dominated the Ravens in their Week 5 matchup, 44-10 . But that was without Lamar Jackson on the field, paired with what was then a dominant defense that was just starting to catch its stride. For this season's matchup against Baltimore, the situation could look a whole lot different.
When combining Houston's recent troubles against opposing quarterbacks, along with their struggles against the run (plus tackling) against an evasive offense led by Lamar and Derrick Henry, I have my reservations about the Texans being able to get a home victory here.
Prediction: Texans Lose, 18-24
This would not be the most ideal outcome for the Texans, all things considered. At 3-1, or even running the table at 4-0, there starts to be a whole lot more optimism in play that Houston can turn their season around for a late bid into the postseason.
But with seven losses in 12 weeks, the Texans would have to essentially win out through the rest of their schedule to have a chance at a Wild Card appearance.
However, that's simply the price to be paid for the Texans' slow start to the season. Margin for error becomes a whole lot thinner, and only a couple of losses across their next four games could be just enough to bury their hopes of clawing into the postseason for a fourth-straight season, let alone win the AFC South.
Of course, there are a lot more games to go, and anything can happen throughout the next 10 weeks. If this is the end result for Houston following Week 12, though, it's going to be hard to feel a whole lot better about the Texans' odds to make a late-season run from what things look like right now.
