title: 3 Texans Players Who Need Bigger Roles After the Bye Week
full_text:
The Houston Texans are heading into their Week 8 bye at a gloomy 2-5 record.
For the Texans to get back on track for the second half of the season, some changes around the roster will have to be made–– even if that doesn't include making a big swing on the trade market ahead of the deadline.
Some of those changes could be as simple as handing a few players around the roster more playing time than they've been accustomed to through the past several weeks.
This Texans roster already has several talented players on both sides of the ball to bank on even if they're three games under .500, so maybe flipping the switch for a few wins could be as simple as distributing more opportunities to a select few players in need of increased snaps.
With that in mind, let's take a look at three players around the Texans' roster who feel due to be more involved coming out of this week's bye:
The Texans have taken a slower approach to get their new wide receiver, Marvin Harrison Jr. involved as a key piece of their offense through the first two weeks he's been in the building.
He's seen less than 30 combined offensive snaps against the Jacksonville Jaguars and New York Giants, and has turned those appearances in for four receptions, 40 yards, and one touchdown.
On one hand, it's probably justified for the Texans to keep Harrison Jr. limited within his first couple of games as a part of this offense. Making sure he's fully adjusted within this passing attack to become the true downfield weapon Houston brought him in to be will be the best course of action for the long term .
But the Texans did give up a second-round pick for this coming draft to bring in Harrison Jr. That's a significant investment in a wide receiver that should encourage Houston's staff to get him more snaps as a complementary piece opposite of Nico Collins sooner rather than later, which might be a bit easier now that the bye week is upon us.
The Texans need to get Harrison Jr. on the field for much more than the sub-30% he's seen over the last two weeks. And if the flashes he's shown through the start of his tenure in Houston are a sign of anything, getting him more touches should be a decision that pays off pretty nicely.
It's become pretty easy to forget about Marlin Klein as a piece within the Texans' offense, considering he's been a healthy scratch ever since his Week 3 appearance against the Indianapolis Colts. But it wasn't too long ago that he was Houston's 58th pick of the 2026 NFL Draft as their third selection off the board.
Klein projected as an intriguing, but raw, talent at the tight end position who has stout 6-foot-6, 250-pound size with upside both as a blocker and a vertical threat for the offense.
His production at Michigan was far from eye- catching, but he did make a few plays in both training camp and preseason (and from a 16-yard reception in Week 1 vs. the Buffalo Bills) that made it feel like he could be an impactful player for this offense to use in heavier 12 and 13 personnel situations.
However, the Texans have essentially shut him out from the game plan entirely throughout the past month. Why? Houston's coaching staff has wanted him to be a more quality contributor on special teams, and to this point, that aspect of his game hasn't clicked––or else he'd be on the field more than he has been.
Regardless of that impact on special teams, though, the Texans have to give Klein a chance to get on the field on gamedays. He was one of Houston's top selections in their most recent draft for a reason, but has yet to really get a chance to spread his wings as the talent this front office brought him in to be.
Another rookie the Texans added in the second round of their most recent draft, yet has been on the field more than Klein throughout the regular season, is defensive tackle Kayden McDonald.
McDonald started the first four weeks of the year stuck on injured reserve with an ankle injury , but has gradually found his way into Houston's defensive line rotation alongside Sheldon Rankins and Tommy Togiai.
And so far, McDonald's integration into that defensive line rotation has put him into a role as Houston's DT3, which is somewhat expected as a first-year talent still fresh off of a weeks-long injury. But the Texans have every reason to get him more involved after the events of their last loss vs. the New York Giants in which they struggled to stop the run, as well as their lackluster ability to tackle.
McDonald, however, was viewed by many coming into the draft as a high-level run defender, and a super productive tackler from his one year starting at Ohio State.
While he might be a bit more raw than the more experienced Rankins and Togiai, handing him some of their snaps in an effort to improve both of those areas defensively could be a huge lift for this struggling unit for the second half of the season.

title: Texans Missed a Golden Opportunity to Trade for Quenton Nelson
full_text:
The Houston Texans just missed their chance to bring a major upgrade on their offensive line.
That's because the Indianapolis Colts just shipped out one of the best interior offensive linemen in the NFL, Quenton Nelson, who was traded to the Seattle Seahawks on Tuesday afternoon as the first domino to fall in the Colts' potential deadline fire sale.
According to ESPN 's Adam Schefter, the Seahawks gave up a 2027 third-round pick and a 2028 fifth-round pick in exchange to bring in Nelson; a major upgrade to Seattle's offensive line that takes their interior to the next level en route to their hopes of another Super Bowl push.
Trade: Colts have agreed to send eight-time Pro-Bowl guard Quenton Nelson to the Seattle Seahawks, per me and @rapsheet . Nelson is on an expiring contract and the Colts are opting to get back draft capital now before they could lose him in free agency. But an all-time Colt now… pic.twitter.com/uKlAEYkPnZ
However, when looking at this deal through a Texans-centric lens, it leaves you wondering: what was stopping Houston from going out to make a move like this?
Now, to address the obvious, it's not often you see two division rivals make a move with one another, especially for a star-level addition like Nelson is. Perhaps Indianapolis would've been totally unwilling to ship off Nelson to Houston in an effort to boost their hopes of winning the AFC South.
However, in the event that the Colts were open to such an outcome, the Texans certainly would've had a comparable package to Seattle's that could entice Indianapolis to consider them as a trade partner as well. And Houston certainly has a dire need on their offensive line that would warrant a big swing like this one.
Yes, the Texans did just trade for Marvin Harrison Jr. a couple of weeks ago for the steep price of a second-round pick from the Arizona Cardinals. Trading away even more draft capital for an expiring contract like Nelson in an effort to boost a 2-5 team could be seen as a bit too short-sighted.
But the Texans' decision to go out and secure Harrison Jr. earlier this month was seemingly done with the mindset that this team was still to be considered mid-season buyers. One loss against the Giants, while a bad loss, shouldn't totally derail that thought process from Caserio and Co., and should at least leave them open to adding even more talent, if the price is right.
Houston's lead decision-makers have remained outspokenly confident with the core group this team has in place. But with consistent offensive line issues— that were on full display this past weekend in the form of their penalty woes — have always been a recurring issue for the Texans' offense to reach its full potential.
Nelson, through the first seven games of the season with Indianapolis, he's found his way to landing the third-best PFF grade for offensive guards (85.7) . He's excelled as a pass-blocker, has allowed just six pressures, one QB hit, and zero sacks through that span. Most importantly, he's been called for just one penalty.
In retrospect, this was the big swing the Texans should've taken to upgrade their roster; not trade for Marvin Harrison Jr. Nelson fills a major need on the offensive line, could've seamlessly fit in at left guard next to Keylan Rutledge and Ed Ingram on the interior, and would've brought a ton of optimism upfront compared to what Houston has been accustomed to in recent memory.
Even if Houston had their eyes set on spending a second round pick to acquire Stroud's former Ohio State teammate in Harrison, this team still had enough future draft picks in their war chest to make a push for Nelson on top of their prior move.
They've got a first, a third, and a fourth round pick for this coming draft, have all of their picks outside of a sixth in 2028, and all of their resources in 2029.
A 2027 third-rounder, paired with a 2028 fourth, could've been just enough to beat Seattle's offer, and should've been at least on the table for the Colts to consider.
Instead, the Texans decided to hold off on Nelson. It remains to be seen whether or not a big deadline swing could still be in the cards, but finding an immediate plug-and-play lineman like Nelson is going to be pretty tough to find elsewhere.

title: Colts, Jaguars Mid-Week Injury Reports Ahead of Divisional Showdown: CJ Allen's First Start?
full_text:
With an AFC South matchup looming Sunday, the Indianapolis Colts and Jacksonville Jaguars are looking to get key players back on the field. Thursday's injury reports offered a better idea of where both teams' health stand heading into the divisional showdown.
Several notable players are working through injuries on both sides, making Friday's final practice an important checkpoint before the weekend. The latest developments could have implications for both teams as they prepare for a game with significant divisional stakes.
The Colts are entering a new era after trading away longtime franchise pillars in LG Quenton Nelson and DT DeForest Buckner, and it's looking like we'll see more young players get their opportunity down the stretch .
After a walkthrough Wednesday, the Colts received encouraging news Thursday, with cornerback Sauce Gardner, guard Matt Goncalves, wide receiver Anthony Gould, and defensive tackle Tim Smith all upgrading to full participation. Gardner missed last week with a calf injury, so his return is crucial for a secondary that's been banged up in recent weeks.
Tight end Tyler Warren remains limited with a groin injury after missing the last two games, making Friday's practice an important checkpoint for his potential return.
Meanwhile, linebacker Bryce Boettcher and cornerback Justin Walley have yet to practice this week. Their continued absences could affect Indianapolis' depth at linebacker and cornerback, particularly with Walley dealing with a knee injury sustained against Minnesota.
Veteran cornerback Cam Taylor-Britt was placed on Injured Reserve earlier this week, keeping him out for at least the next four games. Although the Colts are set to have their starting outside duo available in Sauce Gardner and Charvarius Ward, the slot role remains up for grabs.
If Walley cannot go, the Colts may turn to rookie UDFAs Kapena Gushiken or Kenneth Harris. Both young defenders have flashed at times this season, but neither has carved out a definitive role.
When it comes to linebacker, the Colts are trending towards finally starting second-round pick CJ Allen.
Allen was kept out of most training camp with lingering injuries (groin, hamstring), which led to defensive coordinator Lou Anarumo turning to veterans Akeem Davis-Gaither and Jaylon Carlies while the rookie is slowly but surely ramped up.
The Colts' first pick (53rd overall) of the 2026 NFL Draft has been sidelined for the majority of his rookie season so far, having only played in 11.14% of possible defensive snaps.
Lou Anarumo said earlier this week that Allen was set to make his first start against the Minnesota Vikings in Week 7, but a late-week ankle injury forced the Colts to pivot.
After back-to-back full participation to start the week, one that coincides with the Colts' ongoing fire sale, it appears Owner/CEO Carlie Irsay-Gordon and Co. are officially welcoming in the new era by turning to the promising young players on the roster.
Allen's promising health news is one sign for this, and the Colts' mid-week release of veteran linebacker Germaine Pratt is additional proof.
The Colts will have one more practice Friday before Sunday's road matchup against the Jaguars. The final injury report should provide a clearer indication of which players are trending toward playing and which could be in danger of missing another game. But for now, the prognosis appears positive.
Thursday’s practice report for #INDvsJAX . pic.twitter.com/9hwSTY3ezW
The Jaguars had two players upgrade to full participation Thursday, with cornerback Montaric Brown and tight end Brenton Strange both practicing without restriction. Brown was limited Wednesday with a hamstring injury, so his progress is notable. Brown's availability would give Jacksonville another option in the secondary against Indianapolis' passing attack.
Wide receiver Jakobi Meyers remains limited with a hamstring injury after being listed with the same designation Wednesday. His status is worth monitoring ahead of Sunday's divisional matchup, as the Jaguars look to have their receiving corps available against a Colts defense dealing with injuries of its own.
Meanwhile, safety Antonio Johnson missed his second consecutive practice with an ankle injury. His continued absence could affect Jacksonville's secondary depth, while long snapper Ross Matiscik, defensive tackle Ruke Orhorhoro, linebacker Jahlani Tavai and running back LeQuint Allen Jr. remain limited. We'll have a much clearer idea of who's available and who's not ahead of Sunday after Friday's practice session.

title: Colts Face Franchise-Altering Contract Decision on Breakout Star
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts have plenty of questions to answer as they begin reshaping their roster, but Adetomiwa Adebawore has emerged as an intriguing piece of the team's future .
The young defensive tackle has steadily worked his way into a larger role and is in line to take over starting responsibilities from the recently traded DeForest Buckner . Adebawore's recent progress has positioned him for a big payday, but how much his value could continue to rise may determine what it takes for Indianapolis to keep him around.
A fourth-round pick in 2023, Adebawore is coming off the best season of his young career and has taken another step forward in 2026.
Between his increased production and the current state of the Colts' defensive line, Adebawore has the opportunity to be one of the pillars the Colts build around moving forward.
Adebawore recorded four sacks in 17 games last season, including seven starts, matching his previous career high in tackles for loss with five. Through seven games in 2026, he's already matched that sack total with 10 games left to go.
The most encouraging part of Adebawore's emergence has been his ability to generate pressure in a rotational role. He's played roughly 36% of Indianapolis' defensive snaps this season, yet he's in a three-way tie among all NFL players for the most sacks by a defensive tackle (4).
#Colts DT Adetomiwa Adebawore has the 2nd-most pressures (12) on the team (excl. Buckner) after seven weeks despite only playing 35.9% of snaps. He leads the defense in sacks (4.0), pressure rate (13.0%), and quick pressures (6), and has the second-most stops (13). pic.twitter.com/cqamb6tThI
Adebawore's performance against the Minnesota Vikings last week offered another example of that progress. He recorded two sacks and five pressures, consistently disrupting Kyler Murray to keep the Colts neck-and-neck with the league's last remaining unbeaten team.
The Colts have a potential building block developing along their defensive front. Adebawore is producing at a level that demands attention, and with his role expected to grow following Buckner's departure, he has an opportunity to strengthen his case for a significant second contract.
Adebawore's emergence hasn't gone unnoticed around the NFL. According to NFL Network's Mike Garafolo, teams are already doing their homework on the Colts defensive tackle in case Indianapolis makes him available before the trade deadline.
"If he's made available, this is a guy that other teams might want to pry away from the Colts," he said.
From The Insiders on @nflnetwork : The #Colts ’ trades this week have other teams surveying their entire roster ahead of the deadline. DT Adetomiwa Adeboware has piqued interest in a breakout, contract year. Big payday coming for him soon, whether in Indy or elsewhere. pic.twitter.com/1KE7ojytWK
While the Colts haven't necessarily decided to move on from Adebawore, the leaguewide interest is another indication of how his value has changed. He's just 25 years old and coming off a productive stretch, and still has room to grow, making him an appealing target for teams looking to strengthen their defensive fronts.
That interest could carry over into the offseason if Indianapolis doesn't secure an extension. Should Adebawore continue producing and reach free agency, the Colts could face competition from multiple teams looking to add an ascending interior pass rusher.
A bidding war isn't guaranteed, but the early interest suggests his market could become increasingly difficult for Indianapolis to navigate.
Furthermore, Tennessee Titans star defensive tackle Jeffrey Simmons was traded to the Chicago Bears for multiple first-round picks on Thursday. Even though Adebawore still aspires to be the level of player Simmons is, his emergence coupled with the dwindling defensive tackle market could see premium draft capital come calling Indianapolis's way.
With the Colts entering a new phase as a franchise, Indianapolis needs to act fast if they view Adebawore as a future building block.
Adebawore wouldn't be the first defensive tackle to turn a gradual rise into a lucrative payday. Osa Odighizuwa and Milton Williams offer two useful benchmarks for what the Colts could pay their young defender.
A third-round pick in 2021, Odighizuwa steadily improved over his first four seasons in Dallas before signing a four-year, $80 million extension in March 2025. He was coming off a career-best 4.5 sacks in 2024 and had started all 17 games for the third consecutive season.
Like Adebawore, Odighizuwa developed into a productive interior pass rusher as a mid-round pick. However, he'd established himself as a full-time starter before signing his extension. If Adebawore seizes his opportunity following Buckner's departure, he could earn a similar deal, with Odighizuwa's $20 million annual average serving as a useful benchmark.
A breakdown of the takedowns. pic.twitter.com/11Mbysb1BL
Williams offers a higher-end comparison. After recording five sacks in 2024, he signed a four-year, $104 million contract with New England in March 2025, averaging $26 million annually. He'd combined for 6.5 sacks over his first three seasons in Philadelphia and started just 19 games across his first four years.
Williams' deal shows how quickly a defensive tackle's value can rise with consistent production. However, he entered free agency as one of the top players available at his position after helping Philadelphia win a Super Bowl, making his contract an upper-end comparison for Adebawore.
Ultimately, Adebawore's earning potential will depend on how much more he proves before the Colts decide whether to extend him, potentially waiting until the offseason when they can evaluate his full body of work.
If Adebawore sustains his production and establishes himself as a starter, a four-year deal worth $40 million to $60 million could be a reasonable projection. That would put his annual average between $10 million and $15 million, below Odighizuwa's $20 million benchmark but reflective of Adebawore's limited starting experience.
A four-year contract also makes sense for both sides. Indianapolis could secure a young defensive tackle through the next phase of its rebuild, while Adebawore would receive long-term financial security at 25 years old with another opportunity to reach free agency before he hits 30.
The Colts must also weigh the cost of waiting. An extension now could provide some cost certainty before Adebawore's role expands, but another productive season could make him more expensive to retain.
With Buckner gone, Adebawore has an opportunity to prove he deserves a long-term investment .

title: Colts' Asking Price for Two Defensive Linemen Just Went Up
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts have already shipped out two of their biggest names, and Thursday's blockbuster trade between the Tennessee Titans and Chicago Bears may have just made their next moves a whole lot more interesting.
The Titans are sending All-Pro defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons to the Bears in exchange for 2027 and 2028 first-round picks, plus a 2027 fourth-rounder. Chicago also receives a 2028 fifth-round pick.
Two first-round picks for a defensive tackle.
For Indianapolis, that deal could have serious implications for the trade value of Grover Stewart and Adetomiwa Adebawore, two defensive linemen who could be wearing different uniforms by the Nov. 10 deadline.
Simmons is undoubtedly one of the best interior defenders in football. The 29-year-old earned first-team All-Pro honors in 2025 after recording a career-high 11 sacks and already has four through seven games this season.
But that massive return gives Indianapolis something to work with as teams continue searching for defensive line help.
Now, Stewart and Adebawore aren't Simmons. Nobody should expect an early pick for either player, but the Titans may have just helped the Colts squeeze a little more value out of potential buyers.
The Colts only got a fourth-round pick back for DeForest Buckner, but they also chose to do right by him and Quenton Nelson, thus leaving some better packages on the table as they parted ways with two of their franchise cornerstones.
If Indianapolis waits until closer to the trade deadline on November 10th at 4 PM EST, they may just be able to drive up the price, even if marginally.
Because if this really is a true fire sale, Indianapolis needs to capitalize on every opportunity .
Stewart has spent his entire career in Indianapolis after being selected in the fourth round of the 2017 draft. For nearly a decade, he's been one of the most reliable run-stuffers on this defense.
But at 33 years old, entering the final months of his three-year, $39 million contract, it's time to move on.
I have nothing but appreciation for everything Stewart has given this franchise. Unfortunately, he simply doesn't fit the timeline of what this team is becoming.
By the time Indianapolis is ready to compete again, Stewart could very well be approaching retirement.
ESPN's Adam Schefter has already named Stewart among the Colts who could be moved before the deadline. After Thursday's blockbuster, Indianapolis should be looking to maximize his return .
Fourth-year defensive tackle Adetomiwa Adebawore presents a completely different situation .
At 25 years old, Tomi has recorded four sacks through seven games despite playing a limited number of defensive snaps. His 86.3 pass-rush grade ranks third among interior defenders, according to Pro Football Focus, and he is tied for second among defensives tackles with 4.0 sacks.
#Colts DT Adetomiwa Adebawore has the 2nd-most pressures (12) on the team (excl. Buckner) after seven weeks despite only playing 35.9% of snaps. He leads the defense in sacks (4.0), pressure rate (13.0%), and quick pressures (6), and has the second-most stops (13). pic.twitter.com/cqamb6tThI
That's exactly the kind of young, disruptive player Indianapolis should consider building around .
However, he's also entering free agency after this season, and NFL Network's Mike Garafolo reports that teams are already doing their homework on him in case Indianapolis makes him available.
From The Insiders on @nflnetwork : The #Colts ’ trades this week have other teams surveying their entire roster ahead of the deadline. DT Adetomiwa Adeboware has piqued interest in a breakout, contract year. Big payday coming for him soon, whether in Indy or elsewhere. pic.twitter.com/1KE7ojytWK
Would I love to see Tomi become a cornerstone of this next Colts defense? Absolutely.
But after watching Quenton Nelson and DeForest Buckner get shipped out, it's becoming increasingly difficult to consider anyone untouchable.
The Colts don't even own their 2027 first-round pick, making every additional draft selection that much more valuable.
If another team comes calling with an offer Indianapolis can't refuse, take it.
The next general manager deserves every possible resource to turn this franchise around. If the Colts are committed to tearing this thing down , they might as well squeeze every last bit of value out of it.
Michael Greene is a graduate of Indiana University and the Scouting Academy. He's in his first year covering the Indianapolis Colts and NFL, with a unique focus on fantasy football.

title: Why Colts Should Trade Jonathan Taylor Before the Deadline
full_text:
As the Indianapolis Colts continue their fire sale ahead of the Nov. 10 trade deadline, Jonathan Taylor's future with the team is in the balance.
After moving on from Quenton Nelson and DeForest Buckner , the Colts are facing another major decision about the direction of the franchise. Taylor's situation is more complicated than a typical veteran trade, and the latest reporting has only added to the uncertainty surrounding his future.
Jonathan Taylor has emerged as one of the most intriguing names ahead of the Nov. 10 trade deadline, with multiple teams reportedly exploring the possibility of acquiring the Indianapolis Colts running back.
According to ESPN's Adam Schefter and NFL Network's Ian Rapoport, the Green Bay Packers, Seattle Seahawks, Denver Broncos and Minnesota Vikings are among the teams that have considered a potential trade for Taylor. His superstar status makes him an appealing option for contenders looking to bolster their backfields for a championship push.
Despite that interest, the Colts don't appear eager to move their star running back.
Colts Owner/CEO Carlie Irsay-Gordon views Taylor as "a key part of the organization and a likely mainstay in their rebuild," according to ESPN Insiders Ian Rapoport and Adam Schefter , the latter of whom added that Indianapolis could change its stance if the right offer comes along, leaving the door open without signaling that a deal is imminent.
Head coach Shane Steichen reinforced that uncertainty Wednesday, telling reporters that Taylor had not requested a trade. "Those are hypothetical things right now," Steichen said. "I know there's stuff floating around out there, but JT's on our football team."
For now, the reporting points to a clear divide. Teams are interested in Taylor, but Indianapolis is reluctant to move him. Of course, that could change in the next week and a half, but for now, reports remain unfounded until proven otherwise.
The strongest argument for trading Jonathan Taylor is the opportunity to turn the Colts' most valuable trade assets into draft picks or other players to get Indy through the rebuild stage. Taylor, given his age and elite production, could bring back another significant return as the franchise reshapes its future.
The Colts need draft capital. Plain and simple. Indianapolis has already traded away its 2027 first-round pick at last year's deadline in the deal for cornerback Sauce Gardner, leaving the franchise without a high draft slot in 2027. Trading Taylor could help replenish that draft capital and give the front office more resources to address the rest of the roster.
ESPN's Adam Schefter and Ian Rapoport reported that acquiring Taylor would likely require premium draft compensation, making him a potentially valuable bargaining chip.
Additionally, Taylor's timeline may not match the rebuild. The 27-year-old is still in his prime, but running backs tend to have shorter productive windows than players at many other positions.
If Indianapolis needs multiple seasons to rebuild its roster and return to contention, Taylor will be approaching the latter stages of his career by the time the team is ready to compete again. Trading him now would allow the Colts to capitalize on his current value rather than risk that value declining while the franchise works toward a turnaround.
In other words, the return Taylor would net could be more valuable than keeping him. Taylor is one of the league's most productive running backs, which makes him an attractive target for teams trying to contend in 2027. That gives Indianapolis a chance to acquire premium draft picks or other young talent that could contribute over the next couple of years. With the Colts already willing to move established players, holding onto Taylor simply because he's a star would mean passing up a chance to accelerate the rebuild.
If a team is willing to pay a premium for his services, the Colts have a legitimate reason to consider it.
Trading Jonathan Taylor would give Indianapolis another opportunity to add draft capital, but it would also mean losing one of the NFL's most productive running backs. The Colts need assets to rebuild their roster, but they also need proven talent to help the team compete again. Whether a trade makes sense ultimately depends on what Indianapolis could get in return.
Taylor is still producing at an elite level. Through seven games, Taylor has rushed for 587 yards (5th in NFL) and eight touchdowns (T-1st), putting him among the NFL's most productive running backs. He remains a central part of the Colts' offense and has continued to produce despite the team's struggles. Finding a replacement capable of matching that production would be difficult, even with additional draft capital.
Taylor signed a two-year, $44 million extension in August, keeping him under contract through 2028. Unlike Nelson and Buckner, who were both in the final year of their deals, Taylor isn't approaching free agency. The Colts have time to evaluate the direction of the rebuild without having to trade him before the deadline to avoid losing him for nothing.
A rebuild also doesn't have to mean starting over completely. Taylor is 27, meaning he could still have several productive seasons ahead of him. If Indianapolis can accelerate its turnaround, he could remain a key piece of the offense when the team returns to contention. Keeping a proven star also gives the next edition of the Colts a foundational player rather than forcing the front office to find replacements at every position.
Ultimately, Indianapolis shouldn't trade Taylor just for the sake of it, only if they receive an offer that will benefit the organization moving forward.
At this point, the Colts have more incentive to trade Jonathan Taylor than to keep him.
Indianapolis has already begun dismantling its veteran core, and moving its most valuable remaining player would give the franchise another opportunity to acquire assets for the rebuild. Taylor's stardom makes him difficult to replace, but that alone shouldn't hold the Colts back from making a deal.
The biggest factor is the team's timeline. Taylor is still in his prime, but Indianapolis has significant work to do before it can realistically return to contention. Taylor's career timeline and the Colts' rebuilding timeline don't line up.
By the time the Colts are ready to contend again, Taylor could be nearing the end of his most productive years. Trading him now would allow the franchise to capitalize on his value while giving the next front office more resources.
Taylor's most comparable trade package is that of Christian McCaffrey's blockbuster haul from 2022.
In exchange for McCaffrey, the Panthers received a 2023 NFL Draft second-round pick, a 2023 third-rounder, a 2023 fourth-rounder, and a 2024 fifth-round pick.
The bidding for Taylor likely starts with multiple Day 2 (Rounds 2-3) draft selections, but if a contender comes calling with what they believe will be a late first-round pick, the Colts would be irresponsible to turn it down. Even then, multiple Day 2 picks would be a strong haul.
Keeping Taylor would make more sense if the Colts believed they could turn things around quickly. But the recent trades of Nelson and Buckner suggest Indianapolis is looking beyond the current roster. Holding onto Taylor while moving other established players would make less sense if the goal is to accumulate assets and reshape the team for the future.
Taylor is one of the league's best running backs, and Indianapolis should take the best return package possible. The Colts need to build for their next competitive window, and moving Taylor is an important step toward doing that.

title: Fire Sale: Potential Trade Packages for 3 Remaining Colts Stars
full_text:
Quenton Nelson and DeForest Buckner are gone. Two pillars of the Indianapolis Colts over the past decade were shipped out on Tuesday , and nobody feels untouchable anymore.
Indianapolis received a 2027 third-round pick and a 2028 fifth-rounder for Nelson, plus a 2027 fourth-round pick for Buckner. Both were on expiring deals, but that return still hurts.
At 2-5, the rest of this season could get brutal. All Colts fans can do is appreciate what these guys gave us, collect draft picks and hope the next regime gets it right.
With the Nov. 10 deadline approaching, here are three hypothetical trade packages these Colts might demand.
Proposed Trade: Denver Broncos send a 2027 first-round pick and 2028 fourth-round pick.
I'm not trading JT for a couple of mid-round picks. Unlike Nelson and Buckner, Taylor is under contract through 2028 after signing a two-year, $44 million extension in August.
Through seven games, he has 587 rushing yards and a league-leading eight touchdowns. He's 27, still the centerpiece of this offense, and by far Indianapolis' most valuable trade asset.
Denver is among the teams ESPN has linked to Taylor, although no offer has been reported. Shane Steichen said Wednesday that Taylor hasn't requested a trade, and Adam Schefter reports that owner Carlie Irsay-Gordon wants to keep him .
"[Carlie] Irsay-Gordon views [Jonathan] Taylor as a key part of the organization and a likely mainstay in their rebuild," Schefter said.
Fine by me. But if somebody wants JT, I'm demanding a massive haul. Ideally, you'd send him to an NFC team, but if an AFC contender comes calling with an offer you can't refuse, you have to consider it.
Also, the Colts don't own their 2027 first-rounder, so I want one back for the league's best RB.
Taylor netting a first-round pick would certainly be unprecedented and would no doubt be considered an overpay, but if the Colts play their cards right, they may just convince a potential suitor to pull the trigger.
Taylor's most comparable trade package is that of Christian McCaffrey's blockbuster haul from 2022.
In exchange for McCaffrey, the Panthers received a 2023 NFL Draft second-round pick, a 2023 third-rounder, a 2023 fourth-rounder, and a 2024 fifth-round pick.
The bidding for Taylor likely starts with multiple Day 2 (Rounds 2-3) draft selections, but if a contender comes calling with what they believe will be a late first-round pick, the Colts would be irresponsible to turn it down.
Proposed Trade: Pittsburgh Steelers send a 2027 fifth-round pick and 2028 sixth-round pick.
This one stings. Josh Downs has been one of my favorite young players to watch, and I never expected him to be part of this teardown.
ESPN's Jeremy Fowler reported Wednesday that Downs requested a trade , confirming that his days in Indianapolis are numbered.
Sources: Colts WR Josh Downs is requesting a trade from Indianapolis. pic.twitter.com/rwGaVGMTFf
The 25-year-old has 26 catches for 307 yards and no touchdowns through seven games, and his rookie contract expires after this season.
Multiple AFC teams, including the Pittsburgh Steelers, are reportedly interested in trading for Downs, according to NFL Insider Jordan Schultz .
Two Day 3 picks aren't exciting, but they're better than gambling on potential compensatory help down the road.
I still believe Downs can become one of the league's best receivers in the right offense.
Proposed Trade: Green Bay Packers send a 2027 sixth-round pick.
Big Grove has been holding down Indianapolis' run defense since 2017. He deserves plenty of appreciation for that, but at 33 and on an expiring contract, it's probably time to part ways.
His value is primarily against the run, not as a pass rusher. That limits the market, but I think a sixth-round pick is a reasonable return for a veteran who can still contribute against the run.
Moving Stewart would leave another hole along this defensive line. But a rebuilding team needs those draft picks, and getting something now beats watching another veteran walk in March.
None of this is easy to watch. If Tuesday taught us anything, it's that nobody's legacy guarantees they'll finish their career in Indianapolis.
The memories aren't going anywhere. The front office just needs to turn these departures into future Colts legends.
Michael Greene is a graduate of Indiana University and the Scouting Academy. He's in his first year covering the Indianapolis Colts and NFL, with a unique focus on fantasy football.

title: Biggest Colts Winners of Fire Sale: Two Young Players Get Massive Opportunity
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts may be punting on the 2026 season, but their future has some bright spots on the roster.
Colts' Owner/CEO Carlie Irsay-Gordon has kicked off the team's rebuild with a fire sale of the roster's best players , trading away longtime franchise pillars Quenton Nelson and DeForest Buckner on Tuesday.
The Colts are aiming to add any draft capital they can for the next era by shopping their top players, and this exodus began with the trading of the franchise's most pivotal staples.
Indianapolis's immediate outlook looks bleaker than ever before, but there are two players who have been granted a massive opportunity as a result.
If these two Colts can prove their worth, the next regime's year-one outlook may not be as dire as these trades suggest it'll be.
The biggest winner of the DeForest Buckner trade is Colts defensive tackle Adetomiwa Adebawore.
The fourth-year interior defensive lineman has been an intriguing player since the Colts drafted him in the fourth round (110th overall) of the 2023 NFL Draft.
Adebawore's absurd athletic profile was enough to entice, but his pass-rush potential excited most.
The talented young pass rusher flashed his intriguing skills across his first two seasons in the NFL, but he still had a long way to go in run defense before he could be considered for a bigger role.
Of course, the longtime interior duo of DeForest Buckner and Grover Stewart made it nearly impossible for any defensive tackle to carve out a three-down role in the Colts' defense, but Buckner's departure changes everything.
Not only is the opportunity there, but Adebawore has earned the increased role in question.
Adebawore's first two seasons suggested that he'd likely be a designated pass rusher for the foreseeable future, but a quiet, mini-breakout in his third season single-handedly changed his trajectory.
Below are Adebawore's pass-rush numbers throughout his first three seasons (2023-25) in the NFL:
2023 (rookie): 20.7% playing time, 1.5 sacks, 7.6% pressure rate, 3 defensive stops 2024: 17.9% playing time, 1.0 sacks, 6.7% pressure rate, 4 defensive stops 2025: 46.8% playing time, 4.0 sacks, 10.2% pressure rate, 24 defensive stops
The upward trajectory was apparent, and Adebawore has locked in to fully break out after seven games in the 2026 regular season.
Adebawore struggled to find playing time to start the new year, but has since earned the trust of defensive coordinator Lou Anarumo and the rest of the staff.
After seven weeks, Adebawore is undeniably the Colts' best pass rusher. He is currently tied for second with the most sacks among interior defensive linemen league-wide and leads the team in most major pass-rush statistics.
#Colts DT Adetomiwa Adebawore has the 2nd-most pressures (12) on the team (excl. Buckner) after seven weeks despite only playing 35.9% of snaps. He leads the defense in sacks (4.0), pressure rate (13.0%), and quick pressures (6), and has the second-most stops (13). pic.twitter.com/cqamb6tThI
We've known that Adebawore has some nasty pass-rushing chops, but the biggest development has been his improvement in run defense.
Adebawore has blossomed into a legitimate starting defensive tackle, and it comes at no better time as the Colts have parted ways with their longtime pillar across the defensive line.
However, the Colts' newfound star is on an expiring deal. Adebawore is playing in the final year of his rookie contract, so a big payday is set to come his way.
The Colts are understandably busy shopping their failed era's best assets, but if they want to truly maximize the next regime's early outlook, extending Adebawore should be near the organization's top priorities moving forward.
A similar big opportunity has presented itself for one of the Colts' players still on a rookie contract: first-year guard Jalen Farmer.
Unlike Adebawore's situation, Farmer still has to prove himself as a legitimate NFL player
The Colts drafted Farmer in the fourth round (113th overall) of the 2026 NFL Draft, envisioning that he'll become OL Coach Tony Sparano Jr.'s next installment of successful draft-and-stash projects .
Indianapolis was prepared to treat Farmer's rookie season like a redshirt year as they roll with their proven veteran unit, but Quenton Nelson's departure has changed the trajectory entirely.
Instead, a Hall of Fame-sized hole now sits across the Colts' interior offensive line, and Farmer is set to take over as we approach the midway point of the 2026 regular season.
Although he is an unproven rookie, Tony Sparano Jr. has the utmost faith in Farmer's ability .
As Sparano Jr. famously said following the Colts' combine interview with Farmer, "Let me tell you this much. Draft him, and I'll make it work."
Sparano Jr.’s conviction in Jalen Farmer is so apparent, not only by his own words, but also by the #Colts war room’s reaction when he arrives to celebrate said draft selection. 🎥: @Colts https://t.co/RxH86gKHkC pic.twitter.com/EFmmsUSYYe
In just a few short years with the Colts, Sparano Jr. has successfully developed the likes of LT Bernhard Raimann, RG Will Fries, RG Matt Goncalves, and C Tanor Bortolini.
Second-year tackle Jalen Travis has had an up-and-down start to his first season as a full-time starter, but there's still hope that he can become the ideal longtime Braden Smith replacement.
And it's easy to see why Sparano Jr. believes that Jalen Farmer will be his next successful project.
Farmer sports a strong athletic profile, has ample experience at the position (although he's mainly played right guard), and possesses a ton of raw power.
The Colts' rookie guard will be going from special teams duties to filling the void that Quenton Nelson left.
Even though this season is lost, the Colts have granted themselves a promising evaluation period of pieces that could stick with them through this ongoing fire sale and kick off the new era.
Farmer and Adebawore have a 10-game trial period to prove that they deserve to be long-term pieces of the rebuild.
Noah Compton is the Publisher of Indianapolis Colts On SI. Noah is from the Indy area and has been covering the Colts since 2022, including stops at FanSided, The Blue Stable, and SBNation.

title: Josh Downs' Trade Request Pushes Colts Further Toward Full Rebuild
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts ' roster teardown is gaining momentum, and Josh Downs could be the next player out the door.
The fourth-year wide receiver has officially requested a trade, according to ESPN's Jeremy Fowler, as Indianapolis continues its roster renovation following the departures of Quenton Nelson and DeForest Buckner .
Downs' request presents another pivotal decision for a team that's already begun looking towards the future. With the Nov. 10 trade deadline approaching, the Colts must do right by Downs and get him into a better situation while picking up assets for the future simultaneously .
Downs' trade request, his comments Wednesday and the frustration he's shown in recent weeks all point toward a receiver who wants a change of scenery.
Asked about the possibility of a trade, Downs told reporters, "I'm open to whatever. Whatever comes my way comes my way, and we go from there."
He was also asked whether he would have preferred to sign an extension before the season, responding, "I mean, if it came my way, it came my way, but like I wouldn't say that."
Josh Downs talks potential trade + if he wanted a contract extension: pic.twitter.com/w2KuKEmym3
Downs' frustration is understandable. He's in the final year of his rookie contract and has watched the Colts' season spiral while struggling to influence games himself. Despite Alec Pierce missing significant time, Downs has recorded just 307 receiving yards and no touchdowns through seven games.
With Indianapolis trading away established veterans and shifting its focus toward the future, Downs has little reason to wait around for the franchise to find its footing. A trade would give him a chance to finish the season in a better situation and increase his market value heading into free agency.
The Pittsburgh Steelers have emerged as one potential destination for Downs, with NFL insider Jordan Schultz reporting that multiple AFC teams have expressed interest in the Colts receiver. While a deal wasn't considered likely this week, Schultz reported that a trade is expected to happen eventually.
#Colts WR Josh Downs has received interest from multiple AFC teams, including the #Steelers , and while a deal is not considered likely this week, the expectation is a trade will eventually happen, per sources. pic.twitter.com/lZ5rH5YyIF
The Kansas City Chiefs are another team worth watching.
Kansas City has dealt with injuries to its receiving corps and could use another reliable target for Patrick Mahomes. Downs' ability to work underneath and create separation from the slot would give the Chiefs another option in the passing game. The New England Patriots could also make sense given Downs' familiarity with quarterback Drake Maye from their time together at North Carolina.
Downs is in the final year of his rookie deal, and an acquiring team would have about 10 games minimum to decide if Downs is someone they want to retain, or if he's just a rental.
As for compensation, a Day 3 draft pick seems like a reasonable target for Indianapolis.
Downs hasn't established himself as a No. 1 receiver, and his modest production this season could limit what teams are willing to offer. Still, his age and remaining upside should give the Colts a chance to recoup an asset before he potentially leaves in free agency.
Trading Nelson and Buckner sent a clear message to the rest of the league: Indianapolis is willing to move on from the core it spent years building.
Downs' request makes it even harder for the Colts to justify holding onto players who may not fit their long-term plans.
There are other decisions to make before the deadline. Grover Stewart and Keenan Allen are among the players whose expiring contracts could make them trade candidates, giving interim general manager Ed Dodds more opportunities to recoup assets. Neither move is a foregone conclusion, but both deserve consideration as Indianapolis evaluates what comes next.
The goal shouldn't be to tear down the roster without a plan. It should be to identify the players who can contribute to the Colts’ next competitive window and determine what the others are worth on the trade market.
Downs has made his preference clear, and Indianapolis has already shown it is willing to make moves. The decisions made over the next week and a half should reflect the same commitment to the future.

title: What the Quenton Nelson Trade Means for Colts' Future
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts made a major move Tuesday, trading six-time All-Pro guard Quenton Nelson to the Seattle Seahawks as the franchise looks to find its footing after a disappointing stretch.
Nelson's departure marks a significant change of direction for the Colts, who have gone from attempting to contend for a playoff spot earlier this season to now gearing up for a rebuild.
But there are questions surrounding where the Colts can go from here.
The Colts have a potential replacement for Nelson waiting in the wings already.
Rookie Jalen Farmer could get his first opportunity to fill the void at left guard, giving the team a chance to evaluate whether he can become a long-term starter. Indianapolis selected Farmer in the fourth round of the 2026 NFL Draft, initially as a depth and developmental piece.
Former general manager Chris Ballard said the Colts had targeted Farmer earlier in the draft and compared him to Bernhard Raimann, another offensive lineman the organization developed into a starter.
Offensive line coach Tony Sparano Jr. was equally enthusiastic about the Kentucky product, praising his power, ability to anchor, and run-blocking skills. You may remember Sparano telling fellow staff members, "Let me tell you this much. Draft him and I'll make it work," after the Colts met with Farmer at the NFL Combine.
#Colts OL Coach Tony Sparano Jr.’s combine interview with G Jalen Farmer showcased a match made in heaven of sorts. “Let me tell you this much. Draft him and I’ll make it work.” 🎥: @Colts pic.twitter.com/WH9HDbSy7S
With Nelson now in Seattle, Farmer has a clearer path to playing time. He spent his college career at right guard, so transitioning to the left side would present a new challenge, but not an impossible one.
Still, the Colts' investment in him and their confidence in his potential make him an intriguing option to fill the position beyond just this season. Farmer will have to prove he can handle the responsibilities of an NFL starter, and there will undoubtedly be some bumps at first, but the opportunity is significant.
Rather than immediately searching outside the organization for Nelson's successor, Indianapolis can use the remainder of the season to evaluate whether Farmer can be a part of the plan moving forward.
Losing Nelson creates another challenge for an Indianapolis offense that needs to find more consistency in the run game.
The six-time All-Pro was the team's most reliable blocker - arguably one of the greatest run blockers in NFL history - and his departure leaves a significant hole in the interior of the offensive line.
The Colts have already seen how difficult it can be to establish the run when their blocking struggles. Indianapolis managed just 66 rushing yards against Pittsburgh in Week 5, despite relying heavily on Jonathan Taylor to carry the offense. Nelson was one of the few bright spots in that performance, earning an 81.9 run-blocking grade from Pro Football Focus.
Taylor showed what he can still do against Minnesota, rushing for 95 yards and a touchdown in Sunday's loss, but maintaining that production will become more difficult without Nelson in front of him.
The adjustment also creates an opportunity for the remaining linemen to prove they can handle larger roles. Assuming Farmer gets the chance to start at left guard, his ability to open running lanes for Taylor will be one of the biggest things to watch.
The Colts need to see whether their younger linemen can fill the void left by Nelson without the ground game taking a step backward. And if Taylor is also dealt as part of the Colts' ongoing fire sale, the next era will be fully embraced, but the run game will bring forgotten lows.
By moving off Nelson and his contract, the Colts are giving their next general manager some flexibility as the organization looks to reshape the roster.
The trade compensation gives Indianapolis additional resources to work with. The Colts acquired a third-round pick in the 2027 NFL Draft and a fifth-round selection in 2028, giving the next general manager more draft capital to address the team's needs.
Indianapolis is also projected to have roughly $88 million in salary cap space next offseason, giving the next general manager considerable financial flexibility. Nelson's departure won't directly increase that figure, as his contract was already set to expire after the 2026 season. However, the trade allows the Colts to move forward without having to negotiate a new deal with one of their longtime stars while bringing back valuable draft capital in return.
Nelson's departure gives the next general manager more freedom to evaluate the roster and establish a new direction---his or her own direction. With additional draft picks, significant projected cap space and the opportunity to assess younger players like Farmer, the remainder of the season will help determine who the Colts want to be a part of their rebuild.

title: Colts' Future Comes Into Focus After Parting Ways With Two Trench Staples
full_text:
When it rains, it pours. And it's coming down in buckets over Indianapolis.
The Colts have made two major changes to their roster, trading away two of their most recognizable players as the franchise looks to chart a new course after a disappointing season.
After sending eight-time Pro Bowl guard Quenton Nelson to the Seattle Seahawks for a 2027 third-round pick and a 2028 fifth-round pick, Indianapolis also traded defensive tackle DeForest Buckner to the San Francisco 49ers in exchange for 2027 fourth-round pick.
With both veterans gone, Indianapolis faces significant questions about both its immediate and long-term future. Let's attempt to answer what the next several months may look like.
The Colts have little time to adjust after trading away two of the most established players on their roster. There's still football left to play, but with Nelson and Buckner gone, Indianapolis is officially headed for a lost season.
Rather than mail it in, the Colts should use the remaining games to evaluate the players who are still there. The departures create opportunities for younger players to take on larger roles and show whether they belong in the team's plans moving forward.
Indianapolis could also make more moves before the Nov. 10 trade deadline. Veterans such as Keenan Allen, Grover Stewart and Charvarius Ward could attract interest from contenders if the Colts decide to pursue additional draft compensation for their next general manager to work with.
By the end of the season, Indianapolis should have a clearer picture of which players can contribute to its next competitive roster and where reinforcements will be needed.
Trading Nelson and Buckner leaves significant holes on both lines. Each was an established starter and leader at his position, making their departures consequential beyond the immediate impact on the depth chart.
Offensively, Indianapolis must find a replacement for Nelson at left guard. Rookie Jalen Farmer, a fourth-round pick in the most recent draft, is one option. He should receive a 10-game trial run the rest of the season so the Colts can determine whether he can be part of the team's long-term plans.
Buckner's departure creates a similar challenge on the defensive line. More responsibility will fall on the remaining interior defenders, including Stewart and Adetomiwa Adebawore. The Colts have to find out if Adebawore, a free agent at the end of the season, is a pillar they want to build around.
How Indianapolis handles those vacancies will be a crucial part of its roster evaluation. The goal isn't necessarily to find direct replacements for two established stars, but to build offensive and defensive lines capable of supporting the team's next competitive window.
The Colts' longer-term outlook will depend heavily on who takes over as general manager and how that person chooses to approach the roster. Indianapolis still has talent, but the new decision-maker will have to identify which players he or she deems as viable options moving forward.
The trades also provide additional draft capital. Indianapolis acquired a 2027 third-round pick and a 2028 fifth-round pick for Nelson, adding to the compensation received for Buckner. However, the Colts still don't have their 2027 first-round pick after sending it to the New York Jets for cornerback Sauce Gardner.
That makes the team's remaining draft assets especially important. The next general manager will need to weigh the value of adding young talent against the opportunity to address immediate needs through free agency.
Moving veteran contracts could also create more financial flexibility, depending on the details of each deal. That would give the next GM more options to retain key players, pursue outside additions or continue reshaping the roster.
Ultimately, Indianapolis has created an opportunity to take the team in a different direction. The next general manager will have to decide how much of the current foundation is worth keeping around. Those deemed to not be worth retaining must make their way out of the building one way or another.
Needless to say, primary owner and CEO Carlie Irsay-Gordon has a big hire to make in the not-so-distant future.

title: Thank You, Big Q: Remembering a Colts Legend
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts traded their longest-tenured player to the Seattle Seahawks on Tuesday for a 2027 third-round pick and a 2028 fifth-rounder. Two mid-round picks for one of the greatest offensive linemen in franchise history.
I always thought Big Q would retire in Indianapolis. I thought he would spend his entire career wearing the Horseshoe, walk into the Hall of Fame one day and have the Colts attached to his name forever.
Instead, one of the best players to ever put on a Colts uniform is heading to Seattle.
Nelson was the No. 6 overall pick in 2018, and it did not take long to realize Indianapolis had something special. He became the first guard in NFL history to win Offensive Rookie of the Month and immediately helped change the identity of an offensive line that desperately needed one.
From there, the accolades became almost automatic.
Nelson made the Pro Bowl in each of his first eight seasons, becoming the first player in Colts history to accomplish that and only the second offensive lineman in NFL history to do it, joining Hall of Fame tackle Joe Thomas.
He was also a three-time First-Team All-Pro from 2018-20 before adding three Second-Team selections in 2021, 2024 and 2025.
That is six All-Pro selections in eight completed seasons.
And somehow, the awards still do not tell the entire story.
Nelson brought an edge to this offense that is hard to quantify. He didn't just block defenders; he punished them, played through the whistle, and made sure everyone around him played with that same intensity.
Seriously, how many offensive guards have a highlight tape you would willingly sit down and watch? Big Q was different.
The consistency was just as ridiculous. Nelson started 136 games for Indianapolis and missed only four, all during the 2021 season.
Even at 30 years old, he was still playing like one of the best guards in football. Through seven games this season, Nelson had allowed zero sacks and only six pressures, while his 86.6 PFF grade ranked third among qualified guards.
I understand the business side. Nelson is in the final year of his contract, the Colts are 2-5, Chris Ballard is gone and this franchise is clearly looking toward what comes next.
But some players mean more than the draft picks attached to their name.
Nelson was toughness. He was consistency. He was the backbone of this offensive line for nearly a decade and represented everything you could ask for in an Indianapolis Colt.
In my eyes, Big Q is a future Hall of Famer and one of the best Colts to ever wear the Horseshoe.
Man, I am going to miss watching No. 56 in Indianapolis.
Michael Greene is a graduate of Indiana University and the Scouting Academy. He's in his first year covering the Indianapolis Colts and NFL, with a unique focus on fantasy football.

title: Jaguars Mailbag: Colts Game Could Impact the Trade Deadline in More Ways Than One
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- It is starting to get wild in the NFL.
The NFL Trade Deadline is right around the corner and the action has ramped up throughout the AFC South. With the deadline looming, as does the Jaguars' Week 8 matchup with the Indianapolis Colts in an important divisional battle. We take questions on both of these big events and much more in this week's Jaguars Mailbag.
Are the Jaguars generating enough pressure without relying on sacks, or is their defensive approach leaving too much on the table?
A: I do think the pressure has been relatively fine. I think if the Jaguars had less passes thrown over the secondary's head in the last few weeks, the worries about low sack totals would go away some. But whenever big plays are consistently getting made, the pass-rush is going to draw focus when they are not making the plays to offset any potential coverage woes. The Jaguars could be better here, but I do not think it is an issue of approach. I also think the Jaguars get several sacks this week against Daniel Jones.
Do you foresee any random changes with the offense or defense coming out of the bye? Like certain players getting more snaps/substitutions etc
A: I think we could start seeing more and more snaps for Ruke Orhorhoro and Albert Regis. I think the Jaguars are really happy with the momentum that Orhorhoro was able to build before the bye week, while Regis has gotten praise from both head coach Liam Coen and defensive coordinator Anthony Campanile for his work in practice. This would mean, to me, fewer snaps for both Arik Armstead and Matt Dickerson.
With all the talk of adding a player to the DL - who do you think ends up with the most sacks at the end of the year, and what is their total?
A: Josh Hines-Allen with 9.5. I think he heats up as the year goes on, especially if the Jaguars add some help to change the way protections are shifted to him. Travon Walker isn't a bad shout, either, though I do think Hines-Allen will be set for more chances to close in on sacks than Walker over the next few months.
Some no so serious questions: What's your go-to restaurant? Favorite food? Favorite/Least Favorite moment covering the Jags so far? Jaguars Uniform (Past, present, Rivalries™, etc.) takes? With the holidays approaching, any holiday takes you need to get off your chest?
2) Favorite moment: covering the AFC South title win in 2022. Least favorite? Covering Day 3 of the 2023 NFL Draft. They made a million picks and half of them were grotesque. Some were awesome, though.
3) I love the teal helmets they are wearing Sunday. Still not sure what the heck those white helmets were in 2024.
4) This is the best stretch of holidays. Halloween into Thanksgiving into Christmas.
Is D-line the only trade Gladstone would make or is their another position that could significantly improve the team?
I think the Jaguars could add a number of different positions at the trade deadline that would make them a better team. Defensive end? Check. Defensive tackle? Double check. Safety? Sure! Cornerback? Yep. Even offensive tackle. The Jaguars are a good team, but like any team they still have some flaws to address.
What are the odds of Camp and Udinski leaving in the offseason? And if so, any in house successor candidates or just outside hires?
A: I think the chances are high, especially if the Jaguars keep winning. I would say Udinksi would be the most likely coach to leave since teams tend to lean toward young offensive hires and Udinski would check both of those boxes. I think Campanile will get some interviews, though, and there is always the chance that he gets the nod. I think Shane Waldron getting promoted to offensive coordinator would be a natural move, while defensively I could see Coen going for an outside name with ties. Ejiro Evero , perhaps?
Oklahoma drill, Apollo vs Ketchup…who wins?
A: Ketchup in a landslide. Apollo is a lover, not a fighter. Actually, he isn't even a lover. He just is kind of happy to be there. He is more of a backup quarterback than a lineman. Apollo and Ketchup are mine and Gus Logue's dogs, by the way.
If Montaric Brown comes back fully healthy, do you think Jarrian and Lewis rotate in or is someone the odd man out
A: It does look like the Jaguars will have Montaric Brown back on the field this Sunday against the Colts, which I think is a big deal even with his earlier struggles this season. Without Brown on the field, the Jaguars have been forced to only really rely on their top-three cornerbacks no matter the situations, playy-calls, packages, or matchups. By having Brown available, I think it just gives the Jaguars more options. I think Travis Hunter plays every snap, and then the other three guys play rleatively the same amount of snaps as one another.
if Jags trade for budda or any other safety, who goes to the bench between Eric Murray and Antonio Johnson?
A: I think if there had to be one guy who would see fewer snaps over the course of the year as a result of a safety getting added to the mix, it would be Eric Murray. Antonio Johnson has been their best safety this year, whether in coverage or in space as a tackler. He’s also arguably the best blitzer on the entire defense. With that said, I think the Jaguars’ response to a good problem like this would be to lean on all three safeties, whether with rotations or with three-safety sets.
How many targets does Hunter get on offense rest of season?
A: I am going to say …. 30. There are 11 games left, so at least two per game on average and then a few games where he gets more than that. I could see it get closer to 40 if there are weeks like Houston where he just seems to be the hot hand when it comes to the passing game.
I know I have an issue w/being patient & instant gratification, especially w/3 trades this past week, but any surprise the Jags didnt make a move at the bye? Do you think they're waiting on players availablily? Price to go down? They trust their guys/self-scout made during bye?
A: I think they just aren't in a hurry, and they shouldn't be. We still have a week-and-a-half until the trade deadline, and the Jaguars did not make their move for Jakobi Meyers last year until the day of the deadline despite having checked in with the Raiders as early as the 2025 training camp. I think a move happens, but not until closer to the deadline.
Why aren’t linemen and linebackers wearing full face face masks anymore?
Do opposing QBs having quick release time because of our pressure rate or are receivers getting open that fast because of off coverage? I have to imagine, the reason we get so many picks is because our CBs are counting on the quick release time and can sit on short routes
A: You are exactly right. Anthony Campanile said that a lot of the times aquarterbacks are getting the ball out fast is because the Jaguars' defense is intentional about forcing it out of their hands quickly. This suggests to me that Campanile puts most of the onus for the big plays on the secondary behind the pressures and the blitzes.
How serious are trade talks for btj? Any teams at the forefront?
A: This is just my own take, but I do not think the Jaguars will be actively looking to shop him. I think he is enough of a talent and a big name that his production shops him for the Jaguars, and eventually teams will be aggressive in gauging his value. Since we have yet to see a trade completed, I would say the only assumption to make is that they have yet to get a very serious offer for him. Will that change? Stay tuned over the next few weeks.
If Brian Thomas rebounds and plays well this week, it could obviously affect his trade value, but do you see that having any effect on if he remains a jaguar or not?
A: This is a great quesiton. I really do not think the Jaguars will sell low on Brian Thomas Jr., and I believe it will take something worthwhile for the Jaguars to officially give up on him. With that said, I think even if Thomas has a breakout game for the first time in a long time, he…

title: 3 NFL Trade Deadline Deals the Jaguars Should Explore Right Now in Wide-Open AFC
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The NFL trade market has heated up in a big way this week, with three All-Pros traded from the AFC South alone since Tuesday.
Whether the Jaguars will get in on the trade action remains to be seen, but it is always fun to project anyways. The Jaguars have made a number of trades since James Gladstone took over, with the Jaguars' general manager completing nine non-draft day trades involving players since he was hired.
This includes trading for Jakobi Meyers at the trade deadline a year ago, a move that instantly gave the Jaguars a boost and has paid off since. And while it was a draft-day trade, Gladstone's biggest move as general manager was the 2025 blockbuster for Travis Hunter.
James Gladstone's Player Trades
2026 5th-Round Pick, 2026 6th-Round Pick
CB Tyson Campbell, 2026 7th-Round Pick
CB Greg Newsome, 2026 6th-Round Pick
2026 4th-Round Pick, 2026 6th-Round Pick
In short, the Jaguars have been pretty agressive in terms of trades. They made a move last season with the idea of winning, and it would make sense to do the same this year. But which targets would make the most sense, and which deals could make it happen? We break it down below.
The Offer: Brian Thomas Jr.
Let's get weird? I would also think picks have to be involved, with the Jaguars perhaps sending a seventh-round pick and getting a fourth-round selection in return. Thomas would have much, much more value in terms of draft picks landed in a trade if this was just a player-for-picks deal, but adding a productive veteran like Payne would be enticing. Payne is still in his prime at 29 and is a legit difference-maker against both the run and the pass, but he is under contract for just 11 more games.
Landing Payne as a rental would likely not be ideal, even if the Jaguars would likely be able to recoup something for him in the form of compensatory draft picks in the future. But with several expiring contracts along the interior defensive line, the Jaguars could look to Payne as a defensive version of Jakobi Meyers: a productive, experienced player who can bring an instant impact and sign a deal shortly after as a result.
Letting go of Thomas will always sting a bit for the Jaguars if it does happen. That is why if the Jaguars do trade Thomas, they must get something worthwhile in return. Considering Payne's fit and talent and the need for a difference-maker insider, he would certainly qualify as worthwhile. This could help push the Jaguars' defense over the top and have a minimal impact on the offense. This wouldn't be as explosive as a Jeffery Simmons deal, but Payne could have a similar impact in terms of improving the entire unit.
The Offer: 2027 3rd-Round Pick
Another defensive tackle, and for good reason. As SI's Albert Breer noted, "The Giants and Jaguars are sniffing around on defensive tackles—Jacksonville’s looking for pieces for its defensive front in general." It makes sense considering the Jaguars have a short-term need for a spark inside, as well as a long-term need for a new centerpiece for the interior defensive line. When it comes to potentially available defensive tackle targets, Ojomo is up there with Payne while also being four years younger and still ascending as a talent.
The Jaguars' fit with Ojomo makes a ton of sense off the bat. He has been disruptive against both the run and the pass, he is young and is still getting better each season, he fits the scheme like a glove, and he would give the Jaguars a talent boost at a key position of need. The question, of course, has to do with the fact that he is in a contract year. This could impact what the Eagles do quite a bit considering the options they would have if they didn't trade Ojomo.
If the Eagles opt not to trade Ojomo, then there are only two outcomes for them ahead: signing him to a big deal to give them the most expensive defensive tackle room in NFL history, or letting him walk in free agency for what very likely could be a future third-round compensatory pick, depending on how big of a deal he signs and what other moves the Eagles make. This is exactly what happened with Milton Williams, and it is not hard to see Ojomo cashing in like he did.
If you are the Jaguars, I think you accept the fact that the Eagles' asking price would be a third-round pick today. Jacksonville could live with that depending on how they play free agency next March and depending on just how much Ojomo would improve them. He is worth the swing, though.
The Offer: 2027 5th-Round Pick
It is really easy to make the case for the Jaguars to add a guy like Budda Baker. They are hurting at the safety position, having all three of their top safeties available for just the first three games of the season. Since then, Eric Murray has missed some time, Antonio Johnson is now banged-up, and Caleb Ransaw is on injured reserve. Adding a safety would help the Jaguars quite a bit in the short-term.
Then you add in the fact that Budda Baker has been one of the NFL's best and most productive, reliable, and durable safeties of the last decade, and it is easy to see the fit. Baker played the Rams twice a year during James Gladstone's and Liam Coen's time in Los Angeles, and the 30-year-old would clearly carry a ton of respect in the Jaguars' building, while serving as a legit fit and play-maker.
The Cardinals are not going anywhere during the next season-and-a-half Baker is under contract, and he would allow the Jaguars to confidently play three-safety sets once Johnson is healthy. A trio of Johnson, Murray, and Baker would be quite the group for the Jaguars at the safety position as they look to make a run for the AFC South down the stretch of the year.

title: Jaguars-Colts Thursday Injury Report: What Does Montaric Brown's Return Mean?
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars look like they are getting a big boost to their secondary in Week 8.
The Jaguars had cornerback Montaric Brown listed as a full participant in practice for the second day in a row , a sign that Jacksonville is set to get their highest-paid cornerback back on the field against the Indianapolis Colts.
But what could the potential return of Brown really mean for the Jaguars in an important Week 8 AFC South battle?
Brown has missed all but six snaps over the Jaguars' last three weeks due to the hamstring injury, which first flared up on the Jaguars' injury report in the practices leading up to Week 4 against the Cincinnati Bengals. While Brown was not having a stellar season before his injury, it is worth noting that the Jaguars rank No. 28 and No. 24, respectively, in EPA/Play and success rate against the pass in the three weeks since.
While Brown may not slot in as a starter right off the bat for the Jaguars, he would give them expanded depth at a critical position alongside Travis Hunter, Jarrian Jones, and Jourdan Lewis.
“Certainly, we'd have a guy who's got a lot of experience who knows our system. It'd be good to have him back out there healthy," Jaguars defensive coordinator Anthony Campanile said on Thursday.
Brown did play six snaps in Week 5 against the Philadelphia Eagles but left after allowing a long touchdown pass to Darius Cooper in man coverage, a play that clearly showed the impact of his injury. Without Brown the next week against the Houston Texans, the Jaguars had one of their worst defensive performances in two seasons.
"I know in the Philly game, tough situation where he got hurt there in the game, but he looks good and we gain a veteran presence, and we gain a level of physicality anytime Buster's out there," Campanile said. "I think he's done a great job for us that way on the line of scrimmage, tackling, being physical, even in the coverage element of everything. So yeah, that's what we gain with him in there.”
Getting Brown back at cornerback could allow the Jaguars to do a number of things differently, including getting Hunter more snaps on offense after his dominant game against the Houston Texans. Not having Brown available was the primary reason Hunter didn't play an offensive snap in Week 4 against the Bengals, which to date is the only game in Hunter's career in which he did not take a snap on both sides of the ball.
Getting Brown back also happens at a good time for the secondary since safety Antonio Johnson did not practice for the second day in a row with an ankle injury. Johnson looks unlikely to play against the Colts, which means the Jaguars will need backups like Kaevon Merriweather and reinforcements like Brown to step up in the secondary.
“Every game's different and I think we're fortunate where we got a really good room there, and I think Kaevon [Merriweather] has done a good job coming in here as a new guy who's stepped up and given us the opportunity to have another guy that can kind of play some of those roles," Campanile said.
"I think even watching him in the last game, you see some physicality, and I think he's learning everything we're doing. He's worked really hard at it. I think Perk [Defensive Backs Coach Anthony Perkins] has done a great job with him, getting him up to speed. So, there's some other guys in that room who help us that way. Like any game, you're always adjusting.”
