title: Saints Midseason Stock Report: 4 Bright Spots Amid a Disappointing Start
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints enter their bye week with a disappointing 2-5 record despite the hype around the Saints being contenders to possibly win the NFC South.
While the season has been anything but positive, the team still has bright spots on both offense and defense.
Here's a look at four players who have performed above and beyond as we reach the midseason point.
Tyler Shough hasn't been perfect, but the second-year quarterback continues to show encouraging signs of development under coach Kellen Moore .
Through seven games, Shough has completed 67% of his passes for 1,721 yards, 13 touchdowns and six interceptions. He's also contributed 111 rushing yards and two touchdowns.
His pass yardage and touchdown totals are both in the top 10 as he is tied for seventh in passing touchdowns and ninth in passing yards, but for a majority of the season he was either No. 1 or No. 2 in passing yards.
Those numbers are impressive considering New Orleans' struggles establishing a consistent rushing attack and protecting its quarterback.
Despite occasional mistakes, Shough has demonstrated improved accuracy, pocket presence and command of Moore's offense.
If he continues developing and limits turnovers, the Saints should feel increasingly confident about their quarterback situation.
Wide receiver Chris Olave has shown why the Saints gave him a 4-year, $132 million extension.
Through seven games, the former first-round pick has caught 49 passes (fourth in the NFL) for 636 yards (third in the NFL) and two touchdowns, averaging 90.9 receiving yards per game.
He opened the season with four 100-yard performances in his first four games, including a dominant 182-yard outing against Detroit .
Chase Young has arguably been New Orleans' most impressive player on defense through seven games.
The former No. 2 overall pick has recorded seven sacks, establishing himself as one of the NFL's most productive pass rushers.
Out of 50 edge rushers with at least 125 pass rushes, Young ranked second with a 90.0 Pro Football Focus pass-rush grade.
Young is on pace to record over 15 sacks, potentially putting him in the conversation for Pro Bowl recognition.
Though Young draws much of the spotlight, Carl Granderson is quietly putting together a standout year as well.
Across seven contests, the experienced defensive end has registered 25 tackles alongside 5.5 sacks, highlighted by a 1.5-sack effort versus Pittsburgh .
Granderson's current trajectory puts him on track for roughly 13 sacks, setting up a potential career mark.
Combined, Granderson and Young have racked up 12.5 sacks, forming one of the few reliable highlights for New Orleans' defense.
Even with the unit's broader difficulties, his growth paired with Young gives the Saints a high-caliber pass-rush duo for the future.

title: The Good, Bad and Ugly From Saints' 16-10 Loss to Steelers in Paris
full_text:
Hoping to build momentum ahead of their upcoming bye week after a major victory last week, the New Orleans Saints instead fell 16-10 to the Pittsburgh Steelers on Sunday in Paris, exposing several recurring issues under coach Kellen Moore .
New Orleans' offensive struggles continued as missed scoring opportunities proved costly as the Saints fell to 2-5.
From an emerging young playmaker to a disastrous rushing performance, here is a look at the good, the bad and the ugly from the Saints' disappointing loss to Pittsburgh .
One of the few bright spots in New Orleans' disappointing loss was rookie wide receiver Barion Brown's emergence.
The sixth-round pick got a chance to show his explosiveness, finishing with three receptions for 57 yards and adding another 97 yards on four kickoff returns.
His biggest offensive play came in the first half when he caught a 49-yard pass from Tyler Shough , setting up Daniel Carlson 's 38-yard field goal.
Brown also returned a kickoff 42 yards in the second quarter, setting up a possession that ended with Shough's 1-yard touchdown pass to Devaughn Vele .
Despite those contributions, Brown received just three targets.
That limited involvement raises questions about whether coach Kellen Moore is maximizing one of the offense's most explosive young playmakers.
With rookie Jordyn Tyson still sidelined by a hamstring injury, Brown has a chance to become a more consistent contributor alongside Chris Olave and Vele.
New Orleans gets a vital jolt on offense from Brown's explosive speed and big-play dynamism.
Following a sluggish 281-yard performance against Pittsburgh, integrating him must become a top priority for the Saints. To fully leverage the rookie's skill set, Moore ought to scheme designed touches, vertical routes and run-after-catch opportunities for him. Given how much he has delivered on minimal opportunities, Brown has earned a larger role.
In a narrow 16-10 loss to Pittsburgh, kicker Daniel Carlson missed a crucial 52-yard field goal in the fourth quarter — his fourth failure in 11 attempts this season. This ongoing volatility in special teams poses a critical problem for the 2-5 Saints.
The fourth-quarter miss was particularly damaging because New Orleans had already wasted a promising red-zone opportunity earlier in the second half. Rather than positioning themselves to tie or take the lead with a field goal late in the game, the Saints remained trapped in a six-point deficit.
Carlson's 63.6% conversion rate stands in sharp contrast to Steelers kicker Chris Boswell , who accounted for nine points by flawlessly making all three of his field goals (from 28, 47 and 39 yards).
With three one-score defeats recorded this year, New Orleans simply lacks the margin for error to withstand repeated scoring blunders in tight contests. Carlson's continuous field goal woes add to head coach Kellen Moore's list of bye-week priorities, as unreliable special teams only exacerbate the team's offensive stalls, defensive breakdowns and turnovers.
While much of the focus has centered on Tyler Shough's growth, an inept rushing attack still severely limits the Saints' offensive ceiling.
Sunday's outing represented a new low point for the ground game.
New Orleans generated a paltry 18 rushing yards across 17 carries, resulting in an abysmal 1.1 yards per carry.
The stat line is even more damning because Shough — a quarterback whose primary role isn't to lead the run game — was the team's top rusher with just 7 yards on three carries.
It is downright appalling that primary backs Alvin Kamara (six carries, five yards) and Kendre Miller (eight carries, six yards) both logged more rush attempts than total yards gained.
This embarrassing output highlights a backfield without a true lead option, further compounded by an offensive line that failed to establish leverage up front.
Such complete non-production is intolerable at any level of football—especially when relying on a developing quarterback to sustain drive after drive.
By stifling the run, Pittsburgh's defense put the burden entirely on Shough's shoulders.
Even with Shough connecting on nearly 79% of his passes, New Orleans repeatedly stalled because it lacked offensive balance.
Unfortunately, this isn't merely a single bad afternoon.
The Saints' season-long inability to establish the run has made the offense predictable and easy for physical front sevens to counter.

title: 3 Takeaways From Saints' Loss to Steelers: Same Problems, Different Country
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints traveled across the Atlantic Ocean hoping to build momentum heading into their bye week and salvage their season. Instead, they returned home with its fourth loss in five games and it just seems like another repeating nightmare for Who Dat Nation.
New Orleans fell 16-10 to the Pittsburgh Steelers on Sunday at Stade de France in Paris, dropping to 2-5 through seven games under second-year coach Kellen Moore . It was the NFL's first regular-season game in France.
Despite another efficient passing performance from quarterback Tyler Shough , the Saints struggled to establish their rushing attack, failed to capitalize on scoring opportunities and couldn't get off the field defensively when it mattered most.
The loss marked New Orleans' third one-possession defeat this season, reinforcing concerns about the team's ability to execute in critical situations.
Here are three takeaways from another disappointing performance from the Saints performance.
For all the attention surrounding Shough's development, New Orleans' inability to run the football continues to undermine its offense.
Sunday's performance might have been its most concerning yet.
The Saints finished with just 18 rushing yards on 17 attempts, averaging a dismal 1.1 yards per carry.
Even more alarming, Shough led the team with 7 rushing yards on three attempts. However, he is a quarterback and that is not his job.
But for Alvin Kamara (six carries for five yards) and Kendre Miller (eight carries for six yards) to have more carries than rushing yards is disgusting.
It shows the lack of life in a running back room without a primary option, compounded by an offensive line struggling to create leverage.
That level of production is unacceptable for any offense regardless of the level of play, especially one relying on a young quarterback to consistently move the ball.
Pittsburgh's defense shut down the run, forcing Shough to carry nearly the entire offensive load.
Although Shough completed nearly 79% of his passes, New Orleans could not consistently finish drives because it lacked balance.
The problems extend beyond one disappointing performance.
New Orleans has struggled to generate consistent production on the ground throughout the season, making the offense increasingly predictable against physical defensive fronts.
Because of the rushing problems, the Saints had to rely on Shough again.
Shough did everything you could ask of him, completing 30 of 38 passes for 278 yards and a touchdown. However, one costly mistake ultimately changed the game's complexion.
Trailing 13-10 at the start of the second half, New Orleans put together a 13-play drive that moved the offense inside Pittsburgh's 10-yard line as the Saints appeared positioned to take their first lead of the afternoon.
Instead, Shough threw a pass intended for Chris Olave , which Steelers linebacker Payton Wilson intercepted at the Pittsburgh 11-yard line.
The turnover erased a scoring opportunity and let Pittsburgh respond with a field goal, extending its lead to 16-10.
The interception proved costly, but it also highlighted the impossible position Shough has found himself in because of New Orleans' offensive struggles.
Despite completing nearly 79% of his passes, the quarterback could not afford even one mistake because the Saints had virtually no rushing attack to complement him.
That is an unrealistic expectation for any quarterback, much less one still developing at the NFL level.
Shough showed he could move the football against a Pittsburgh defense, distributing the ball effectively and keeping New Orleans competitive despite a one-dimensional offensive approach.
However, his play reinforced a troubling reality: when Shough plays well, the Saints can win; when he makes one mistake, the operation unravels.
Until Moore builds a credible run game and finishes drives, Shough bears an unreasonable load and New Orleans must create an offense where its quarterback does not need to be perfect to win.
Unless the Saints give Shough a credible rushing attack and adequate protection, they risk repeating a familiar chapter in franchise history: asking a talented young quarterback to overcome problems far beyond his control, much like Archie Manning decades ago.
Daniel Carlson 's fourth missed field goal in 11 attempts this season — a 52-yarder in the fourth quarter — kept New Orleans trailing in a 16-10 loss to Pittsburgh, highlighting a critical special teams weakness for the 2-5 Saints.
The missed 52-yard attempt came while the Saints trailed 16-10 in the fourth quarter, keeping Pittsburgh's lead at six points. Carlson's 63.6% success rate contrasts with Steelers kicker Chris Boswell , who converted all three attempts (28, 47 and 39 yards) for nine points.
The fourth-quarter miss was especially costly as New Orleans had already squandered a promising red-zone drive earlier in the second half. Instead of entering the final minutes needing only a field goal to tie or lead, the Saints remained six points behind.
Carlson's kicking struggles add to head coach Kellen Moore's bye-week concerns. For a team hampered by offensive inefficiency, defensive lapses and turnovers, unreliable special teams further shrink a narrow margin for error.
With three one-score losses this season, New Orleans cannot afford missed points. Sunday's loss highlights that the Saints lack the margin for error to overcome recurring scoring mistakes in tight games.

title: Saints Fans Should Know These 3 Things About the Steelers Before Sunday
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints (2-4) enter Sunday's historic matchup against the Pittsburgh Steelers (4-2) at Stade de France, looking to build momentum after their 34-27 win over the New York Giants .
However, Pittsburgh presents a considerably different challenge.
Under first-year coach Mike McCarthy , the Steelers have established themselves as a competitive AFC North contender, winning four of their first six games despite an offense that has struggled to consistently produce explosive plays.
Pittsburgh enters Sunday's contest averaging 22.8 points and 320.5 yards per game, ranking 18th and 21st in the NFL, respectively. However, its defense has been considerably more effective, allowing 307.5 yards per game, the ninth-fewest in the league.
For Saints coach Kellen Moore , Sunday's matchup offers a chance to secure consecutive wins for the first time this season before the team's Week 8 bye.
Here are three things Saints fans should know about the Steelers.
While 42-year-old Aaron Rodgers continues to anchor Pittsburgh's offense with his elite ability to read defenses and capitalize on errors, the Steelers' aerial game has produced fairly modest results.
Across six games, Rodgers has completed 61.4% of his pass attempts for 1,487 yards, throwing 12 touchdowns against five interceptions.
Despite these respectable individual metrics, Pittsburgh ranks just 18th in the league through the air, averaging 221.3 passing yards per contest.
Physical wide receiver DK Metcalf gives Rodgers a dependable downfield threat capable of winning contested balls and creating opportunities on intermediate routes.
However, Rodgers' statistical split against specific zone schemes presents a critical storyline for this matchup.
NFL Next Gen Stats reveals that Rodgers has struggled against Cover 3, registering a 32.9% success rate—the third-lowest figure among qualified quarterbacks—compared to a 52.9% success rate against all other zone schemes.
This dynamic is especially relevant given that New Orleans deploys Cover 3 on 55.9% of defensive dropbacks, leading the entire NFL.
Consequently, defensive coordinator Brandon Staley must balance disciplined zone coverage with an effective pass rush to contain Pittsburgh's passing attack.
While Rodgers draws significant focus, the Steelers' ground attack could pose a greater threat to New Orleans.
Running back Jaylen Warren has rushed for 460 yards on 84 carries, averaging 5.5 yards per attempt.
His ability to gain yards after contact, identify lanes and contribute in the passing game gives Pittsburgh multiple offensive options.
That creates a difficult matchup for New Orleans.
The Saints allow 138 rushing yards per game, ranking 30th in the NFL, while Pittsburgh averages 99.2 rushing yards per game, ranking 20th.
Despite Pittsburgh's modest team average, Warren's efficiency indicates the Steelers can exploit the Saints' run defense.
While returning veteran linebacker Kaden Elliss should bolster the Saints' run defense, containing Warren remains a critical priority. Allowing Pittsburgh to establish its ground game early will open up play-action opportunities for Rodgers.
While Pittsburgh's offense has experienced inconsistencies, its defense remains the team's most reliable strength.
The Steelers enter Sunday's matchup allowing 21.3 points and 307.5 yards per game, ranking 12th and ninth in the NFL, respectively.
A key part of its defense has been its ability to defend the pass as the Steelers have surrendered just 204.3 yards per game, the eighth-fewest in the league.
Pittsburgh has also recorded 16 sacks and six interceptions through six games, contributing to a plus-three turnover differential.
Outside linebacker T.J. Watt , who has a team-high 4.5 sacks, remains one of the league's most disruptive defensive players.
Alex Highsmith provides another formidable presence on the edge, while veteran defensive tackle Cameron Heyward anchors the interior.
The Steelers also one of the league’s top cornerbacks, eight-time Pro Bowler Jalen Ramsey , giving their secondary an experienced playmaker who can create turnovers.
For Saints quarterback Tyler Shough , protecting the football will be especially important.
Shough has thrown for 1,443 yards, 12 touchdowns and five interceptions this season, but his performance against zone coverage presents a potential concern.
According to Next Gen Stats , Shough has thrown five interceptions against zone coverage this season, tied for the second-most among qualified quarterbacks.
Pittsburgh has utilized zone coverage on 82.8% of opposing dropbacks, with five of its six interceptions occurring against zone concepts.
This creates a compelling schematic test between Moore's offense and Pittsburgh's defense.
If Pittsburgh generates pressure without compromising coverage, Shough may struggle against an opportunistic unit. To build on last week's win, New Orleans will need to establish the run, avoid clear passing downs, and minimize turnovers.

title: Saints vs. Steelers: Injury Concerns Mount Ahead of Historic Paris Showdown
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints face several injury concerns as they prepare for Sunday's historic international matchup against the Pittsburgh Steelers at Stade de France in Paris.
Running back Alvin Kamara and starting offensive guard Cesar Ruiz headline New Orleans' injury report, while Pittsburgh is monitoring several key defensive players, including T.J. Watt, Alex Highsmith and Jalen Ramsey.
According to the Saints' official Thursday injury report , 11 New Orleans players were listed Thursday, with three missing practice and three participating on a limited basis.
The Saints (2-4) are looking to build momentum following Sunday's 34-27 victory over the New York Giants, which snapped a three-game losing streak. Meanwhile, Pittsburgh (4-2) enters the matchup seeking its second consecutive victory.
Both teams have several injury situations worth monitoring before Friday's final practice report.
The Saints' biggest offensive concerns involve Kamara and Ruiz, who have been dealing with back and knee injuries, respectively.
Kamara was limited for the second consecutive practice Thursday, leaving his availability worth monitoring heading into Sunday's game.
The veteran running back remains an important part of Kellen Moore's offense, particularly as New Orleans attempts to establish a more consistent rushing attack.
Ruiz's situation is potentially more concerning. The veteran offensive lineman missed practice Wednesday and Thursday because of a knee injury, raising questions about his availability against Pittsburgh's defensive front.
However, Jeremiah Wright played well in his absence during New Orleans’ win over the Giants last week.
Meanwhile, linebacker Kaden Elliss (calf) and edge rusher Anfernee Jennings (knee) were limited for the second consecutive day. During today's player roundtable , Elliss was asked if he would be available to play Sunday, and he said, "Yes."
There was some encouraging news for New Orleans.
Shough, who appeared on the report with a left-hand injury, participated fully in both practices. Cornerback Kool-Aid McKinstry (head) and defensive lineman Nathan Shepherd (illness) also practiced without limitations.
Running back CJ Donaldson (shoulder) improved from limited participation Wednesday to a full practice Thursday.
Kicker Daniel Carlson missed his second consecutive practice because of a personal matter unrelated to injury (he and his wife are having a baby), while defensive lineman Davon Godchaux received a rest day Thursday.
Backup quarterback Spencer Rattler was added to Thursday's report with a knee injury but participated fully.
Pittsburgh is also dealing with significant injury concerns, particularly on defense.
The most notable development Thursday was star edge rusher T.J. Watt, who was limited with a calf injury after sitting out Wednesday's practice for rest.
Watt's status matters, given the Saints' offensive line concerns. The former NFL Defensive Player of the Year has 4.5 sacks through six games.
Fellow pass rusher Alex Highsmith remained limited with a groin injury, while veteran defensive tackle Cameron Heyward missed his second straight practice for rest.
The Steelers also received encouraging news about star cornerback Jalen Ramsey, who returned to practice on Thursday, albeit in a limited capacity. He missed Wednesday's session with a wrist injury.

title: Saints Stock Up: 3 Heroes From New Orleans' Win Over Giants
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints earned a much-needed victory over the New York Giants as they broke a three-game losing streak.
Now, the Saints are in Paris as they turn their attention to the Pittsburgh Steelers to win consecutive games for the first time this season. However, it will be a tough task: Pittsburgh still has a solid quarterback in Aaron Rodgers at 42, and the offense has plenty of weapons; on defense, they have a solid pass rush.
After fully reviewing the Saints’ win over New York and looking at which players have been trending upward, here are three players whose stock is rising.
The Saints historically produce standout special teams performers, including Morten Andersen , Michael Lewis , and Steve Gleason .
Linebacker Isaiah Stalbird has continued that tradition this year, keying special teams unit success and executing the decisive sequence of the game.
Down 10-3 late in the second quarter, New Orleans seemed poised for a halftime deficit before Stalbird made a game-altering play on coverage.
The second-year backer stripped the ball from Charlie Jones on a kickoff return, which tight end Oscar Delp recovered to set up New Orleans inside the red zone.
Shough converted the takeaway into points, finding rookie Bryce Lance for a game-tying touchdown right before the break.
That turnover shifted game momentum entirely and helped spark a 31-point unanswered run that gave New Orleans a 34-10 lead before the Giants mounted a furious fourth-quarter comeback.
Cornerback Martin Emerson Jr. posted his top outing of the year in the 34-27 victory, accumulating seven tackles, two interceptions, and four pass breakups.
His effort earned an 88.4 defensive rating and a 90.2 coverage rating from Pro Football Focus, leading all team defenders in Week 6. Emerson was named NFC Defensive Player of the Week for his efforts.
Emerson held opponents to four catches on 10 targeted passes while picking off throws from Jameis Winston and J.J. McCarthy . The performance provided valuable depth after Kool-Aid McKinstry exited due to a migraine.
Rookie guard Jeremiah Wright capitalized on unexpected playing time against New York, filling in when starter Cesar Ruiz left with a knee injury in the second quarter.
If one thing is certain, the run game started to click when Wright went into the game as he added toughness to the interior line, anchoring a run game that piled up a season-best 175 yards. If you want to know how much of an impact Wright had? When the Saints ran to the right, they averaged just over 5 yards per carry. When they ran to the left? 3.1-yards a clip.
The fourth-round selection surrendered just a single QB pressure in his most extensive action of the season.

title: Bold Trade Idea for Giants: Cash In on John Michael Schmitz Before the Deadline
full_text:
If nothing else, the New York Giants have proven that they’re not afraid to shake up the roster, especially with their eyes firmly on winning the NFC East.
And with the league’s trade deadline fast approaching, there’s been plenty of talk about who the Giants might acquire, but little about who, if anyone, they might move to recoup draft picks.
So here’s a thought about the latter: Why not see if the Green Bay Packers would be interested in acquiring center John Michael Schmitz in exchange for a draft pick?
Crazy, you say? Perhaps. But let’s explore this wild scenario anyway.
Simple. Injuries have hit their offensive line hard. They are already on their third center this season after losing Sean Rhyan, their Week 1 starter, to a high ankle sprain in Week 7 and backup Jacob Monk to a quad injury that same week.
Rhyan is expected to miss between four and six weeks . Right now, the Packers are down to John Williams, their seventh-round pick in 2025, who stepped in for Monk against the Detroit Lions last week.
Per PFF , Monk has allowed 11 pressures this season, and Williams has allowed five. Is it that hard to believe the Packers would want a better option at center moving forward, as they also fight to win their division?
Why not? It’s obvious that after losing his starting job to Bryan Hudson back in Week 4, Schmitz, who, by the way, is in the final year of his rookie contract, isn’t in the long-term plans for the Giants.
Rather than let him walk in the 2027 free agency cycle and risk getting nothing in return, why not see if the team can get a draft pick for him from a club in need, such as the Packers?
Doing so not only guarantees a 2027 pick, but also adds to a haul that already includes five picks, plus a potential extra fourth-round pick projected to come the Giants’ way via the compensatory system.
If the Giants can get extra picks for players who don’t have a long-term future with the team, why not pursue that avenue?
To win now. If Green Bay isn’t happy with its current center situation, it makes the upgrade now and worries later about whether anyone on an expiring contract will be back.
And let’s say, for argument’s sake, that the Giants and Packers made this trade. Would it be a rental? Probably. But remember, the Packers signed Rhyan to a three-year, $33 million contract in March of this year, so it's probably safe to say that he’s their starter moving forward.
And Schmitz? Since he’s in the final year of his rookie deal, he’d cost the Packers approximately $230,823 for each week he’s on the roster, which isn’t a huge financial strain for a team that currently has $6.422 million in salary cap space.
Per Tankathon , the Packers are projected to have 11 draft picks in 2027. That haul includes two fourth-round picks, three fifth-round picks (two of which are projected compensatory picks), and two sixth-round picks (one compensatory pick).
If the Packers are desperate for an upgrade at center, would anyone balk at trading a fifth-round pick for a center who was a second-round pick in his draft class?
Currently, Schmitz is listed as Hudson’s backup after losing his starting job, meaning there is no other center on the roster at the moment.
But the Giants do have a couple of players on the practice squad who could be options for promotion to the 53-man roster if the team moves on from Schmitz via a trade.
The most obvious is Kendrick Green, a veteran who has been in the NFL since 2021 and has played 975 snaps at center , most recently in 2024 with Houston.
Green also spent the 2025 season in Cleveland with Giants offensive line coach Mike Bloomgren, so he is probably already ahead of the curve in adapting to the techniques Bloomgren teaches.
Another option would be Lodi, N.J. native Geno VanDeMark. VanDeMark is still a young player looking to get his NFL footing, but he played 161 snaps at center over his college career at both Michigan State and Alabama.

title: Two More Defensive Tackles the Giants Can Pivot to After Simmons and Buckner Trades
full_text:
The New York Giants couldn’t have asked for a better time for their Week 8 bye, just two Sundays before the NFL’s annual trade deadline, when plenty of players are expected to change jerseys as priorities shift in the second half of the 2026 season.
For the Giants, who sit at 4-2-1 atop the NFC East during their bye week, the focus is on making the improvements needed to help John Harbaugh’s roster pile up more wins and potentially capture their first division crown since 2011 and first playoff berth since 2022.
One area that could stand in the way of that goal is the defensive line, once again one of the league’s least productive units. It has allowed the fifth-most rushing yards per game and the second-highest yards per carry in the league.
The Giants have to be largely pleased with the efforts of their two veteran signings, D.J. Reader and Shelby Harris, who were brought in to provide experience after the Dexter Lawrence II trade left a massive void.
Behind them, the rest of New York’s young core just hasn’t been rising to the occasion, leaving observers to question whether the franchise should bring in another veteran before the trade deadline so the unit doesn’t keep going off the rails whenever Reader and Harris come off the field.
With DeForest Buckner and Jeffrey Simmons, arguably the top two defensive linemen on the trade block, now gone, here are a few additional options the Giants could consider if they want to shore up their defensive line depth.
With the Giants’ limited cap space a big factor in their trade deadline activity, the main question is whether they want to gamble on a rental or go for a player with more contract security.
For the latter route, a possible option is Roy Lopez of the Arizona Cardinals. Lopez, 29, is in the first year of a two-year, $10.5 million contract.
If the Giants struck a deal with Arizona for Lopez, he would cost them $117,647 in base salary for every week he is on the roster, plus $20,000 per game played this year. In 2027, he’d cost them $4.11 million total (including roster bonuses and a workout bonus).
Lopez has been active for 85 of 87 career games since 2021. He has also been one of the more productive gap stuffers at his position, making 18 tackles, including 16 run stops, tied for the fourth-most in the league among defensive tackles with at least 200 snaps.
If the Giants wanted to roll the dice on a player who would probably cost them very little in salary cap space and definitely wouldn’t cost them a draft pick, they could look at old friend Austin Johnson, a free agent.
Johnson, 6-foot-4 and 314 pounds, started his career with the Tennessee Titans in 2016 and spent the 2020 and 2021 seasons with the Giants. After that, he spent time with the Chargers, Bills and Jaguars before landing back on the Bills’ practice squad this year, where he was released on Oct. 27.
Johnson has played 10 NFL seasons, appearing in 145 games with 56 starts. He has 272 tackles (136 solos), 17 tackles for loss, 19 quarterback hits, 9.5 sacks and 13 pass breakups.
His best season came in 2021 with the Giants. That year he recorded career highs in tackles (72), sacks (3.5), tackles for loss (6), and quarterback hits (7).
Again, Johnson’s appeal is that he could be a bargain, and the Giants, already down to six draft picks for 2027, wouldn’t have to give up any assets to get him.

title: Cam Skattebo’s Road Back: 5 Takeaways From the Giants’ New Documentary
full_text:
New York Giants running back Cam Skattebo has become something of a cult hero, no, make that a superhero, among Giants fans who have embraced his youthful enthusiasm for the game, his blue-collar running style, and his overall fan-friendly demeanor.
But despite his larger-than-life personality, even Skattebo faced an emotional crossroads. He fought back from a devastating season-ending ankle injury suffered last year in Week 8 against the Eagles, when linebacker Zack Baun tackled him.
“I always said I wasn’t going to play if I got a major injury,” he said in the opening minutes of Skattebo: The Road Back .
“I know I’m going to be the same, if not better. I want to prove to myself that I’m going to be the same, if not better, and to prove to everyone else that I ain’t going nowhere.”
That is among the revelations in the team-produced documentary that follows Skattebo’s nearly yearlong journey, which began with him being carted off the field on October 26 in Philadelphia and ended with his return to the field last month in a thrilling Week 1 victory over the Dallas Cowboys on Sunday Night Football.
Skattebo opened up about his journey back to the field in an hourlong documentary, at times showing his vulnerability as he recounted the peaks and valleys of his long comeback and his personal growth through adversity.
Here are more takeaways from the documentary. (Warning: spoilers below.)
Skattebo spoke about not being a patient person by nature, and that if he could have, he would have started running a lot sooner than he eventually did once he was cleared. But if there was a silver lining to his injury and rehab process, it was that he learned to be patient.
“Am I a patient person? Absolutely not,” Skattebo said. “I missed maybe two football games my entire football career. Patience is not in my vocabulary, that’s for sure.
“(Giants Director of Rehabilitation/Physical Therapist) Leigh (Weiss) has to fight me off every day to make sure I’m doing the right thing and not doing too much because if it was up to me, I’d try to run tomorrow, and I know that’s not the right thing to do. So it’s teaching me patience.”
As much as Skattebo loves football, he said that the process taught him that football isn’t everything in his life.
“I’m a football player, and I’m good at what I do, but I’ve been finding other ways and aspects to go about life. That’s something I really didn’t have before this injury. I’ve been trying to find other things I can do in life if (football) gets taken away.”
That outlook comes as his profile has grown off the field, too. Skattebo has become an advertiser’s dream, earning numerous endorsements in his spare time, including State Farm, The Farmer’s Dog, Nike, Whatnot, and BUM Energy, to name a few.
He has also hosted youth football camps for young athletes who aspire to follow in his footsteps.
After completing a rehab session, Skattebo jokingly said to Weiss, “Time to do a backflip.”
Weiss responded, “I told you that’s your marker.”
Skattebo later did a backflip at the Brian Burns Charity Softball Game in late May and again at a Fanatics event in July, just before heading off to the team’s training camp. He didn’t land the second one cleanly. But he had actually done a backflip much earlier.
There’s an asterisk, though. Skattebo’s first post-surgery backflip came in a pool during a rehab session, after doctors cleared him to shed his walking boot and crutches. It was in water, but it was still progress for the determined running back.
For some players who suffer a season-ending injury, being around their teammates and the game can be a painful reminder of what they lost, though usually only temporarily.
While Skattebo had to get used to not being able to practice or play in games, he stayed part of the team by continuing his rehab with the team’s training staff and doing whatever activities he could, as allowed by league rules.
Once medically cleared, he even showed up on game days as an unofficial mascot for his teammates, who were going through a rough season of their own, a four-win 2025 campaign.
Many players enter the NFL aiming to be the best at their position, regardless of the legends ahead of them.
“Obviously I want to be the best running back ever to do it,” he said. “That’s a high standard to set for yourself, so I said I want to be the best running back that I can be.”

title: Should the Giants Trade Kayvon Thibodeaux Before the Deadline?
full_text:
With the NFL’s November 10 trade deadline on the horizon, the New York Giants ’ brain trust is undoubtedly spending part of the team’s bye week scanning the league for ways to improve the thin areas of John Harbaugh’s roster.
Their focus is likely on positions like the defensive line, which needs more productive depth , and the offensive backfield, which had a bounce-back performance against the Houston Texans yet is missing a true three-down running back to shoulder the bulk of Harbaugh’s run-heavy aspirations.
Questions also loom about whether the franchise might consider moving any of its own players from healthier parts of the roster to accrue assets that will help strengthen the roster moving forward.
The player most often mentioned in that scenario is outside linebacker Kayvon Thibodeaux, whose contract is nearing an end and whose long-term status with the Giants hangs in the balance.
The 6-foot-5, 258-pound Thibodeaux lived up to his draft hype in his first two seasons in blue, notching 98 total pressures and 17 sacks, including his lone double-digit sack campaign in 2023, which tied for seventh-most among edge rushers.
The Oregon product also contributed to the Giants’ run defense at a respectable clip, logging 70 tackles, including 58 run stops, and forcing five turnovers in that same span.
Since that career-high season, he hasn’t sustained that production. Injuries sliced his availability down to 22 games over the next two years. Even when he was on the field, Thibodeaux’s pass-rush efficiency dipped as he struggled with tackling and his effort seemed inconsistent from snap to snap.
All of that has sparked speculation and calls from the fanbase to put Thibodeaux on the trade market to see what value they could get for a former first-round pick still in his prime but not meeting expectations that match his draft pedigree.
Seven games into the 2026 season, it’s been another relatively quiet start for Thibodeaux in a banged-up Giants defense, prompting another round of pleas for Big Blue to move on and get something in return from another team desperate to add experienced pass-rushing depth.
Thibodeaux is in the final year of his rookie contract, which pays $14.8 million, all of it guaranteed, the second-highest cap hit on the Giants’ roster.
He is currently costing the Giants $867,706 in base salary per week, which is what the Giants would save for every week Thibodeaux is not on the roster. That money would add to the $7.4 million in cap space they currently have, which they could use to keep upgrading the roster or potentially extend someone like cornerback Deonte Banks.
Earlier this year, there was some speculation that the Giants were looking for a high Day 2 pick for the former Oregon star. But in history, the Washington Commanders traded defensive end Chase Young to the San Francisco 49ers during the final year of his rookie contract in exchange for a compensatory third-round pick.
That said, does a trade really make sense?
Probably not, unless the Giants receive a sweetheart offer in which a willing trade partner grossly overpays for Thibodeaux.
The team suffered a huge blow when Brian Burns went down for the rest of the season with a Week 4 ACL tear.
Before losing their most talented pass rusher, the defensive front was already hurt by Roy Robertson-Harris’s preseason exit with the same ailment, and Chauncey Gholston’s season-ending neck injury.
When Burns returns in 2027, he’ll reclaim his spot as the top option alongside rising teammates on the edge. While the Giants have to love the impact they are getting at the second level, depth remains a massive concern.
Thibodeaux hasn’t been a disaster, despite what some fans might want to believe. He’s actually started to play better of late, having logged three pressures in each of his last three starts while making nine of his 11 tackles, including six run stops.
And there is also the question of where the Giants stand right now. At 4-2-1, they sit atop the NFC East, their eyes firmly on winning the division, which would put them in the postseason. Does it really make sense then for them to part with guys who have played a role in that, no matter how small?
That said, with there being no guarantee of the Giants getting a compensatory pick for Thibodeaux if he were to walk away in free agency, plus with a compensatory pick, even if awarded, not arriving for the Giants’ use until 2028, the option of moving Thibodeaux needs to remain on the table until the NFL declares “pencils down” on any more trade activity.

title: New York Giants at the Bye: 5 Factors That Fueled a 4-2-1 Start
full_text:
The New York Giants have become one of the NFL’s surprise stories in 2026.
With a new-look, motion-based offense and an aggressive defense, Big Blue has weathered the season’s ebb and flow to earn a 4-2-1 record and sole possession of first place in the NFC East, a feat last achieved in 2015.
Still, New York’s road to redemption has not been smooth. From losing starting quarterback Jaxson Dart and outside linebacker Brian Burns to season-ending injuries to struggling to run the ball and defend the run, the Giants arrived at their bye week as a battle-tested squad ready to pursue their first playoff spot since 2022.
While their season has been far from perfect, more has fallen in New York’s favor than to its disservice. In that regard, here are five key factors that have helped shape the Giants’ renaissance during coach John Harbaugh’s first year at the helm in East Rutherford.
After a dismal running-game performance in the Giants’ 34-27 loss to the New Orleans Saints in Week 6, the NYG HC knew something had to change.
Second-year back Cam Skattebo had been held out of the game after his costly fumble against the Washington Commanders in Week 5.
His remaining trio of running backs (Najee Harris, Tyrone Tracy Jr. and Devin Singletary) combined for just 34 rushing yards against the Saints. In fact, Harris was released just two days after voicing his displeasure with the Giants’ running back rotation.
“One of those guys needs to step up,” Harbaugh said from his Week 6 postgame podium. “Somebody needs to step up and be the ‘Back.’ None of those guys have done that yet.”
In Week 7 against the Texans, following what Harbaugh described as a “heck of a week” at practice, Skattebo rose from the ranks, rushing for a career-high 124 yards on 17 carries with a touchdown, along with a crucial 42-yard gain in overtime. Singletary ran for 41 total yards, including the 30-yard game-winning score.
Collectively, the Giants’ runners compiled 188 rushing yards. The unit not only reestablished itself as a key component of coordinator Matt Nagy’s offense, but Skattebo also seemed to answer his coach’s challenge as New York pushes for the postseason.
After a disappointing performance in 2025, Giants cornerback Deonte Banks appeared to be nearing an unceremonious end to his tenure with Big Blue. After all, New York had declined the fifth-year option on his rookie contract, leading many to project him as little more than a situational reserve option heading into 2026.
Banks entered the season determined to prove his doubters wrong. The 24th overall selection in the 2023 NFL Draft hit the field with renewed vigor under the tutelage of both Harbaugh and defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson, his eyes firmly set on regaining a starting job.
The Giants’ coaches chose to deploy Banks as a true matchup cornerback, and he has delivered beyond expectations. In five appearances (making five starts) this season, the 25-year-old has compiled 20 total tackles, 10 passes defensed, and one interception, which he returned for a 98-yard touchdown against the Arizona Cardinals in Week 4.
Still, Banks’ best showing came during New York’s Week 7 win over the Houston Texans. When directly matched against star receiver Nico Collins, the Giants’ defensive back held him to just one catch for four yards on four targets.
Though the coaching staff may have re-opened his talents, Banks has been successful in “closing down” his opponents on game day.
While Nagy is known for his run-centric, motion-based offense, he isn’t afraid to throw deep. With top-tier talents such as Malik Nabers at receiver and Isaiah Likely at tight end, New York’s aerial attack has come alive.
Before the Giants’ 28-20 Week 1 win over the Cowboys, Nabers had not seen regular-season action since suffering an ACL tear in Week 4 of the 2025 season. Yet, just one year after his season-ending injury, Nabers leads all Giants pass-catchers with 605 receiving yards on 48 catches with two touchdowns.
Not only has the sixth overall pick in the 2024 NFL Draft logged receptions of 46, 42, and 39 yards this season, but he has also compiled 158 yards after the catch.
Likely has been equally impressive as a productive red-zone target at the tight end position. After spending his first four NFL seasons with the Baltimore Ravens, Likely signed a three-year, $40 million contract with the Giants, joining Harbaugh, who also came over from Baltimore.
Through the first seven games of the season, the five-year veteran has caught 41 passes for 395 yards and five touchdowns. In the process, he has established himself as New York’s top tight end option.
With both Nabers and Likely playing at a high level, Giants quarterback J.J. McCarthy will have no shortage of pass-catching weapons heading into the season’s home stretch.
Alongside strong showings from defensive stalwarts such as safety Jevon Holland and linebacker Abdul Carter, Giants rookie Arvell Reese is already establishing himself as a game changer.
After a stellar performance throughout training camp and into the preseason, Reese earned the starting spot on the weak side of Dennard Wilson’s defense. Through seven games this season, he leads the team with 56 total tackles. The fifth overall selection in April’s draft also has 1.5 sacks and 5.5 tackles for loss.
In New York’s Week 4 victory over the Arizona Cardinals, Reese turned in a defensive masterpiece, logging nine solo tackles, one tackle for loss, three passes defensed, one quarterback hit, and one interception.
Reese became the fifth Giants rookie with three or more passes defensed and an interception in a game, and the only Giants rookie since 1994 with nine or more tackles, three or more passes defensed, and at least one interception. For his efforts, Reese earned Pepsi NFL Rookie of the Week honors.
As he continues to develop, Reese will be asked to take on a more prominent role within the Giants’ defense. Fortunately for Big Blue, he looks to be more than ready to accept the challenge.
After Dart’s season-ending injury, the Giants sent a 2027 fifth-round draft pick to the Minnesota Vikings in exchange for McCarthy, hoping to shore up a thin quarterback room.
In doing so, they may have saved their season.
The 10th overall pick in the 2024 NFL Draft quickly grasped the Giants’ playbook and showed comfort in coordinator Matt Nagy’s offense.
Though he was used only in select packages in the Giants’ 27-27 Week 5 tie with the Washington Commanders, McCarthy took the offensive reins with 11 minutes remaining in the fourth quarter of the team’s Week 6 loss to the Saints, after starter Jameis Winston’s second interception of the day.
McCarthy finished the game having completed 11 of 21 passes for 243 yards and one touchdown. He logged the most fourth-quarter passing yards by any player this season. For his efforts, Harbaugh named McCarthy the Giants’ new starting quarterback.
In his first start, McCarthy delivered, completing 20 of 28 passes (71.4% completion) for 252 yards for a passer rating of 99.1. Across four quarters and overtime in his first start, the 23-year-old showcased his multifaceted skill set while staying calm, cool, and collected.
Based on his performance, McCarthy has apparently secured his spot as the Giants’ starter. Though he may be best suited to an offense built on zone reads, designed runs, and RPO packages, the former Michigan Wolverine has also shown his prowess in the deep passing game.
If McCarthy keeps improving each week, the Giants may head to the postseason as NFC East champions for the first time since 2011.

title: Giants Rise in Latest MMQB Power Rankings Poll
full_text:
The New York Giants made a statement when head coach John Harbaugh benched quarterback Jameis Winston and handed the starting job to J.J. McCarthy for the team’s final game before the bye week, against the Houston Texans.
Still, very few people were buying into what was being labeled a “desperation move.”
McCarthy, for whom the Giants traded a fifth-round pick to the Minnesota Vikings to back up Winston after Jaxson Dart went down for the season, came in relief of the veteran gunslinger in the fourth quarter against the New Orleans Saints and nearly authored an incredible comeback. Even so, the reaction was far less enthusiastic than the crowd's cheers at MetLife Stadium.
The former No. 10 pick responded perfectly for all the doubters, completing 20 of his 28 pass attempts for 252 yards while picking apart a more feared Texans defense to lead the Giants to a shocking 27-21 overtime win in a game they entered as double-digit underdogs.
Not all of his individual stats were flashy. Still, the victory made many, including SI’s Conor Orr, realize something had changed with this version of the Giants as they improved to 4-2-1 and gave themselves a bigger cushion in the NFC East heading into the off week.
Orr admitted his faults in questioning the decision to turn the offense over to No. 18 and made amends by raising New York to No. 17 in his latest MMQB NFL power rankings .
“I posted this on Sunday, and I want to echo it here: I am fully aboard the Giants’ bandwagon (mostly because my 5-year-old has adopted them as his team),” Orr said. “But I deserve to pay an entrance fee first in the form of a public flogging, given that I was very, very hard to convince.”
Entering the 2026 season, much of the Giants’ potential promise rested on Dart and whether he could make it through a full season without succumbing to injury.
When Dart’s campaign ended two weeks in, much of the belief in Harbaugh’s locker room seemed to go with it. Skepticism only grew as injuries to key figures like linebackers Brian Burns and Tremaine Edmunds piled up, and the switch to McCarthy, whose early NFL career hadn’t inspired much confidence, emboldened the doubters further.
Granted, McCarthy came in after missing his entire rookie year with the Vikings because of a knee injury, then started only 10 games in 2025, posting a 6-4 record but a mediocre 57.6% completion percentage and an 11-12 touchdown-to-interception ratio.
Questions also lingered about McCarthy’s fit with the culture Harbaugh was quickly building in East Rutherford, but none of that mattered to the established head coach. Like any of his bold moves so far, it aligned with what gave his team the best chance to win football games.
As split as Orr and others may have been on Harbaugh’s handling of certain roster decisions in his first six games in command, McCarthy was validated by his performance and by how the rest of the players rallied around their new starter against the Texans.
With a full game under his belt, McCarthy displayed total poise in the pocket, throwing at a 7.5-yard clip that marked the highest single-game average with at least 20 completions by a Giants quarterback this season.
His ability to take off with the football also helped revive the RPO-style offense that Matt Nagy had been eager to run with Dart. The run game exploded for 188 yards and three touchdowns as the Texans had to respect the mobile quarterback.
Along with a better performance from the defense, those elements sparked a massive win over Houston that sends the Giants into the bye week with a two-game lead in the division and, suddenly, the respect of the rest of the league, with a chance to make some noise as the calendar flips to November.
The Giants will get some well-deserved rest in Week 8. Still, as their rivals continue dealing with their own issues, Big Blue could return with a chance to cement its first claim to the NFC East crown since 2011, including by handling its remaining divisional business over the next two months of the regular season.
Harbaugh certainly isn’t leading a perfect group into the second half, and a few more surprise moves could come as the trade deadline looms, helping plug holes on both sides of the ball and get better for a postseason push.
For those who keep questioning how he is leaving his fingerprints on the organization or entrusting McCarthy to light the torch for the offense in the weeks to come, it has all been done with competitive balance in mind.
Neither Harbaugh nor his players are backing down from the goals he set on the first day of camp just because injuries have taken away a few talented leaders or because the schedule gets tougher after the break.
He sees a leader in McCarthy who can take the Giants the distance, and he isn’t buying the stories about his starting quarterback’s past after what he's seen in two short weeks of game action.
So far, the results speak for themselves, and the hope is that Harbaugh’s vindication continues when the Giants return and prepare for a big matchup with the Philadelphia Eagles two Sundays from now.

title: Five Potential Trade Targets for the New York Giants
full_text:
The New York Giants are “in it to win it.”
Through the first seven weeks of the season, Big Blue has driven its way to a 4-2-1 record and sole possession of first place in the NFC East for the first time since 2015.
Though few may have expected such a rapid turnaround, coach John Harbaugh and his staff have helped cultivate a team that is (for the most part) playing opportunistic, fundamentally sound football.
In fact, Harbaugh all but confirmed that the team plans to keep the pedal to the metal after New York’s impressive 27-21 overtime victory over the Houston Texans.
“Now, you've got to make something of it. It doesn't mean anything if you don't build on it,” Harbaugh said.
“It doesn't mean we're going to win a championship yet. But it means we have an opportunity, though. We're going to be in this thing until the end now.”
Still, the Giants know where they need to improve. They'll use the current bye week to fine-tune their on-field planning and execution, and they will also be diligent in upgrading their personnel by the Nov. 10 NFL trade deadline .
Beyond their biggest need at defensive tackle, the team is expected to fortify its depth at running back and along the offensive line.
With that in mind, here are five players the Giants may look to acquire via trade in the coming days.
Given their need for a physical interior run defender, Tomlinson would make a great deal of sense for Big Blue. The 10-year veteran originally entered the NFL as a second-round selection by the Giants in the 2017 NFL Draft. He spent four seasons in New York, starting all 64 games in which he played.
The 32-year-old signed a one-year, $7.5 million contract with the Chargers this offseason, but he has failed to work his way into the Bolts’ starting lineup. Tomlinson has compiled eight total tackles, 0.5 sacks, and one run stuff in four appearances for Los Angeles while backing up starter Jamaree Caldwell.
If moved, the veteran defender would leave the Chargers with no dead money, while costing the Giants just north of $150,000 per week.
Perhaps a second tour of duty in East Rutherford, under defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson, could spark an on-field renaissance for Tomlinson while addressing Big Blue’s need at interior defensive line.
With two-time All-Pro DeForest Buckner headed back to the San Francisco 49ers, the Colts have all but confirmed their plans to rebuild. Though Buckner may have arguably been the more intriguing option, Stewart could also help fill New York’s need.
Through seven games this season, Stewart has logged 22 tackles, 0.5 sacks, and one pass-breakup. Last season in 17 games played, the 33-year-old tackle racked up 55 tackles, 0.5 sacks, a forced fumble, an interception, and four passes defended.
Trading Stewart would give the Colts approximately $12.3 million in cap savings — a valuable windfall for a team looking to spend this offseason. For the Giants, the 6-foot-5, 295-pound nose tackle could provide a massive upgrade to a run defense which currently ranks 25th in the NFL.
Although intra-divisional trades are rare in the NFL, the Commanders may be enticed to move on from their Pro Bowl defensive tackle for the right offer.
At 1-4-1, Washington is falling fast in both the division and conference standings. With Payne in the final year of his contract, the club is reportedly listening to offers.
Payne’s $16.4 million salary may deter some teams, but New York can take on a rental who knows the NFC East well. Despite his declining pass-rush ability, the 6-foot-3, 320-pound lineman is still an effective run defender.
In six games this season, Payne has seven total tackles, five quarterback hits, two tackles for loss, two run stuffs, and one forced fumble. His divisional knowledge and on-field experience could be a valuable asset to a young team making a playoff push.
Even if their focus remains on upgrading their defensive front, the Giants may still be in the market for a veteran running back to bolster their newly resurrected run game.
Before arriving in Tennessee in 2024, Pollard spent five seasons running the ball for the Dallas Cowboys. His elusiveness in the open field, combined with his abilities as a backfield receiver, makes him a provocative target — even at age 29.
This season, the Pro Bowl back has rushed for 478 yards on 112 carries (4.3 yards per attempt) with four touchdowns. He has also caught 11 passes for 50 yards. Being in the final year of his deal, the Titans may look to move his $6.7 million base salary for the right price.
If Tyrone Tracy Jr.’s hamstring keeps him out longer than the minimum four games he’s required to spend on IR, Pollard could help strengthen New York’s running back corps, which includes Cam Skattebo, Devin Singletary, the newly acquired Greg DeRosiers, and practice squad rusher Phil Mafah.
Despite its roller-coaster journey this season, the Giants’ offensive line has performed well. Though their play hasn't been perfect, they've done their jobs well in both pass protection and run blocking. Still, the Giants may be wise to keep a close eye on available talent to fortify their interior depth.
Center John Michael Schmitz likely headed to free agency after being replaced in the starting lineup by Bryan Hudson; New York could look to the Seahawks’ center as an interior depth piece. Olu Oluwatimi is in the final year of his rookie deal and is scheduled to be an unrestricted free agent this offseason.
With Oluwatimi having lost the starting center job to Jalen Sundel, Seattle may be motivated to move the 6-foot-3, 309-pound lineman rather than risk losing him in free agency. The Giants should be interested, provided the price is right.

title: Joe Schoen Explains Why the Giants Extended Jameis Winston's Contract
full_text:
The New York Giants extended Jameis Winston’s contract by two years and $13 million before Jaxson Dart’s season-ending knee injury forced the backup quarterback to step in.
Dart went down seven snaps into the team’s Week 2 game, and Winston, the Giants’ hand-picked backup, stepped in.
The extension, which added two years to a deal that was due to expire after this season, lowered his cap hit and ensured Winston remains with the club through 2028.
Yet rather than stick with Winston, New York gave up a fifth-round draft pick to acquire J.J. McCarthy from the Minnesota Vikings, a quarterback Big Blue intends to start for the rest of the season.
Knowing Winston might not have been the ideal fit to run the Giants’ offense as designed full time, if something happened to Dart, why did the Giants bother to extend him?
The answer is that Winston was never meant to be a long-term answer, but rather a guy who could step in for a series or a game or two, which is exactly what he did.
“When you’re talking about a backup quarterback that also has leadership, that can lead not only that room, but the team,” general manager Joe Schoen said.
Winston, Schoen noted, has kept the Giants in games where they held a fourth-quarter lead or at least a tie, which is what the team wants from a backup when he's pressed into action.
But for the Giants and how their offense was designed to operate, having Winston run the offense for most of the season was something that raised questions about the sustainability of the plan.
Winston may not have been an ideal fit to go the distance in this offense, but his value to the organization remains high because he brings veteran leadership.
Despite his role as QB2, he was voted a team captain and sits on the eight-man leadership council chosen by head coach John Harbaugh.
Schoen recognized the importance of having a veteran quarterback after learning the lesson during his time in Buffalo when after the Bills drafted quarterback Josh Allen, they didn’t have a solid veteran presence in place to help the young signal caller.
Having seen how Winston has helped McCarthy and Dart in the meeting room has made the investment in keeping Winston around undoubtedly worth it for Big Blue.
Winston, to his credit, has been the picture-perfect model of professionalism despite the outside noise surrounding his play, dubbed “The Jameis Winston Experience,” and his demotion from the starting lineup.
The coaching staff hasn’t totally cast him aside in game planning. Last week, he successfully ran the Giants’ version of the “Tush Push.”
But his biggest contribution, which is what initially endeared him to the organization, lies in his willingness to lead by example.
“Serving leadership is very important in everything that we do. First, by example, out there on the field, how you go about your work, how you apply it in the film room, how you’re open and sharing things through your experience that you have encountered,” Winston said.
With McCarthy now under center, Winston’s job is to keep the quarterback room steady, a role the Giants valued enough to pay for before Dart ever got hurt.

title: What the Giants Must Fix Before Returning from Bye Week
full_text:
The New York Giants are enjoying a much-needed bye this week, sitting atop the NFC East, a position they’ll keep regardless of what happens in the division this coming weekend.
While the players are off enjoying a mini vacation of sorts, general manager Joe Schoen and head coach John Harbaugh are not resting; both want to ensure the Giants maintain their place atop the division when they resume play in Week 9 with a road game against the Philadelphia Eagles.
While Schoen, Harbaugh, and the rest of the Giants’ braintrust plot how they intend to handle the final days before the trade deadline and future roster moves, here are two things that should be at the top of their to-do list to keep them in the crow’s nest.
By far the most disappointing development of the 2026 season has been the performance of the defensive line depth behind starters Shelby Harris and D.J. Reader.
Second-year man Darius Alexander, whom the team undoubtedly hoped would continue to build on the flashes he showed at the end of last season, has been hot and cold, particularly in run defense.
C.J. Okoye has been a disappointment since the Giants acquired him in a trade with Baltimore, which received the Giants’ 2028 seventh-round draft pick.
Okoye has played 82 defensive snaps, 41 against the run, and has four tackles to show for it, two of them for loss. He was a healthy scratch for the team’s Week 6 game against the New Orleans Saints.
And rookie Bobby Jamison-Travis, who has played 38 defensive snaps (27 against the run), is still getting his feet wet after being inactive for the first five games of the season.
As a result, when Harris and Reader need a breather, the Giants have become more susceptible to big-play runs, with opposing rushers averaging 4.4 yards per carry when one or both are on the field and 5.2 yards per carry when neither is.
The Giants have added defensive lineman Dean Lowry to the mix, signing him to the practice squad this week. But if Big Blue does nothing else this week, it has to zero in on the defensive line, given what the braintrust has seen so far from the depth.
The Giants’ running game had a huge moment last week against the Texans, exploding for a season-best 188 yards (the fourth-best rushing total in the league in Week 7) on 34 carries, with 180 of those yards coming from the running backs.
But overall this season, most of the Giants’ rushing woes have come on between-the-tackles runs.
Per Next Gen Stats, only Tyrone Tracy Jr. (+1.6) and Devin Singletary (+0.3) have positive Rush EPA figures, while lead running back Cam Skattebo sits at -8.8.
Further, Skattebo’s rushing success rate between the tackles this season is 37.3%, the fourth-lowest among 15 running backs with at least 50 attempts.
While not all interior rushing struggles fall solely on the offensive line, it’s still an area Big Blue would like to improve moving forward. Some of those struggles have been on Skattebo himself for not always following his blocks.
Whatever the issue, the Giants will want to fix it when they return from the bye, especially with the Eagles (11.6% run stuff rate, 26th in the league) and Commanders (10.5% run stuff rate, 31st in the league) struggling to stop runs between the tackles.

title: Schoen: Giants “Happy Where We Are,” but Still Exploring Deadline Moves
full_text:
The New York Giants are in a rare situation, at least lately, sitting alone in first place in the NFC East with a 4-2-1 record at the halfway mark of the 2026 season, which coincides with their bye.
What makes it unusual is that the Giants, given what they’ve accomplished under head coach John Harbaugh, don’t necessarily have to be buyers or sellers with the November 10 trade deadline approaching.
But far be it from the Giants to be content with where things stand with their roster, which, despite their winning record, has lost several key players such as quarterback Jaxson Dart, outside linebacker Brian Burns, defensive lineman Chauncey Golston and returner Braxton Berrios.
General manager Joe Schoen, who, like Harbaugh, has the NFC East crown firmly in his sights, said he’s “happy where we are” and that he “really likes the team.”
But that doesn’t mean he’s about to rest on his laurels. Rather, he’s looking to keep improving the roster, and how the team goes about it matters.
“There are a lot of factors into it, in terms of where we are pick-wise. We don’t have a fourth or a fifth right now. So, you take that into account,” Schoen said on Tuesday.
“In some situations, that may rule some players out. Maybe that’s their value. Maybe a third is too rich or a sixth isn’t enough, so you start looking at future picks and contract status, and where we are depth-wise. So, a lot of factors that we’ll look at and who’s going to be available, who’s really available.”
The Giants’ biggest needs, at least for the short term, include defensive line depth, but given Harbaugh’s recent comments about longing for a Derrick Henry type of situation, running back is clearly on the team’s radar as well, even though the unit had a breakout game last week against the Houston Texans’ run defense, which was ranked third in the league at the time.
Questions remain about whether the Giants will make an offer for Colts running back Jonathan Taylor, who is rumored to be available as part of Indianapolis’ fire sale.
Schoen and his staff have also been exploring other scenarios around the league in their quest to give Harbaugh what he needs to keep the team competitive through its postseason push.
But there is also a question of what makes sense, whether that’s making a trade, signing a street free agent or plucking someone off another team’s practice squad, such as what the Giants did in signing running back Greg Desrosiers on Tuesday.
In other words, not every move has to be a big splash.
“It’s easy to say, go sign X, Y, and Z position, but if a team’s really not ready to get rid of somebody where they’re asking too much, it doesn’t match up with where you see the value, then it doesn’t make sense to do it,” Schoen said.
“So, we’re going to look at all the available options. And, certain teams have already started some trades, and we’ve been in contact with those teams and have a pretty good idea of who may or may not be available. And again, it’s got to make sense, short-term and long-term, when you make those moves.”

title: Ashton Jeanty's Comments Put Jets at a Crossroads Ahead of Week 8 vs. Raiders
full_text:
It's been a rough couple of weeks for the Jets' defensive line. In their last two games, they have given up a combined 304 yards to AFC East rivals in the Patriots and the Dolphins.
Those struggles recently led a member of the Jets' upcoming opponent to talk a little smack leading into Sunday's contest against the Raiders. Former sixth-overall rookie Ashton Jeanty made it clear that he thought his team could do whatever it wants against New York .
Why? Because the Jets were soft.
" I think we can definitely get the run game going. Get back on track ," Jeanty said (h/t Ari Meirov). "A couple guys out there that don't really want to tackle, but I'm not going to say names."
Jeanty's comments are a direct slap in the face to the Jets defensive unit. The group has looked improved from last season, but has struggled again to start the year. When a running back who has failed to record 100 yards in two games this season, it will lead to even more embarrassment for the franchise.
Even if the players aren't taking the bait.
"Obviously, certain things can add a little more fuel to the fire, but at the end of the day, I got to go out there and do my job," Minkah Fitzpatrick said. "I think most guys in this locker room operate in the same fashion.”
If the Raiders are smart, they will look to continue the success other teams have had on the ground against the Jets. That leaves New York with two options going into Sunday.
New York can talk about not letting Jeanty's comments affect them, but there's no denying how important Sunday's game has become for the group. The Jets cannot allow Jeanty to have a stellar performance after calling into question the group's effort.
They must show some semblance of a backbone and shut down Vegas from running the football effectively.
That's where the choices are for New York.
If the Jets contain Jeanty, they prove they have the mental fortitude to defeat any opponent and remain a team playing hard for their coach. Should they struggle to stop the run, though, then the Jets will be known as the team that rolled over and did nothing to stop a player from smack-talking them before the game and dominating after.
It's a matter of pride for the Jets' defense, whether they want to admit it or not. As the team sits at 2-5, there aren't many more chances to prove they are willing to fight for their pride.
New York will be at a disadvantage going into Sunday as well.
David Bailey has missed the first two practices this week with a groin injury, while Joseph Ossai and T'Vondre Sweat are both considered "week-to-week" by head coach Aaron Glenn. They are outmanned and outnumbered going into the day.
Still, Jeanty called out their will this week. Star players or not, the Jets need to rise to the occasion to bring respectability back to their unit.
Anything less, and things will get much worse for the roster.

title: Jets Front Office Looking Even Smarter After Jeffery Simmons Trade
full_text:
Position value in the NFL matters more than it ever has. Top interior linemen can change defenses on a dime when playing compared to quality linebackers and safeties.
When the Tennessee Titans opted to trade All-Pro defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons on Thursday, they did so knowing they were parting ways with not only their best player, but with a star in a key position of their defense.
For the Chicago Bears, it didn't matter that Simmons cost two first-round picks. His star power alone could turn the Bears into a Super Bowl favorite.
A blockbuster trade like this will naturally affect many organizations around the league. For the New York Jets, the trade remains a major win for their front office.
One that shows they are finally heading in the right direction.
Tennessee was smart to get two first-round picks out of the best player on the roster. The Jets were in a similar situation last season, when they sent Sauce Gardner to the Indianapolis Colts for a pair of first-round picks.
But it's that Gardner trade specifically that highlights how much better off the Jets are compared to the Titans.
Tennessee moved Simmons to a sure-fire NFL contender. Chicago is in second place in the AFC North, but remains extremely talented and well coached with Ben Johnson and Caleb Williams leading the way. Over the next two years, the Titans' first round picks from Chicago are most likely going to pick in the later parts of the first round. While that can allow them to be flexible, it does take them out of elite prospects.
The same cannot be said for the Jets. When New York made the Gardner deal with Indianapolis, the Colts were 7-1. But they were also led by Daniel Jones, not a former top overall pick like Williams is in Chicago.
As things stand, the Jets are projected to have a top-10 pick from the Colts this season after their abysmal 2-5 start. If New York and Indianapolis continue to struggle, there's a good chance the Jets could own two picks in the top five overall selections in the 2027 draft.
It's significantly different from what the Titans will be dealing with in a post-Simmons world.
That's also not even counting the fact that the Jets also own the Dallas Cowboys' first-round pick as well this year. Dallas could very well finish below .500 and give New York another pick in the top 10.
Where star players are traded can matter just as much to rebuilding teams as the decision itself. In the case of the Jets, they are in a much better situation because of their trade with the Colts compared to the Titans shipping Simmons out to Chicago.
It's another important distinction and win for the Jets front office.

title: Jets' Key Offseason Trade Looks Even Smarter After Titans' Jeffery Simmons Blockbuster
full_text:
The Jets traded for T'Vondre Sweat for Jermaine Johnson during the offseason, unloading a contract of a player they had no intention of re-signing. Since the 2026 season started, Sweat has been more than serviceable for New York, fueling the idea that the Jets won the trade in spades .
Lucky for Gang Green, that trade has looked better due to recent developments.
On Thursday, the Titans traded their star defensive tackle amid their lackluster start to the 2026 season, as the Bears acquired Jeffery Simmons for two first-rounders and a fourth-round pick.
While New York was not involved in the Simmons trade, the NFL's latest blockbuster should leave Gang Green feeling even better about the trade that brought Sweat to Gotham.
When the Jets acquired Sweat in exchange for Johnson, they gave up no draft capital, meaning the Jets maintained all 10 draft picks for the 2027 draft. While the trade suggests the Sweat acquisition was a flyer, the defensive tackle's performance shows it as another Darren Mougey masterclass.
Sweat has been great during his time in New York. Pro Football Focus has the 25-year-old as the 19th-best defensive tackle this year. For comparison, Quinnen Williams—whom Sweat replaced— is ranked 48th . New York successfully replaced a player they traded for a first- and second-round pick with someone they traded an unwanted player for.
The Jets' front office looks even better considering the current trade market for defensive tackles. Deforest Buckner, whom PFF ranks 44th at the position , went to the 49ers for a fourth-round pick. Simmons ranks 12th , making the Jets' trade look like a steal compared to the slew of picks the Bears sent.
New York is far from a complete team. Despite the trade for Sweat, they still look to be in the market for defensive interior . But the trade for the former Titan has left them better off than other teams in a similar situation. The Titans, for example, are in sell mode and now are without the two starters from last season at the position.
The Bears and the 49ers also potentially hurt their future with their trades. Obviously, those teams are looking to win now, but they have depleted significant draft capital in that pursuit. New York is on a different side of the coin.
The Jets obtained a top-20 defensive tackle and have 10 picks in the next draft, something none of the other teams mentioned can boast.
Sure, the Jets' performance on the field has been poor, but the front office's moves have aged quite gracefully.  New York holds three first-round picks in this draft, something no other team can claim. Gang Green also has a top-20 DT that they didn't have to mortgage their future for.
It's early, but Thursday's Jeffery Simmons splash just serves as a reminder of how good the T'Vondre Sweat trade has been.
