title: Washington’s No. 2 Blitz Rate Hasn’t Solved Dan Quinn’s Pass-Rush Problem — Commanders Daily
full_text:
The Washington Commanders are in an odd spot: they rank second in the NFL in blitz percentage, behind only the Minnesota Vikings, but are tied for 14th in pressures and tied for 22nd in sacks. Those numbers need some context, though. Washington has played six games, while some teams have played seven, and the pressure and sack totals include plays when defensive coordinator Daronte Jones didn't blitz. Commanders HC Dan Quinn identified coordination between the rush and coverage as an area the staff examined during the bye. An extra rusher needs time to arrive. An immediate, uncontested throw can beat the pressure before it reaches the quarterback, leaving the defense at a natural disadvantage if the offense executes. "I'd love to see us, whether it's blitzing or rush coverage together, really being in sync with that," Quinn said.
Great to see Commanders DT Johnny Newton back at practice today. The team opened his 21-day window to return. He's been IR with a torn pectoral muscle. pic.twitter.com/rRPJXgNPwJ
Washington opened defensive tackle Jer'Zhan Newton's 21-day window to return after surgery on his pectoral injury. He practiced in a limited capacity Wednesday. With Javon Kinlaw missing practice because of a knee injury and Charles Omenihu limited with groin/ankle injuries, there are real questions about the rotation heading into Sunday night's game. Getting Newton back in practice is a good sign, but it doesn't guarantee he'll suit up anytime soon. To get after Tanner McKee , Washington needs to disrupt his timing while covering the quick throws so he can't get the ball out before the rush arrives. Sacks make a world of difference in games, but so do hurried incompletions, throwaways, and pressure that help end possessions. At 1-4-1, Quinn needs that work to show up against McKee on Sunday night.

title: Austin Ekeler Is Ready for More as Commanders Face Eagles With Croskey-Merritt Still Out
full_text:
After Austin Ekeler's first three games back with Washington, Commanders head coach Dan Quinn updated everyone on the running back Wednesday: "Now I think the play time can now increase; he's ready for that." That news couldn't come at a better time, as the team prepares for Philadelphia, already without Jacory Croskey-Merritt for at least the next three games while he's on injured reserve. To put things in perspective, Ekeler played 17 snaps against the Colts , six against the Giants, and seven against the 49ers. Against the 49ers, Rachaad White played 46 snaps, and Jeremy McNichols played 12. Quinn's comments give real hope that Ekeler will get more opportunities in an offense that needs more consistent production. "I feel his quickness, I feel his decisiveness. And so now that he's back, we'll need to lean in more, and he's able to handle a bigger workload now," Quinn said.
Ekeler described how a simpler offense could make assignments more universal, allowing multiple players to fill the same spot. “Maybe it's not as many different types of personnel groupings. Maybe not as many combinations of different types of players,” he said. "And so I think it's something that helps us play faster, but I think it's still an offense that you can go attack and have a diversified game plan," Ekeler said. That could suit Ekeler, who can take a handoff or give Jayden Daniels an outlet out of the backfield without Washington having to substitute. A matchup with a linebacker in space could let Daniels get the ball out quickly and give Ekeler room to create after the catch. Against Philadelphia, those opportunities need to help Washington sustain drives. A productive first-down carry or a short reception that sets up third-and-manageable would give the offense more options and take some pressure off Daniels to manufacture a big play. Ekeler doesn’t have to carry the offense, but helping keep it on schedule would be a good place to start.

title: Lucas Patrick’s Sack-Free Start Hasn’t Settled Commanders’ Center Question
full_text:
The Washington Commanders entered the 2026 season saying they had their center position filled, but they didn't take long to change course when they signed Lucas Patrick on September 16, then turned to him as the starter in Week 3. In his 258 offensive snaps at center, including 169 pass-blocking snaps, he hasn't given up a sack. Patrick took over at center for the Commanders against Seattle when Nick Allegretti moved to right guard after Sam Cosmi was injured. Patrick was named the starter soon after.
Pro Football Focus has him at a grade of 60.9 overall, including a 56.2 pass-blocking grade, which is not the greatest. He's allowed five pressures: three hits and two hurries.
Source: PFF Premium Stats ; 2026 regular season, Weeks 3–6. He had his best pass-blocking game so far against the New York Giants, the team that cut him in August, earning an 84.1 grade in Week 5. The problem is it fell to 35.3 against the 49ers the very next week. Three of his five pressures came during his largest pass-blocking workload: 51 snaps against San Francisco. PFF grades can reflect a lost block even when the quarterback releases the ball before pressure develops. That's why grades and pressure totals can tell different stories. His run blocking needs attention, too. PFF gives him a 61.1 grade on 89 run-blocking snaps. His best mark came against Indianapolis at 73.0, followed by 54.7 against the Giants and 55.0 against San Francisco. Dan Quinn pointed to “more strategy than personnel” when asked Monday about offensive-line adjustments after the bye . He emphasized finishing runs and blocks, including downfield blocking and moving the pile. His answer covered all 11 players, including the tight ends, receivers, and "the quarterback carrying out fakes."
#Commanders C Lucas Patrick in 5 games with the team: • 93% pass block win rate • 97 wins out of 104 plays (6th-best among NFL IOL) • 0 sacks allowed • 5 total pressures allowed (6th best) pic.twitter.com/bqaoCeSxaX
PFF lists Patrick 19th among 35 qualified centers overall . That puts his first four starts near the middle of that group. I’d keep working with him, but he needs a steadier level of play in both phases before I’d call the center position "fixed." Philadelphia is next . A complete performance Sunday would give Washington more confidence in its decision and David Blough one less position to worry about as he tries to get the Commanders' offense moving . title: The Eagles Have a Second-Half Scoring Problem. Washington Can’t Be the Answer — Commanders Daily
full_text:
On Sunday night football, the Washington Commanders and Philadelphia Eagles will meet for the 187th time. A rivalry steeped in disdain has already seen one chapter this season and will now shift to Northwest Stadium for chapter two this week . The Eagles come into this game having scored 37 total points after the second quarter (5.3 per game) in seven games, while Washington has given up 98 (16.3 per game) in six. Against Dallas, Philadelphia's backup quarterback Tanner McKee led a 17-play, 84-yard drive that took 9:16 and resulted in a touchdown that put the Eagles ahead 21-20 to open the second half. The only problem with that drive? It was Philly's first third-quarter touchdown of the season, and they never scored again, losing 38-21. The Commanders had a defensive breakthrough after allowing 95 points following halftime in their first five games; they held San Francisco to just one field goal. Washington head coach Dan Quinn summed it up in one quote: "I'd love to have all four quarters together. That's what we're chasing, and that's what I'm certain we're gonna get after [the bye week]." Washington lost the first meeting 24-22; the Eagles scored 10 second-half points that day, including seven from Jalen Hurts’ 43-yard touchdown pass to Dallas Goedert in the fourth quarter. The big question heading into this game is what Washington changed or worked on during the bye week , and whether we see any differences on the field. Can Daronte Jones’ defense carry its second-half performance against San Francisco into the Eagles game? That one needs an answer and will likely determine the fate of the 2026 Washington Commanders and how their season ends. The Birds might be wounded, but they have a knack for playing up to Washington no matter the situation. Washington can’t let Philadelphia take nine minutes off the clock on another third-quarter drive, and it can’t wait until halftime to start making stops. Quinn needs this win to show he has a grip on this roster and the direction is solid. Losing at home to a 2-5 Eagles team starting Tanner McKee would be a horrible look for Quinn and Adam Peters in year three.

Saquon Barkley returned Monday after missing a couple of games with a hamstring injury and had seven carries for 62 yards and a touchdown despite dealing with a back issue that limited his time on the field. His backup, Dameon Pierce, left Monday's game with an injury. After the game, Barkley said, "My hamstring came out great," and he doesn't expect the back issue to keep him out of Sunday's game. The Giants placed RB Tyrone Tracy Jr. on injured reserve Tuesday with a hamstring injury he sustained against the Texans this past weekend, meaning he'll miss a minimum of four games. To fill the spot, the team signed Gregory Desrosiers from the Chargers' practice squad to the active roster as they enter their bye week at 4-2-1 and alone in first place in the NFC East. New York GM Joe Schoen wants everyone to know the Tracy move is temporary: "This won't be something that's going to be long-term -- fortunately," Schoen said.
